knowledge: The author 坪谷邦生 is a practitioner (not a researcher) who, at age 25, left engineering for HR in order to improve exhausted workplace conditions; he later spent 10 years as an HR staff member/manager and 10 years as an HR consultant/advisor, building systems and supporting organizational development for 50+ companies (25 years of practice in total).
Core definition of 人事: 「人を生かして事をなす」 — accomplishing work by fully utilizing people (bringing their capabilities to life).
「人を犠牲にしてでも、事をなす」 is not HR; it is 搾取 (exploitation).
「人がイキイキとしていても、事がなされない」 is not HR; it is ぬるま湯 (a lukewarm, complacent environment).
True 人事 is the simultaneous realization of both 人 and 事: each person’s abilities are fully demonstrated and the organization’s purpose is achieved.

The book’s aim is not another collection of specific 採用 (recruitment) techniques, but a systematic introductory treatment of the prior question: 「そもそもどう考えるべきか」 (how one should think about recruitment in the first place).

This volume is the fifth independent title in an illustrated introductory series (after talent management, organizational development, goal management, and labor affairs); volumes can be read in any order. It was co-authored with 秋山統樹, director of the 採用市場研究所.

The book 『図解採用入門100のツボ』 consists of 100 independent 'tsubo' (points). Each tsubo is self-contained on a two-page spread, enabling 'snack-style' reading of individual points of interest, while reading all 100 provides an overall picture of recruitment. Typical layout: Q&A at the top, explanation on the left page, diagram on the right page, and practical hints at the bottom right.

Corporate recruitment (採用) is the activity of acquiring new talent. It is not merely increasing headcount; it is securing the people the organization needs so that the organization can achieve results through its business.
To understand recruitment correctly, examine four elements in sequence: Results (成果), Business (事業), Organization (組織), and Recruitment (採用).

Results (成果), per P.F. Drucker, are the value an organization provides to customers and society. What matters is not internal effort but the value visible from the outside. As Drucker wrote in The Practice of Management, 'Results exist outside the organization.' Contribution to customers and society is therefore the criterion of results.

Business (事業) is the continuous activity of providing value: creating products or services and receiving revenue in return. It comprises the overall mechanisms and actions that enable a company to grow while developing and delivering offerings.

An organization (組織) is required to keep producing results through business. The characters mean 'weaving together': people linking toward a common purpose, dividing roles, and collaborating. HR functions (recruitment, labor affairs, talent management, talent development, organization development, goal management, etc.) are indispensable for the organization to function smoothly. Recruitment is the first and especially important core HR function.

Recruitment is the activity of bringing in the talent needed for the organization to achieve results through its business. If the hired person fails to adapt to the organization, contribute to the business, or produce results, the recruitment has failed.

Done well, recruitment injects expertise, new ideas, and previously missing capabilities, accelerating business growth and expanding value. Example: hiring talented engineers can enable new product development and competitive advantage. Future executives must also be hired; they do not otherwise exist inside the organization.

Even in large, long-established companies, everyone except the founder entered the organization through recruitment. Recruitment is therefore not mere talent acquisition but a key that creates the company's future and that shapes organizational culture and growth speed.
HR (人事) means 'making things happen by utilizing people' (人を生かして事をなす); here '事' refers to results (成果).
Recruitment (採用) is not merely gathering people; it is an endeavor in which an organization and people encounter each other and together shape the future.
Through recruitment activities one can experience the significance of touching the essence of an organization's philosophy (理念), culture (文化), and business (事業).
The orientation of recruitment should shift from 'selecting people' (人を選ぶ) to 'building relationships' (関係性を築く).
The chapter uses many highly abstract concepts, so readers may find it hard to see exactly what concrete actions to take.
Readers expecting practical discussion of job-posting media (求人媒体) or talent-introduction agencies (人材紹介) may feel disappointed.

Recruitment (採用) in a company is the activity of acquiring new talent, but it is not merely increasing headcount. It means securing the talent necessary for the organization to achieve results through its business.
To correctly understand recruitment, four elements must be grasped in order: 成果 (results), 事業 (business), 組織 (organization), and 採用 (recruitment).

Results (成果) are the value an organization provides to customers and society. P.F. Drucker defines results as the value the organization creates for customers and society. What matters is not the amount of internal effort but how much value was provided as seen from outside. Quote: “Results exist outside the organization” (P.F. Drucker, The Practice of Management / 現代の経営).

Business (事業) is the sustainable activity of generating value that society and customers need and receiving revenue in return. It refers to the total of mechanisms and actions by which a company continuously develops and provides products/services and grows.

Organization (組織) is required to keep achieving results through business. The characters mean “joining together and weaving.” An organization is people shouldering a common purpose, dividing roles, and collaborating. HR functions (recruitment, labor affairs, talent management, talent development, organization development, goal management, etc.) are indispensable for the organization to function smoothly. Recruitment is the first and especially important core HR function.

Recruitment (採用) is the activity of bringing in the talent needed so that the organization can achieve results through its business. If the hired person cannot adapt to the organization, cannot contribute to the business, or does not lead to results, the recruitment is a failure.
Proper hiring brings organizational expertise, new ideas, and capabilities that did not previously exist, which accelerates business growth speed and expands company value.
Example: In IT companies, hiring talented engineers leads to new product development and establishment of competitive advantage.
Future executives must be hired into the organization; they will not exist there otherwise.
Even in historic, large companies, everyone except the founder joined the organization through hiring.
Hiring is not merely talent acquisition; it is a major key to creating the company's future and an element that determines organizational culture and growth speed.
An organization brings in new talent (人材) in order to achieve results (成果) through its business activities (事業).
Recruitment (採用) is the process by which a company (企業) welcomes new personnel so the organization can produce business outcomes.
Figure 001 illustrates company recruitment of talent in relation to customers (顧客).
事とは「人を生かして事をなす」ことである（人を活かして物事を成し遂げること）。
「事」とは成果のことである。
Corporate recruitment activities have four main impacts: organizational growth, organizational activation, individual career formation, and social employment creation.

Organizational growth: By welcoming appropriate talent, the organization absorbs new ideas, knowledge, skills, and technologies. Recruitment for growth consists of two types: 増員 (staff increase) and 補充 (replacement/filling vacancies).

増員 (staff increase): Recruitment to achieve strategies and plans such as business expansion or launching new projects. It secures the talent needed when a company enters new markets or develops new services, enabling the firm to seize growth opportunities and raise competitiveness.

補充 (replacement): Recruitment to fill vacancies arising from retirement or transfers. Immediate contributors (即戦力) are often required. This supports continuous organizational operations, minimizes business interruptions, and prevents productivity decline.

Organizational activation: Organizations create order through success experiences, but becoming settled in that order leads to inactivation and an inability to generate new things. Bringing in new talent introduces 'chaos (disorder)' that disrupts existing value systems and implicit rules; this chaos leads to activation (related to chaos theory, as discussed in Osawa Takeshi's Psychological Management).

Individual career formation: Recruitment provides working people with opportunities to demonstrate their abilities and grow. In Japan's shrinking labor population and resulting seller's market, it becomes increasingly important that workers perceive the opportunity as advantageous for their own careers (related to recruitment CX design, covered in Chapter 8).
The fourth impact of recruitment (採用) is social employment creation (社会の雇用創出).
Recruitment plays the role of providing stable employment that is indispensable to society.
Viewed broadly, recruitment is an initiative that forms the foundation for developing society as a whole.
The next section (ツボ 003) covers the constituent elements of recruitment.
Recruitment (採用) grows and activates the organization (組織を成長させ、活性化する).
Recruitment consequently helps the career formation of working individuals (働く個人のキャリア形成を助け).
Recruitment creates employment in society (社会に雇用を創出する).
The impact of recruitment (採用の影響) spans three levels: the organization (growth and activation), the individual (career formation / キャリア形成), and society (employment creation / 雇用創出).
The employment ice age (就職氷河期) in Japan involved companies restraining or holding back on hiring (採用を控えた).
This hiring restraint during the employment ice age greatly shook (大きく揺らぎました) the foundation (基盤) of Japanese society (日本社会).
Recruitment (採用) as a whole is structured around three components: the Recruitment Team, the Recruitment Process, and Recruitment CX (Candidate Experience) Design.

The Recruitment Team is the group that actually executes recruitment activities. It functions through collaboration among HR personnel, field managers, field members, executives, and external partners.

The Recruitment Process is the short-term mechanism for acquiring needed talent. In general, 'recruitment activities' refer to this process (also called the Arrow Feather Model / 矢羽モデル). It is composed of Recruitment Requirements, Sourcing, Selection, and Adaptation.
Recruitment Requirements (採用要件) are the verbalized image of the person the company wants to hire. They serve as the standard that runs through the entire recruitment activity.
Sourcing / Recruitment (募集) consists of activities that widely deliver information to talent matching the requirements, combining diverse channels such as job sites and talent-introduction agencies.

Selection (選考) assesses mutual fit between candidate and company. Document screening and interviews are used to judge the match of skills and stance. Aptitude tests such as SPI or GAB are used for more objective evaluation of abilities and personality traits.

Adaptation (適応) means that after joining, new employees become accustomed to the work and organizational culture so they can demonstrate their abilities. The supporting mechanism is called onboarding (オンボーディング).

Recruitment CX (Candidate Experience / 採用CX) is everything the candidate 'experienced' at all touchpoints from application through joining. Speedy communication, careful responses, and moments of feeling company culture influence offer-acceptance rates and post-joining adaptation.

採用マーケティング (recruitment marketing) is an activity that nurtures the relationship between candidates and the company. It improves recruitment branding by adjusting and improving the recruitment process (the contact point between both parties) and by disseminating information (see Chapter 9).

採用戦略 (recruitment strategy) aligns management strategy and business strategy with candidates' needs. It clearly defines when, what kind of people, and how many people are needed, and determines how to recruit them (see Chapter 10).
The text poses the question of when Japanese companies' recruitment took its current form and states that the next section (ツボ004) will cover the history of recruitment in Japan.
Recruitment strategy is framed around five elements (採用戦略の5要素), presented as the overall structure and constituent parts of hiring (図表003 採用の全体構造と構成要素).
The recruitment team (採用チーム) is composed of the recruitment process (採用プロセス), recruitment CX design (採用CXデザイン), recruitment marketing (採用マーケティング), and candidates (候補者), including candidate fit.
Recruitment operates across short-term (短期) and long-term (長期) horizons and must address gaps between them.
Candidate experience (候補者体験) is a core component of the recruitment structure and is tightly linked to recruitment marketing.

Recruitment strategy must align with business strategy (事業戦略), the organization’s mission-vision-values (ミッション・ビジョン・バリュー), and broader HR functions covering labor affairs, talent management, organization development, and goal management (人事: 労務・人材マネジメント・組織開発・目標管理).
Adaptation (適応) and onboarding (オンボーディング) sit adjacent to the recruitment system and are treated as related stages in the overall talent lifecycle.
Study method for recruitment (採用): first grasp the overall structure in a broad/big-picture way, then begin learning each constituent element.
Key statement: 採用の全体構造を大きく捉えたうえで、各構成要素の学習にとりかかりましょう (After capturing the overall structure of recruitment at a high level, let's start studying each component.)

Meiji-era modernization brought Western-style, academic-credential-focused elite hiring into Japanese government offices and companies, concentrated among government agencies and zaibatsu firms that recruited only a limited elite stratum.
In the Taisho and early Showa periods, large companies began mass recruitment of factory workers (職工) and clerical staff (事務員), gradually laying the foundation for lifetime employment (終身雇用).

Post-WWII reconstruction saw companies explicitly adopt long-term employee development; Japanese-style employment practices crystallized around new-graduate hiring, including mass simultaneous recruitment (大量一括募集), seniority sequencing (年功序列), and in-company education (企業内教育).

During high economic growth, joining a large firm became a symbol of “stability and success.” University students typically entered the labor market together via job agreements (就職協定) and school recommendations; junior-high and high-school graduates also moved into factory and clerical jobs through school recommendation quotas.

In the 1970s–1980s, lifetime employment and internal training were taken for granted; the strong company–employee trust relationship was viewed as a distinctive Japanese strength and attracted overseas attention.

The 1990s bubble collapse marked a turning point: changing business conditions exposed the limits of lifetime employment and seniority, prompting growth in experienced-hire recruitment (経験者採用), dispatch workers, and contract employees, plus abolition of job agreements and liberalization of hiring calendars that altered the new-graduate system.

In the 21st century, IT and globalization further diversified hiring. Simultaneous new-graduate hiring persists, yet year-round recruitment (通年採用) and internships aimed at identifying immediately productive talent (即戦力) have expanded; foreign-affiliated and venture firms increasingly adopt job-based (ジョブ型) and meritocratic (能力主義) approaches, recently reinforced by work-style reform (働き方改革).
Remote hiring (リモート採用) and online interviews (オンライン面接) have become widespread, making talent-acquisition methods more flexible.
Japanese corporate hiring has shifted from mass simultaneous hiring (大量一括) to individual optimization (個別最適).
The shift is intended to respond to diversified talent needs (多様化した人材ニーズ).
Japanese recruitment practices continue to evolve daily after this transition.
The next key point (ツボ 005) covers differences between Japanese and American hiring.

James C. Abegglen's '日本の経営' (The Japanese Factory; first edition 1958, Diamond; new translation 2004, Nikkei) is a classic systematic analysis of how Japanese corporate culture—especially lifetime employment (終身雇用) and seniority ranking (年功序列)—was formed and became entrenched.
Koike Kazuo's '仕事の経済学' (1991, Toyo Keizai) systematically organizes Japanese workplace labor-management relations, education and training, and the mechanisms of the seniority system.
Saguchi Kazuo's '雇用システム論' (2018, Yuhikaku) summarizes modern Japanese corporate employment systems and hiring practices in light of their historical development.

Kondo Ayako's '就職氷河期世代 データで読み解く所得・家族形成・格差' (2024, Chuokoron-Shinsha) uses data to examine social effects of the post-bubble collapse and employment ice-age generation from the 1990s onward, covering income, family formation, and inequality.
Japanese hiring history (図表 004) can be periodized as: Meiji; early Showa; postwar reconstruction; high-growth era (1950s–1970s); around the 1990s; and the 21st century onward.

Meiji-era hiring emphasized academic credentials and elite recruitment, centered on government offices and zaibatsu firms and limited to a narrow stratum; modernization brought Western-style corporate organization and rising demand for university graduates as education systems developed.

Postwar reconstruction featured mass hiring, gradual spread of lifetime employment, the start of long-term internal development policies, and large-scale recruitment to ease labor shortages; employment at large firms became a symbol of stability and long-term company–employee relations were valued.

In the high-growth period (1950s–1970s), simultaneous new-graduate hiring (新卒一括採用) became established, seniority governed promotion and pay, and university–firm coordination (school recommendations, employment agreements) intensified as firms expanded.

Around the 1990s, limits of lifetime employment and seniority became visible; the bubble collapse transformed the business environment, cost-cutting and restructuring weakened employment security, and simultaneous new-graduate hiring entered a period of change.

From the 21st century, year-round hiring and internships grew; mid-career, dispatch, and other diverse forms expanded; job-type hiring, meritocracy, and foreign-firm practices spread; IT and globalization diversified talent needs; online interviews and SNS recruiting increased; and work-style reform and remote work became more common.

Japanese recruitment is characterized by 新卒一括採用 (new-graduate mass hiring): many firms hire large numbers of university graduates all at once, timed to graduation, then train them from zero as new employees.

U.S. recruitment is characterized by 通年採用 (year-round hiring): firms fill specific positions with people who already have the needed skills whenever those positions open; students typically build practical experience via internships and then search for a matching employer after graduation.

Japanese hiring criteria emphasize 組織への適応度 (organizational fit) and potential more than current job skills; interviewers therefore look at student-era activities and personality to judge whether the person is likely to stay and grow over a long career.
U.S. hiring criteria emphasize immediate スキル (skills) and 成果 (results); selection often includes job-specific tests such as coding tests for engineers or case-study interviews for consultants.

Japanese firms still commonly assume 長期雇用 (long-term employment) and use ジョブローテーション (job rotation) across departments so employees become generalists; large companies often run weeks-to-months of collective new-graduate training covering business manners, internal rules, and specialized knowledge.

U.S. firms predominantly use ジョブ型雇用 (job-type employment): required skills for each position are clearly specified, individuals are expected to drive their own career development, and training is typically tailored to personal needs with an emphasis on self-directed learning.

Japanese companies' bulk/simultaneous hiring (一括採用) of new graduates and long-term employment (長期雇用) give both employees and the firm room to grow together and strengthen organizational capability (組織力), but can lack flexibility for speedy innovation and global responsiveness.

U.S. companies' year-round hiring (通年採用) and skill-focused approach (スキル重視) make it easier to achieve the right person in the right role (適材適所) and to deepen individual expertise, but labor markets are more fluid and employment stability is weaker.
These contrasting hiring and employment systems illustrate a trade-off between internal growth/organizational cohesion (Japan) and talent matching/specialization plus market fluidity (U.S.).

Japanese employment traditionally emphasizes lifetime employment (終身雇用) through simultaneous mass hiring of new graduates (新卒一括採用) timed to graduation, followed by intensive post-hire training and development rather than hiring for immediate skills.

Japanese recruitment focuses on organizational adaptation and potential, long-term employee growth, more interview rounds (including group interviews, group discussions, and written exams), comprehensive batch training plus OJT, and frequent job rotation.

Advantages of the Japanese model include strengthening organizational capability from a long-term perspective and high employee belonging/loyalty; disadvantages include slower adaptation to change and restricted hiring windows.

U.S. recruitment is typically year-round to continuously fill needed roles, targeting immediate contributors based on skills, results, job experience, and practical ability, with usually 2–3 interviews and practical assessments such as coding tests or case interviews.
The U.S. approach stresses self-responsibility, self-development, and specialization in an individual's professional domain rather than broad rotation.

Advantages of the U.S. model include easier acquisition of ready talent and high labor-market mobility/flexibility; disadvantages include difficulty stably securing talent plus intense competition and higher turnover.

New graduate recruitment (新卒採用) at Japanese companies targets students expected to graduate from universities, graduate schools, vocational schools, and similar institutions, and in most cases takes the form of batch hiring (一括採用).

The defining feature of Japanese 新卒採用 is that companies recruit large numbers of students at a fixed time each year and select primarily on potential (ポテンシャル), with an eye toward future growth rather than current skills.

A typical 新卒採用 process is: students apply (entry) via job-information sites or company pages; document screening and aptitude tests follow; multiple interviews are held; a job offer (内定) is issued. Final interviews often involve executives or the president to judge cultural fit and long-term potential.
Compared with experienced-hire (mid-career) recruitment, the contact period between company and candidate is characteristically longer in 新卒採用.

Long-term development is assumed: many firms run concentrated training before or after joining, covering everything from business manners to job knowledge. After assignment, job rotation across departments is used to develop generalists—a major cultural feature of Japanese new-graduate hiring.
Because a cohort of same-year joiners (同期入社) is created, company culture is easier to share and organizational unity (一体感) is easier to foster.
Students can therefore learn practical work gradually while building a career under a long-horizon system.

Recent practices to avoid missing strong students include year-round recruitment (通年採用), scouting, and internships; some firms lock candidates in at the internship stage to gain an advantage in later selection.
A shift is occurring from traditional comprehensive-job batch hiring (総合職一括採用) toward job-type hiring (ジョブ型採用), in which specific duties and required skills are clearly defined in advance.
Hiring methods continue to diversify through technology, notably the spread of online interviews.

Employment in Japan is entering a major period of transformation, yet the framework of 新卒一括採用 (shinsotsu ikkatsu saiyo: simultaneous bulk hiring of new graduates) remains deeply rooted. Under this system, companies hire large numbers of students at once and train them from scratch.
Japanese companies’ new-graduate hiring has historically functioned as a mechanism for nurturing long-term employment relationships and transmitting internal corporate culture.
Going forward, firms are expected to continue combining 新卒採用 (new-graduate hiring) and 経験者採用 (experienced/mid-career hiring) according to each company’s own policy in order to secure talent.
The next unit (ツボ 007) covers experienced-hire recruiting.
Traditional Japanese new-graduate (新卒) hiring emphasizes potential (ポテンシャル重視) over a student’s current skills or experience; recruiters assess future growth potential and fit with corporate culture.
Batch hiring (一括採用) aligns recruitment with university graduation cycles so that a large cohort of new employees joins at the same time.
The system is built on a long-term employment premise (長期雇用前提), with a complete educational pipeline running from business-manner training through departmental assignment.
After graduation, talent is developed from zero via structured training and job rotation (ジョブローテーション).
Training together with the same-year cohort (同期) readily produces horizontal networks and a sense of unity.
OJT and internal transfers (job rotation) are used for long-term career formation; many firms therefore develop generalists (ゼネラリスト) rather than specialists.

Emerging shifts away from the traditional model include direct recruiting (ダイレクトリクルーティング), greater use of internships (インターンシップの活用), job-based hiring (ジョブ型採用), and the spread of year-round recruitment (通年採用).
新卒採用 (shinsotsu saiyō, new-graduate recruitment) is described as an employment practice unique to Japan.
This practice should be understood in relation to 終身雇用 (shūshin koyō, lifetime employment) and 年功序列 (nenkō joretsu, seniority-based ranking/pay).

経験者採用 (experienced-hire / mid-career recruitment) targets people with prior work experience and evaluates them primarily on practical experience and specialized skills, rather than potential to be trained from scratch.

For positions that require management experience or advanced specialized knowledge, experienced hiring functions as a way to secure immediate, ready-to-perform talent that new-graduate hiring cannot provide.

Core premise difference: new graduates are hired on the assumption of 'nurturing/growing' them (育てる), while experienced hires are hired on the assumption of 'entrusting' them with work (任せる). Therefore, whether the candidate can deliver performance immediately after joining is the most important evaluation factor.

Demand for experienced hires is fluid and often sudden: it arises from organizational movements such as vacancy replacement or new-business launches, not from a plan fixed at the start of the fiscal period.

Hiring timing and required qualifications typically originate from the field/business situation. Decision-making is therefore often led by the business unit; HR generally plays a supporting role in system design and coordination.
The assignment/destination is frequently already decided at the time of hire, so flexible and agile decision-making is required.

Contact with candidates is limited, so the priority is reliably hiring people who match the requirements. Selection is individualized (1-on-1 interviews, meals, etc.) rather than group interviews, with emphasis on understanding the person deeply and attracting them.
Start date, compensation, and work style must be negotiated and aligned individually with each candidate.
Selection is simultaneously a 'place to choose' and a 'place to be chosen'; firms must also win against competing employers.
Effective experienced hiring requires adapting to a changing environment; evaluation should not rest on specialized skills alone (the source text cuts off as it begins to introduce a further shift).
In changing work environments, continuous learning ability and flexibility to keep "adapting" to new situations are increasingly valued over static skills.
Workers' values are diversifying; organizations must design roles that respond to individual hopes regarding fulfillment (やりがい) and flexible working styles.
The recruitment market has become more fluid, so meeting strong talent requires proactive ("offensive") methods such as scouting and employee referrals (リファラル); these are now indispensable.
Post-hire onboarding (オンボーディング) support systems are increasingly recognized as directly determining whether a new hire performs and delivers results (referenced in Chapter 7).
Experienced/mid-career hiring (経験者採用) is not mere headcount replacement; it is a practical activity tightly linked to corporate strategy.
The following section (ツボ 008) examines common failure patterns in hiring.
Experienced hiring (経験者採用) emphasizes immediate contribution (即戦力) and specialized expertise (専門性), targeting people who already have professional work experience (社会人経験).

Selection and evaluation in experienced hiring are based on practical experience (実務経験) and specialized skills (専門スキル), serving as a means to secure ready-to-contribute talent under the premise of 'entrusting' (任せる) them with work.

Chart 007 describes characteristics and changes in experienced recruitment. A key feature is field-led (現場主導) decision-making: hiring needs arise suddenly according to organizational movements such as filling vacancies or launching new businesses, and business departments often lead hiring decisions.

Another characteristic is individualized handling (個別対応): there are few contact points with candidates, so the process emphasizes deeply understanding the person and attracting them; selection, negotiation, and condition presentation are all handled individually, and the employer must win against competing recruiters.
Additional noted shifts in experienced hiring include emphasis on adaptability (適応力重視), diversification of values (価値観多様化), and more aggressive/offensive methods (攻めの手法).
経験者採用（中途採用）は基本的に即戦力を求める。
募集の背景や必要スキルを明確にすることが重要である。

Typical Japanese-company hiring failures fall into four patterns: (1) ambiguous requirements, (2) overly personalized selection, (3) a gap between recruitment messaging and actual workplace reality, and (4) lack of strategy tied to long-term organizational needs.

Ambiguous hiring requirements: companies fail to clarify what talent is truly needed and insufficiently align with the field, proceeding vaguely with phrases such as 'we want excellent people.' Applications may arrive, but post-hire skill mismatch produces early turnover and internal confusion.

Personalized selection process: interviewers overweight intuition and personal likes/dislikes, so hiring decisions become idiosyncratic. This easily diverges from the organization's target profile and raises the risk of poorly assessing ability and culture fit.

Information-vs-reality gap: over-prioritizing recruitment PR leads firms to over-beautify vision and workplace conditions. New hires then feel 'this is different from what I was told,' generating distrust, early resignation, lower retention, reputational damage, and long-term harm.

Lack of strategy: hiring is not linked to management strategy or long-term organizational vision and stays at filling immediate vacancies or headcount. Consequently the firm cannot have talent ready when needed, cannot systematically develop future leaders, and competitiveness erodes gradually.

Ikujiro Nonaka et al.'s 'The Essence of Failure' (失敗の本質) argues that the Japanese military in the Pacific War exposed structural organizational defects: successive short-term operations, personalized leadership, Imperial Headquarters-style information manipulation plus optimism, and absence of comprehensive strategy with a local-battle orientation.

Those military defects map closely onto hiring failures: (1) short-term operations = rushing to fill numbers without solid requirements, producing repeated mismatch; (2) personalized leadership = interviews and criteria depending on a charismatic boss or HR person's subjectivity rather than organization-wide direction; (3) HQ-style info manipulation = recruitment PR that highlights only positives and hides negatives, causing post-join gaps and early turnover; (4) no comprehensive strategy / local-battle focus = symptomatic hiring that never builds a future leadership layer, so competitiveness is lost.

Core lesson: obsession with temporary tactical success, failure to create fundamental strategy, and reliance on personal judgment plus excessive 'appearance' rebound as large medium-to-long-term failure.
We must learn from the experiences of our predecessors (先人たち) and evolve going forward.
The next section (ツボ 009) addresses the future of recruitment/hiring (採用の未来).

Without a recruitment strategy, organizations fail. Common traps include clinging to temporary successes, relying on person-dependent judgments, and chasing excessive 'appearance' (見た目) rather than substance.

Four core recruitment failure patterns and the underlying essence of failure: (1) repeated short-term, person-dependent local operations; (2) leadership that depends on a commander's intuition; (3) a gap between information sent out and actual workplace reality; (4) absence of strategy.

Hiring requirements are often too vague. Field teams and HR hold mismatched views of what is needed. Interviewers' intuition and subjectivity decide pass/fail. Evaluation criteria are not standardized, so results have low reproducibility. Required skills and aptitudes are never clearly defined.

Information-reality gap: companies over-produce or manipulate information that diverges from actual conditions, emphasizing only convenient facts for outsiders. New hires then discover 'it is different from what I was told,' which increases turnover.

Strategic vacuum: hiring is not linked to management strategy or long-term vision. Future-leader development is ignored, eroding competitiveness. Organizations get stuck in partial, local-battle tactics and lose sight of the overall picture.
Future Japanese corporate recruitment (5–15 years) faces a major turning point driven by population decline and labor shortage.
Retirement-age extension and active use of senior talent will advance; working into the 70s if health conditions are met will no longer be unusual.
Acceptance of foreign workers will accelerate to offset domestic labor shortages; multinational and multi-generational workforces mixing inside organizations will become normal.
Cross-cultural understanding and communication will become indispensable skills in every aspect of daily work.
AI and robot technology will automate most routine tasks, sharply reducing manpower needs in offices and factories.
Demand will rise further for creative talent who create new value from data generated and analyzed by AI.
Job-type employment (ジョブ型雇用) will increase; individuals will polish specialist skills and raise market value through job changes or side jobs as needed.
Companies will actively use experienced-hire recruitment and freelance contracts to secure immediately productive talent.
Emerging industries such as biotechnology and greentech will grow, increasing the need to secure global specialist talent.
Remote hiring of overseas PhD holders and researchers, plus international teams that ignore time zones and geography, will become common.
Traditional manufacturing, retail, and banking will see unmanned and online operations, so large-scale mass hiring will decline.
Side jobs and project-based contracts becoming socially established will erode the equation “employee = full-time regular employee.”
Job-matching services will be used so that people hold multiple concurrent work arrangements.

Contract-based work arrangements with companies are expanding, prompting firms to secure people who have the required skills only for the period they are needed rather than through permanent staffing.
The company–individual relationship is shifting away from long-term employment toward an equal partnership whose purpose is to maximize mutual growth and results.
Fixed-post, slot-filling hiring is being replaced by more flexible recruitment styles that will become the norm.

Japanese corporate hiring is being forced to adapt to structural change driven by demographic shifts and technological innovation, and therefore must make use of talent diversity and specialized expertise.
The subsequent section (Tsubo 010) turns to recruitment as a function within human resources.
Japan's recruitment future is projected across 2025–2040 amid a seller's market for talent, with intensifying competition for workers due to chronic labor shortages.
2024 spring new-graduate employment rate reached a historic high of 98.1%; METI predicted an IT talent shortfall of about 430,000 people by 2025 driven by DX needs.
Women's employment (ages 25–39) hit 81.5% in 2022; from April 2025 companies are obligated to secure employment until age 65, expanding senior continued employment.

Foreign workers in Japan numbered about 2.3 million as of 2024 (more than double in 10 years); potential additional labor supply includes +1.02 million from women, +1.63 million from seniors, and +0.81 million from foreigners.
Over 40% of 2025 students desire lifetime employment; side jobs are generalizing, with MHLW asking companies to publicly disclose conditions for permitting them.

Remote work and AI are spreading into recruitment processes; companies increasingly use welfare-benefit enhancements and job-type (role-based) employment, especially via experienced hires, headhunting, and professional roles at large firms.

Project-based / hybrid employment is rising: more freelancers and specialists contracted per project, combining core employees with fluid external talent teams; overseas professionals can be hired remotely.

In the 100-year-life era, multiple careers become normal; retirement extension and work past age 70 are promoted; hiring shifts toward qualitative matching of candidates' thought/philosophy with the organization's.

Production-age population estimates: ~71.70 million (around 2025) with ~5.05 million talent shortage; ~67.73 million (2030) with ~6.44 million shortage; ~62.13 million (2040) with 65+ reaching 35% of the population.

By 2030, absolute labor-force shortage intensifies especially in AI, data science, green tech, and DX/IT; rapid technological progress could automate 27% of work, potentially replacing ~16.60 million jobs with machines.
By 2040, even previously cautious policies such as immigration acceptance may become unavoidable; AI and robotics advances are expected to raise GDP per capita despite demographic decline.
Telework adoption (around the mid-2020s): 45.9% of companies, 10–20% of workers.
Recruitment (採用) is the activity of bringing in the talent an organization needs in order to achieve results through its business.
The HR (人事) function is indispensable for making the organization operate smoothly; recruitment is one of the functions that HR possesses.

人事 literally means “bringing people to life in order to accomplish things.” It is not performed only by the HR department or HR staff; executives, line managers, and every working person are involved.
HR consists of multiple overlapping functions such as labor affairs (労務), talent management (人材マネジメント), organization development (組織開発), and management by objectives (目標管理).

These functions are arranged in a holon structure (ホロン構造), a nested, ring-like hierarchy in which lower layers support upper layers while upper layers encompass the lower ones and increase complexity—the principle of “transcend and include.”

Upper layers (e.g., MBO, organization development) are more complex, analogous to how a cell is more complex than a molecule, which is more complex than an atom; occupying an upper layer does not make a person “superior.”
If a lower layer fails, the layers above it cannot function: without atoms there are no molecules or cells.
Example: if labor affairs are not functioning, talent-management investments are wasted because workers’ livelihood, health, and internal order are already disrupted.

Example: if talent management is not functioning, organization-development efforts produce a “lukewarm-water” (ぬるま湯) organization that only talks and declines because it lacks a rational structure for winning.
Every layer is mutually dependent; if any layer is missing, the company’s overall HR function cannot stand.

Within the holon, recruitment’s role is to bring in “the people who accomplish things.” As the lowest layer it is the starting point of everything and, in that sense, the most fundamental root function.
If recruitment does not work, talent simply does not exist, so none of the other HR layers can produce results.

Even if highly talented people are successfully hired, they will not take root in the organization (leading to turnover or unused capability) unless other organizational layers/functions are also working.
Recruitment is very important but is only one part of the overall HR (personnel) function.
Recruitment’s impact is maximized only when it is coordinated and linked with other HR functions.
The following chapter covers the recruitment team.
A holon structure is a nested (annual-ring-like) hierarchical structure in which each higher level transcends and includes the levels below it; it is not a ranking for domination.
Lower levels of a holon are essential: without them the higher levels cannot exist. Higher levels have greater complexity and are harder to restore if lost.
Examples of holon nesting: atoms < molecules < cells; characters < words < sentences. (Concept drawn from Ken Wilber’s Integral Theory.)
HR panorama (人事の全景) frames the purpose of people management as “bringing people to life so that work gets done” (人を生かして事をなす).
Purpose and goals are used to spiral-up the relationship between people and work.
Intervention focuses on “the space between people” so that work arises autonomously.
Investment in people’s talent maximizes work over the medium-to-long term.
The livelihood and order of workers (people who get things done) must be protected.
The organization must welcome in people who get things done.
Source of the HR panorama framework: Kunio Tsuboya, “人事の全景”.
すべての人事機能は「人を生かして事をなす」ために存在する。
人事（HR）の各機能の存在意義は、人を活かして仕事・事業を成し遂げることにあるという原則。
Key Japanese HR/management principle: every personnel function exists to bring out people's potential in order to accomplish work.
Recruitment (採用) is the most important theme directly connected to executing management strategy; it is not merely headcount securing but the entrance that shapes the organization's future.

Executives should use the purpose of recruitment (key points 001 and 002) and failure factors (key point 008) as a trigger to deeply consider how management positions recruitment and converts it into organization-wide capability.

Recruitment is not only the HR department's job but an important practice that field managers should carry out; they must re-recognize their roles and responsibilities across the full process of who to hire, how to develop, and how to retain people.
Key points 003 and 007 address recruitment components and the preparation of acceptance/onboarding systems, providing content that connects directly to field practice.
Recruitment officers stand on the front line connecting the company and candidates; they must understand both strategy and the field rather than treating work as mere operations.
Recruitment officers should design the full experience including branding, the selection experience, and talent retention, viewing the work comprehensively rather than as isolated tasks.
Key points 003 and 009 cover the overall picture of recruitment and future changes; key point 008 organizes common failure patterns in detail.
The chapter summary presents role-specific messages for executives, field managers, recruitment officers, and all working members, emphasizing that recruitment strategy must be owned beyond HR.
Everyone has the experience of being welcomed or hired (迎えられた経験) and will eventually stand on the welcoming/hiring side (迎える側).

Hiring (採用) is connected to individual careers and to society as a whole; it is not someone else's business (他人ごとではない) but a theme that concerns one's own way of working (働き方) and the nature of the organization (組織の在り方).
Readers are encouraged to consider how to welcome future colleagues (未来の仲間をどう迎えるか) by overlaying that question with their own experiences.
The next section (Chapter 2) addresses the hiring team (採用チーム).

採用 (recruitment) is the act of bringing new talent into an organization so the organization can achieve results through its business. It grows and revitalizes the organization and, in turn, supports working individuals’ career formation.
Recruitment creates employment in society and is built from elements such as the recruitment team, recruitment process, and recruitment CX design.
Core components of recruitment include recruitment marketing and the five elements of recruitment strategy.

Japanese recruitment history: lifetime-employment-based 新卒一括採用 (mass new-graduate hiring) was long the mainstream; recently ジョブ型雇用 (job-type employment) and experienced-hire recruitment have expanded.
A defining feature of Japanese recruitment has been 新卒一括採用 that emphasizes lifetime employment.
新卒採用 (new-graduate hiring) characteristics: ポテンシャル重視 (emphasis on potential), 一括採用 (mass/batch hiring), and a premise of long-term employment.
経験者採用 (experienced-hire recruitment) characteristics: emphasis on 即戦力 (immediate contribution) and specialist expertise, field-led decision-making, and individualized handling.
Recruitment fails when there is no strategy—when organizations cling to short-term success, rely on person-dependent judgment, or chase excessive “appearance” (見栄え).
Future recruitment must respond to structural change from demographics and technological innovation, and must use talent diversity and specialist expertise.
In HR, recruitment is a core function: welcoming into the organization people who 事をなす (get things done).
Recruitment, particularly executive search, is described as having the power to completely overturn or reverse a company's situation (盤面をひっくり返す力がある).

Egon Zehnder is a firm specializing in executive-level (経営層) recruitment; Yasushi Maruyama, Partner and former Tokyo office representative, is interviewed on the appeal of recruitment work and the career path of recruitment professionals.

Executive search assignments are obtained through distinct career phases. Early on, as a beginner with no relationships or track record, one must intensively pursue sales by visiting many potential client companies.
The interview explores how companies come to entrust executive search (エグゼクティブサーチ) work to specialists and how recruitment practitioners build their careers over time.
A talent connector or recruiter can operate like a whiskey master blender: when company or organizational needs arise, they see which elements to mix so the combination clicks into place.

Maintaining constant curiosity about people—who they are, what they want to do, and with whom they should partner—turns every encounter with a leader into a potentially useful connection that can activate when the timing is right.

Two main client-support approaches in talent work: (1) executive search and hiring when there is a people gap relative to a desired goal; (2) coaching and developing people already inside the organization.

Hiring has clearly stronger short-term power than coaching to ‘flip the board’ (radically change the situation) by adding one person, even though coaching and development remain important and effective.

The appeal of recruitment lies in the possibility that bringing in the right person can drive large-scale organizational change and growth, even if the contribution is not always a direct business-line impact.
Working with people is extremely interesting, complex, and deep, so there are infinite ways to find enjoyment in the work.

An attractive career model in this field is meeting many leaders, thinking integratively about who fits which situation, and connecting them; this path is approachable even if one cannot immediately operate at an expert blender’s level.
A firm that historically did only executive search can still incorporate substantial coaching work as a complementary practice.
Executive search (サーチ) and coaching are originally very close activities, which is why combining them works well.

Hiring via executive search often involves an identity shift (アイデンティティシフト) for the leaders involved, along with changing one's way of thinking and ongoing learning; this makes it highly compatible with coaching.

Maruyama Yasushi (丸山泰史) is a Partner at Egon Zehnder (formerly Tokyo office representative) and a visiting researcher at Stanford University; he works on executive search, C-suite assessment, and leadership development.

He studied under Harvard professor Robert Kegan, focusing on adult development and growth, and uses Kegan's Immunity to Change (ITC) method for coaching Japanese company presidents, successor candidates, executive teams, and organizational transformation consulting.
Credentials include: University of Tokyo (BSc, MSc in Information Science), INSEAD MBA with Distinction, and Certified Immunity to Change Coach.

In a ~100-person IT company centered on technical roles, a newly appointed HR person (former engineer) questioned the value of new graduate hiring (新卒採用), because the people who were actually thriving appeared to be experienced mid-career hires (中途入社) and HR already had a heavy workload, making new-grad recruiting seem like a low-ROI use of time.

The president’s reply was that both he and the HR person ‘couldn’t do anything at first’ (はじめは何もできなかった). They became experienced professionals only because their first employers taught them the basics of being a working adult and trained them.

Mid-career hiring of people already trained elsewhere is indeed effective in the short term. But if every company pursued only its own short-term advantage and hired only experienced people, no one would raise new members of society (新社会人).

Therefore the company continued new-graduate hiring and development despite the burden, for as long as it had the capacity to do so. This stance embodies social contribution (社会貢献), paying it forward (恩送り), and the common good (共通善)—ideas the author did not yet know by name.

The president looked one circle larger than HR headcount cost or short-term corporate profit, infused each measure with intent, and tried sincerely (even while embarrassed) to make an immature employee understand that intent.
Once the ‘significance’ (意義) of hiring inexperienced people landed, the author committed fully to new-graduate recruitment.
In hiring/recruitment, readers will understand their own role and how to collaborate with surrounding colleagues.
Hiring is not solely the work of the HR department; it is an organizational endeavor (組織的営み) in which the workplace/frontline, management, and all employees are involved.
The behavior of interviewers and other related parties forms a structure that shapes candidates' impressions of the organization.
There is no clear, definitive answer to who should do what in hiring; readers may be left with lingering ambiguity (モヤモヤ) after the chapter.
Trying to map the chapter's ideas onto one's own company structure may instead make misalignments and constraints more noticeable.
Chapter 2 focuses on the hiring team and why recruitment should be conducted as a team rather than by individuals.

Three merits of team-based hiring: A. Diverse perspectives prevent mismatches because executives bring business strategy, field managers bring operational reality, recruiters bring market trends and candidate experience, and external partners bring a wide talent pool; overlaying these views enables early detection of risks such as sufficient skills but poor culture fit.

B. Collaboration balances speed and quality: processes such as application intake, interview scheduling, evaluation, and offer negotiation require different expertise; dividing roles and processing in parallel prevents delayed candidate responses and opportunity loss, while standardizing evaluation criteria and communication preserves quality.

C. Team learning converts results into organizational assets and raises hiring capability: because the talent market changes rapidly, a mechanism to turn outcomes into learning is essential; individual experience stays personal, but team sharing (e.g., circulating post-interview questionnaires to accumulate good questions and improvement points) improves subsequent interview accuracy.

Five conditions for a learning hiring team that maximizes the above merits: (1) Common purpose and goals—all members pursue the same purpose and targets, e.g., succeeding in a three-year business plan as purpose, with fill rate and post-hire performance as goals.

(2) Clear role division—explicitly define roles of executives, field managers, external partners, and recruiters; a RACI-style table visualizes who decides, who executes, who advises, and who is informed.
(3) Open information—progress and evaluations are shared with the entire team in real time, typically via an ATS (Applicant Tracking System).
Hiring teams should make retrospectives a habit: for example, use monthly reviews to verbalize successes and failures and then improve processes.
Everyone on the hiring team should be candidate-centric, staying conscious of candidate experience (採用CX / recruitment CX) and thoroughly delivering prompt, sincere responses (see Chapter 8).
If a team that continues this kind of learning can be built, a virtuous cycle emerges in which the organization grows stronger with every hire.
The next section (ツボ 012) covers the organizational form of the hiring team.

Hiring as a team has three core merits that should be maximized: (A) diverse perspectives that prevent mismatches, (B) collaboration that balances speed and quality, and (C) knowledge accumulation that turns experience into organizational assets.

The purpose of team-based hiring is expressed as using diverse viewpoints to avoid mismatches, collaborating to achieve both speed and quality, and converting experience into assets through the accumulation of knowledge.

A learning hiring team (学習する「採用チーム」) is defined by five conditions: (1) a shared/common purpose (共通の目的), (2) clear role division (明確な役割分担), (3) open information sharing (オープンな情報), (4) a habit of reflection/review (振り返りの習慣), and (5) a candidate-centered approach (候補者中心).
These five conditions are presented as the practical requirements for turning a hiring team into a learning organization that continuously improves recruitment outcomes.

The Japanese term 組織 (soshiki, organization) is explained through wordplay on 組む (kumu, to join/assemble) and 織る (oru, to weave): 組織とは組んで織りなす (an organization is formed by joining together and weaving).
An organization consists of people who, toward a common purpose (共通の目的), put their shoulders together (肩を組み), collaborate (協働して), and weave their respective roles (役割を織りなします).
Key conceptual statement: Organization is not merely a structure but an active process of people assembling and interweaving their contributions around a shared goal.
Recruitment team structure (採用チームの形態) changes with company size and growth phase; organizations typically combine types or migrate between them rather than using a single fixed model.

Five representative types of recruitment teams: 1) Decentralized / field-led (分散型・現場主導), 2) Dedicated / centralized (専任型・中央集権), 3) Hybrid / matrix (ハイブリッド型・マトリックス), 4) Project / time-limited (プロジェクト型・期間限定チーム), 5) Outsource / external-asset (アウトソース型・外部アセット活用).

Decentralized (現場主導): Typical of founding-stage, very small organizations with no HR department. Founding members hire for their own departments. Advantages: direct check of needed skills and fast decisions. Fits small companies and specialist hiring. Risk: inconsistent methods by department and uneven candidate experience.

Dedicated/centralized (専任型): An in-house recruiting team inside HR handles job posting through interview scheduling in one place. Advantages: information concentrates and employer-brand messaging is consistent. Suits larger headcount. Risk: mismatch with actual work if there is no mechanism to hear from the field.

Hybrid/matrix (ハイブリッド型): Dedicated team owns planning and candidate-pool building; first interview onward is handed to the field. Combines decentralized speed with dedicated quality. Often used by rapidly growing companies. Ambiguous roles make responsibility unclear—share a RACI-style table of who does what.

Project/time-limited team (プロジェクト型): Mixed team assembled for a finite, high-volume need (e.g., launching an overseas site). Dissolves when the goal is met. Delivers concentrated short-term results, but learned know-how must be captured or the same challenge will be hard next time.

Outsource type using RPO (Recruitment Process Outsourcing): External specialists run recruiting operations; a small internal team focuses on planning and final decisions. Enables immediate hiring despite staff shortage. Over-reliance leaves no in-house know-how—periodically review and record learnings.
Indicators for choosing or migrating structure: company scale, growth phase, hiring volume, scarcity of required skills, and internal culture.
Realistic migration example by headcount: ≤50 employees → decentralized for speed; >100 → dedicated to unify standards; >300 → hybrid to balance quality and agility.
Recruitment team structure should not be treated as fixed; it must be regularly reviewed in response to changes in the business and the market.
Look back at whether hired people are actually thriving/performing, and keep the flexibility to update what is needed.
A habit of continuous improvement is what builds a strong recruitment team.
Apply these ideas to your own company rather than treating team form as static.
The next key point (013) covers role division within the recruitment team.
There are five types (類型) of recruitment teams (採用チーム): 分散型 (distributed), 専任型 (dedicated), ハイブリッド型 (hybrid), プロジェクト型 (project), and アウトソース型 (outsource).

分散型 (distributed type): Each workplace/site (現場) directly handles its own hiring. Suited to small-scale organizations and specialist/professional hiring. Strength: fast decisions. Weakness: quality and process vary by department.

専任型 (dedicated type): Hiring is handled solely by the HR department. Suited to mid-sized organizations and new-graduate (新卒) hiring. Strength: information, plans, and standards are aligned. Weakness: can drift out of alignment with the actual workplace (現場).

ハイブリッド型 (hybrid type): Dedicated recruiting team and the workplace share roles. Suited to rapidly growing organizations. Strength: combines the speed of the distributed model with the quality/consistency of the dedicated model. Weakness: ownership of responsibility can become ambiguous.

プロジェクト型 (project type): A time-limited mixed team assembled for a specific large-volume hiring effort. Strength: can deliver concentrated results in a short period. Weakness: learning and know-how (学び/知) tend not to remain in the organization.

アウトソース型 (outsource type): Uses RPO (Recruitment Process Outsourcing) so that internal staff can concentrate on planning and decision-making. Strength: can be started quickly even when internal headcount is short. Weakness: learning and know-how tend not to remain inside the company.

When conducting recruitment as a team, the most common stumbling block is ambiguous role division of 'who does what.' Unclear roles cause processes to stall midway, delay candidate communications, and ultimately lead to candidate withdrawals or early turnover.

Executives (経営者) show the 'direction' of recruitment. Their concrete responsibilities include: (1) approving talent requirements linked to business strategy, (2) setting recruitment budget and investment-recovery (ROI) targets, and (3) personally communicating the employer/recruitment brand in their own words.
Executive actions such as appearing in employer-branding videos or talking about company vision on SNS rapidly increase candidate trust and also strengthen internal stakeholder cohesion.

Field managers (現場マネージャー) guarantee 'workplace fit' (職場適合). Their concrete responsibilities include: (1) defining requirements for each position, (2) evaluating skills and stance in first- and second-round interviews, and (3) creating post-hire onboarding plans.
Field managers must do more than just attend interviews: they should share evaluation criteria with recruiting staff and possess explanation skills that improve the candidate experience.

External partners (job media, staffing agencies, RPO, etc.) raise recruitment 'efficiency.' They mainly form candidate pools and supply market information (accessible candidate segments, competitor movements, compensation market rates) so that internal decision-making can be sped up.
The recruiter (採用担当者) functions as a 'hub' (ハブ) that connects management (経営), the field/operations (現場), and external parties (外部).

Core responsibilities of the recruiter as hub include: (1) designing the recruitment strategy and the overall process, (2) progress monitoring and extracting issues, and (3) quality management of the candidate experience (候補者体験).
Role division (役割分担) is established and made durable through a three-stage cycle: write it down (書いて), share it (共有し), and update it (更新する).
Practically: first document the roles, place the document where everyone can view it, and rewrite it promptly whenever the situation changes.
Once this write–share–update cycle is running, the recruitment team can keep a strong collaborative structure while still securing talent quickly.
The following section (ツボ 014) addresses the role of executives (経営者) in recruitment.
図表 013 presents a four-role framework (4つの役割) with assigned functions.
経営者 (executive/management): 方向を示す — sets and shows direction.
現場マネージャー (frontline/on-site manager): 職場適合を担う — owns workplace fit and adaptation.
外部パートナー (external partner): 効率をあげる — raises efficiency.
採用担当者 (recruiter/hiring officer): 関係者をつなぐ — connects the relevant stakeholders.
Team development should go beyond mere role division (役割の分担) and also cultivate awareness of the shared 'ba' or place of dialogue (対話の“場”).
Key statement: 役割の分担だけでなく、対話の“場”を意識してチームを育てましょう (Not only divide roles; be conscious of the dialogue field and grow the team).

Executives (経営者) are the final responsible party (最終責任者) and the biggest champion/flag-waver (最大の旗振り役) for hiring; how seriously top leadership engages with recruitment directly affects both candidates and internal company morale.

Role 1 — Show the direction (方向を示す): Break sales plans and new-business roadmaps down into concrete talent needs and share them with the hiring team. Example: convert “aim for top share in market X in ○ years” into “hire 3 senior salespeople and 2 product managers within ○ years.” Without this reverse-calculation (逆算), hiring becomes ad-hoc.

Role 2 — Show your face (顔を出す): Candidates care about “who they will work with.” When executives personally articulate the vision in their own words and appear on SNS and events, candidate empathy rises. Short video messages and webinar Q&A are effective. A “company where the top is visible” signals seriousness and lifts application and offer-acceptance rates.

Role 3 — Decide quickly (迅速に判断する): Timing decides hiring outcomes. Do not delay offer approvals or extra-budget decisions. Treat hiring as an investment: justify recruiter fees and scouting costs via business ROI and secure the funds. Design a zero-wait decision flow so high-caliber talent is not lost to competitors.

Role 4 — Talk about culture (文化を語る): Strong pay cannot compensate for a mismatch between company culture and candidate values. Executives must embody “this company’s uniqueness” through daily behavior and internal systems, then translate it into hiring messages. Example: if the culture “welcomes challenge,” install evaluation systems that do not punish failure and share failure stories at internal events so actions back the claim.
The role of executives (経営者) in recruitment is to show direction, appear in person (顔を出す), make decisions quickly, and talk about the culture (文化を語る).

Consciously practicing these executive behaviors enables the recruiting team to develop strategy with confidence, the workplace (現場) to participate proactively, and candidates to realistically imagine their future after joining.
When top leadership commits to recruitment, the hiring activity is already half successful; this is not an exaggeration.
These practices by leadership connect to building trust in the recruitment process.
The next key point (ツボ 015) covers the role of field/on-site managers in recruitment.
Executives (経営者) have four core roles in recruitment: 1) show direction (方向を示す), 2) show their face (顔を出す), 3) make rapid decisions (迅速に判断する), and 4) talk about culture (文化を語る).

Role 1 — Show direction: Connect business strategy with hiring strategy. Translate sales and growth targets into talent requirements; set hiring headcount and deadlines by reverse calculation. This concrete translation becomes the axis of hiring measures and prevents random/haphazard hiring (場当たり採用). Hiring team involvement: hand over quantified requirements and use them as the starting point for strategy planning.

Role 2 — Show face: Serve as the face of recruitment branding. The executive personally talks about the vision and delivers passion/heat (熱量) to candidates via SNS and events. Visibility of the top’s face improves application rates and offer-acceptance rates. Hiring team involvement: coordinate communication materials and speaking opportunities so the brand stays unified.

Role 3 — Decide rapidly: Rapid decision-making and resource allocation. Instantly approve offers and additional budgets; treat hiring as an investment and allocate resources without stinting. Zero-wait-time decisions prevent losing excellent talent. Hiring team involvement: present required funds and ROI estimates to obtain fast approval.

Role 4 — Talk culture: Embody and communicate organizational culture and values. Live the culture through daily words/actions and systems, then translate it into hiring messages. Cultural consistency supports post-hire retention and performance. Hiring team involvement: turn examples into stories and communicate them in interviews and publicity.
Show items 013 and 014 to managers (経営者) so they recognize their roles (役割を認識してもらう).
This is presented as a HINT for engaging executives with specific numbered materials or documents.

In hiring, the frontline (on-site) manager is decisive because the candidate ultimately judges whether they want to work with this person, and the manager is responsible for creating an environment in which the new hire can perform after joining.

Frontline managers are expected to fulfill five key roles in recruitment (with collaboration tips); the first is requirement verbalization (要件言語化): clearly specifying which work, at what level, and by when the person should take it on, expressed in concrete actions and results rather than abstract traits.

Vague requirements cause mismatches. Example: instead of an abstract phrase such as “someone with communication skills,” use a behavioral/results description such as “sales experience of 3+ years who can handle three customer negotiations per week.”

The second role is assessing skills and stance (スキルとスタンスの見極め). Because the manager is the professional in the actual work, interviews should probe skills through specific examples while also checking whether the candidate’s stance fits the team culture.

Culture-fit questions should be prepared in advance (e.g., “Can they share failures?” “Do they have an attitude of autonomous learning?”) and scores recorded on an evaluation sheet so that assessment becomes more objective and quantified.

The third role is staging candidate experience / CX (CXの演出). The interview with the manager is the moment the candidate imagines their post-joining self; a smiling welcome plus honest talk about the role and its challenges builds trust.
Practical CX tactics include inviting the candidate to Slack before and after the offer so they can interact with team members and experience the team atmosphere; this raises offer-acceptance rates.

The fourth role is adaptation / onboarding support (適応支援). Many people who leave within the first three months felt that job expectations had been vague; the manager should therefore set 30-day and 90-day achievement goals aligned with the job description, assign a mentor, and schedule weekly follow-up meetings.
Structured 30/90-day goals plus weekly mentor check-ins increase ramp-up speed and early retention rates.
Hiring/recruitment is not finished at the moment of offer acceptance or joining: the process continues with post-hire result verification (結果検証).
Hiring managers must track new joiners’ on-the-job performance (活躍具合), retention/settlement rate (定着率), and engagement after they join.
Managers should jointly review those outcomes with recruiters so they can update RA requirement definitions and interview design, then set concrete next improvement actions.
When line/field managers proactively own these verification and feedback roles, overall recruiting-team results improve dramatically and the organization becomes sustainably stronger.
The following section (ツボ 016) covers the role of external partners in recruiting.

Field (on-site) managers play five core roles in hiring: (1) verbalizing requirements, (2) assessing skills and stance, (3) staging candidate experience (CX), (4) supporting adaptation/onboarding, and (5) verifying results via a feedback loop.

Requirement verbalization: translate hiring needs into concrete, action-based language—explicitly state assigned duties, performance standards, and deadlines as observable behaviors; eliminate abstract wording and recast them as measurable outcomes. The recruiting team shares a verbalization sheet and uses it to optimize job postings.

Skill and stance assessment: evaluate both expertise and culture match. In interviews, dig into specific past examples to judge whether skills and stance fit. Quantify questions and scoring sheets so subjective bias is reduced. The recruiting team registers evaluation sheets in the ATS and distributes them to interviewers.

CX (candidate experience) staging: the field manager is the public face who raises candidate experience. Speak frankly in interviews about both the role’s challenges and its attractions; share team atmosphere in advance (e.g., Slack invites). The recruiting team embeds networking/exchange events into the interview flow.

Adaptation support: design onboarding and mentoring. Set 30-day and 90-day goals plus a mentor structure; run weekly follow-ups to prevent expectation gaps and isolation. The recruiting team standardizes (templates) onboarding and tracks progress.

Result verification: close the hiring feedback loop. Measure post-hire performance (活躍度) and retention (定着率), then update interview processes and requirements. Use data to raise accuracy of the next hiring cycle. The recruiting team shares metrics in quarterly reviews and folds improvement actions back into the process.

Cross-cutting pattern: each of the five manager roles has a paired recruiting-team action (sheets, ATS, events, onboarding templates, quarterly reviews), so hiring quality is co-owned rather than left solely to the hiring manager.
現場マネージャーと採用担当者は対話を通じて「いい人」像をすりあわせましょう (On-site/field managers and hiring/recruitment staff should align their shared image of a "good person" / ideal candidate through dialogue.)
External hiring partners complement internal shortfalls in resources and expertise and act as collaborators that raise both the speed and quality of recruiting.
Four partner types and their expected roles: job-media (求人媒体), talent-introduction agencies (人材紹介), direct/scout recruiting services, and RPO (Recruitment Process Outsourcing).

Job media are a high-volume entry point: advertising slots plus search functions broadcast openings widely, lower the application hurdle, reach tens of thousands of viewers (including anonymous latent candidates), secure candidate volume, and create initial employer-brand awareness.
Click and view histories stored inside job media also function as market sensors that make visible the interests of people who never applied.
Talent-introduction firms are specialist guides: they mine industry networks for immediately productive or senior talent that rarely appears on job boards, then recommend them.

Agency consultants raise matching quality by aligning a candidate’s aspirations with the company’s problems, negotiating terms, and organizing concerns; they also accumulate daily compensation benchmarks and competing-offer trends that inform management decisions.

Scout / direct recruiting is an offensive, same-day approach: the company searches résumé databases and sends pinpoint messages to people who already possess the required skills and experience, thereby securing scarce talent quickly.
Real-time view and reply logs from scout platforms let internal teams iterate outreach based on actual candidate reactions.

RPO (Recruitment Process Outsourcing) is a model in which an external specialist team takes over the entire practical recruitment workflow—from job posting creation, candidate-pool formation, document screening, interview scheduling, through to offer communication—and bears responsibility through achievement of agreed KPIs.
Using RPO lets the in-house team concentrate on higher-value work such as strategy design and candidate-experience improvement.
The outsourced team also delivers standardized process reports, so labor-hour reduction, process optimization, and know-how accumulation can be realized at the same time.
Understanding each party’s role and combining them enables recruitment to proceed efficiently and smoothly.
As AI technology advances, external partners’ roles are expanding (e.g., substituting for interview/selection functions and optimizing scouting).
The following section (ツボ 017) examines the role of the in-house recruiter.

External recruitment partners have complementary roles summarized as: job media (求人媒体) for mass exposure, talent introduction agencies (人材紹介) for quality guarantee, scouting for direct contact, and RPO for outsourcing.

Job media (求人媒体) functions as mass exposure and a market sensor. It is an entry point that publicizes openings at scale to reach even latent/potential candidates, and viewing plus application data is used to measure market interest. The recruiting team’s involvement is to regularly share job-ad (原稿) improvements and application-volume trends.

Talent introduction (人材紹介) guarantees quality and supplies market-rate (相場感) insight. Agencies individually recommend scarce, immediately productive talent from proprietary networks and bridge gaps between company and candidate through condition negotiations. The recruiting team’s involvement is to periodically review requirements and yield (歩留まり) KPIs.

Scouting accelerates direct contact. A resume database enables same-day outreach to precisely targeted talent via search; response data is used to run a fast improvement cycle. The recruiting team’s involvement is to track reply rates and continually update message templates (文面の型).

RPO (Recruitment Process Outsourcing) is full process outsourcing: the vendor operates everything from job-ad creation through offer communication as a single flow. Processes are standardized and optimized via SLA and KPI. The recruiting team’s involvement is to concentrate on strategy and candidate-experience design while regularly reviewing outcomes.
Building a relationship of trust with external partners (外部パートナー) is the key to successful recruitment/hiring (採用成功の鍵です).
Key statement: 外部パートナーと信頼関係を築くことが採用成功の鍵です.
The recruitment officer (採用担当者) acts as a “hub” connecting executives, field managers, and external partners, and as a “promoter” who leads recruitment activities from design through execution.
Five core roles of the recruitment officer: (1) Recruitment Strategy Planner, (2) Recruitment Process Designer, (3) Information Coordinator, (4) CX Designer, (5) Organizational Learning Facilitator.

Role 1 — Recruitment Strategy Planner: Interprets business strategy and business plans and translates them into recruitment strategy and recruitment plans. Reverse-calculates “by when / what kind of people / how many” to create an annual roadmap. Conducts market research and competitive analysis, adjusts the mix of recruitment channels, and allocates budget accordingly.

Role 2 — Recruitment Process Designer: Designs the end-to-end process from hiring requirements through onboarding. Sets purpose, owner, deadline, and evaluation metrics for each step. Uses an ATS (Applicant Tracking System) to visualize yield rates and interview times and quickly implements improvements when bottlenecks appear.

Role 3 — Information Coordinator: Aggregates the executive vision, field requirements, and external partners’ market insights and documents them so all parties operate from the same map. Shares numbers and issues in weekly progress meetings and reflects decisions in the ATS the same day to prevent misalignment.

Role 4 — CX Designer: Designs the speed, transparency, and warmth candidates experience from first application through offer acceptance. Example: confirming interview schedules within 24 hours and sharing interview question themes in advance via an interviewer-introduction email increases candidate security and lowers decline rates.
Key terms: ATS (Applicant Tracking System / 採用管理システム); recruitment CX (candidate experience); yield/歩留まり; bottleneck improvement; reverse-calculation of hiring targets into an annual roadmap.
Because the recruitment environment changes rapidly, a mechanism for reflecting on results and learning from them is essential.
Interview evaluations and post-offer questionnaires should be databased; monthly 'success factors and improvement points' should be shared with the entire team.
Cycling between tacit knowledge (暗黙知) and explicit knowledge (形式知) accumulates highly reproducible recruitment knowledge (採用ナレッジ). See ツボ 020.
A recruitment specialist is a multi-functional player who draws plans, organizes flows, circulates information, polishes experiences, and promotes learning.
Consciously practicing those functions raises the performance of the whole recruitment team and accelerates the organization toward business goals.
The next section (ツボ 018) covers the results, actions, skills, and stance required of recruitment staff.

Five core functions of a recruitment specialist: draw plans (計画を描く), organize the flow (流れを整える), circulate information (情報を流通させる), polish candidate experience (体験を磨く), and promote organizational learning (学習を推進する).
