Role 1 — Recruitment strategy planner (採用戦略プランナー): Translates business strategy and business plans into recruitment strategy and recruitment plans, and creates an annual roadmap. Uses market research to optimize the mix of media vs. scout sourcing and allocate budget. Executive holds priority job types and budget; field managers provide required skills; external partners share target profiles.

Role 2 — Recruitment process designer (採用プロセス設計者): Maps a single end-to-end line from job posting through pre-joining follow-up, making process steps, deadlines, and KPIs explicit. Monitors conversion (歩留まり) in the ATS and immediately refines bottlenecks. Executive confirms decision/approval points; field shares interview workload; external partner acts as a single coordination window.

Role 3 — Information coordinator (情報コーディネーター): Aggregates the top’s vision, field requirements, and market data into documents. Synchronizes numbers in weekly meetings and reflects them the same day in the ATS. Executive confirms messaging; field updates requirements; external partner supplies market reports.

Role 4 — CX designer (CXデザイナー): Designs speed, transparency, and warmth from application to offer in order to reduce candidate drop-off. Visualizes ‘life after joining’ via pre-shared questions and Slack interaction. Executive provides vision videos; field designs interview touchpoints; external partner reports candidate sentiment/temperature.

Role 5 — Organizational learning facilitator (組織学習ファシリテーター): Turns interview evaluations and retention rates into data and shares success factors plus improvement points in monthly reviews. Converts knowledge into a wiki to raise reproducibility of the next hiring cycle. Executive approves KPI retrospectives; field submits outcome data; external partner supplies benchmark cases.

Stakeholder interaction pattern used across all five roles: 経営者 (executive) for strategy/budget/message/KPI approval; 現場 (field/managers) for skills, workload, requirements, and performance data; 外部P (external partners) for targeting, single-window coordination, market reports, candidate sentiment, and benchmarks.
The adopted approach or style is mixed martial arts (総合格闘技 / sōgō kakutōgi).
Do not rush (焦らずに); master techniques one at a time (1つずつ技を身につけていきましょう).

Recruiters are expected to deliver two kinds of results that balance quantity and quality: (1) fill rate—whether the planned number of hires was completed by the deadline, expressed in numbers; and (2) post-hire performance/quality—tracked via 6-month goal-achievement and retention rates after joining.

A concrete example goal that unifies the whole process: “Hire 5 engineers during Q2 and maintain 90% retention after six months.” Setting such a target lets the recruiter operate with a consistent view from candidate-pool building through onboarding support.

Core repeating actions that produce results are visualization, sharing, and correction. Examples include: at launch, set headcount, deadline and evaluation criteria then update the ATS every morning and notify stakeholders; in interviews, immediately verbalize mismatches between requirements and background and send follow-up questions the same day; after offer, weekly contact until start date, log concerns and hand them to the hiring team. Immediate response raises selection speed and candidate experience (CX).

Five skill domains that support recruitment work: (1) basic knowledge of labor law and employment contracts; (2) mastery of the recruitment process (ability to apply the book’s content); (3) interview and selection evaluation skills; (4) data literacy (funnel/yield analysis and simple statistics); (5) tool operation (ATS, scout media, AI matching). Combining them produces the sequence “appropriate channel selection → evidence-based pass/fail decisions → numerical explanation of results.”

Recruitment is emotional labor (like customer-service or hospitality work): the recruiter must manage and express emotions. Required stance includes sincerity that respects each candidate’s background and aptitude for market change (text cuts off).

Recruitment officers require a set of professional stances that cannot be omitted: curiosity, the endurance (忍耐力) to persist even when coordination and adjustments drag on, and the composure (落ち着き) to make calm judgments even immediately before deadlines.
These stances can be developed and strengthened by continuously combining external feedback from those around you with ongoing self-dialogue.

Recruitment personnel are expected to deliver outcomes that simultaneously satisfy both quantity and quality, to take actions that never interrupt the flow of information, to possess knowledge and skills across five domains, and to maintain a stance suited to emotional labor consisting of sincerity (誠実さ), curiosity (好奇心), persistence (粘り強さ), and calmness (冷静さ).
The following section (ツボ 019) examines the career of the recruitment officer.

Recruitment personnel must deliver results that balance quantity and quality, take actions that keep information flowing without interruption, possess knowledge and skills across five domains, and adopt a stance suited to emotional labor (感情労働).

Figure 018 presents an iceberg model of what is required of recruitment staff (採用担当者に求められるもの), adapted from the corporate personnel capability iceberg model in Osawa Takeshi, Shiba Yuujun, and Nimura Hideyuki’s Personnel Assessment Handbook (人事アセスメントハンドブック).

Visible (above-the-surface) elements include uninterrupted visualization, sharing, and correction (滞りない可視化・共有・修正) plus five domains of knowledge and skills: (1/4) basic knowledge of labor law and employment contracts (労働法と雇用契約の基礎知識), (2) basic knowledge of the recruitment process (採用プロセスの基礎知識), (3) interview and evaluation skills (面接・評価スキル), data literacy (データリテラシー), and tool operation (ツール操作).
Invisible (below-the-surface) elements include personal qualities such as sincerity (誠実さ) and calmness/composure (冷静さ), which support the emotional-labor demands of the role.
Behavior (行動) is visible, but knowledge/skills (知識・スキル) and stance/personality (スタンス・性格) are not visible.
This distinction treats observable actions as the visible layer and internal attributes (knowledge, skills, attitude/stance, and character) as the invisible layer.

Recruitment (採用) is the work of identifying people who connect with an organization's culture, values, and business strategy, and of designing encounters with them. It is close to 'decision-making that creates the future' (未来をつくる意思決定).
Recruitment officers are specialists who stand at the 'forefront of HR strategy' (人事戦略の最前線).

Recruitment is the contact point between company and society and is strongly affected by changes in technology, values, and ways of working. Examples of such change include AI interviews, SNS-based recruiting, and cross-industry (越境) recruiting.

Responding to these waves of change requires a stance of continuous learning: studying other companies' cases, deepening knowledge through books and seminars, and joining recruitment study groups. The habit of cycling between information gathering and practice raises a recruiter's value.
Serious dialogue with the front line and with management expands one's perspective beyond the HR domain; daily work of this kind hones professional expertise.
Not all insight gained in recruitment fieldwork becomes accumulable know-how. Dialogue with candidates, alignment with the field, and the atmosphere of interviews yield 'practical knowledge' (実践知).
Management scholar Ikujiro Nonaka (野中郁次郎) argues that this practical knowledge is the source of leadership that guides people and organizations.
Career formation for recruiters therefore also means forging one's own leadership through this 'invisible knowledge' of practical knowledge.

Recruiters are simultaneously beings who create the organization's future and beings who carve out their own future. In each practice of selecting, delivering, connecting, and supporting, one's own work satisfaction (働きがい) and strengths (強み) also grow.

Recruitment is a deeply creative endeavor that stands at the intersection of people and organizations. Believing in that appeal and accumulating practice develops the power to carve out one's own career. Career options for recruiters are diversifying.
Recruitment specialists (採用担当者) have many future career options rather than a single linear path.
One path is promotion within overall HR to roles such as manager or HRBP (HR Business Partner).
Another path is to remain specialized in recruitment and deepen skills as a Talent Acquisition (タレントアクイジション / 人材獲得) professional.
An increasing number of people become independent as freelance recruitment supporters or recruitment consultants.
New job types are emerging in the recruitment field, including scouting (スカウト), branding (ブランディング), and RPO (Recruitment Process Outsourcing) operations.
These roles enable professionals to work and succeed beyond a single organization's boundaries.
The next section (ツボ 020) addresses organizational assets that recruitment teams should systematically accumulate.
Recruitment career development theme: hone professional expertise while contributing to organizational growth, accumulate practical knowledge (実践知), and thereby carve out one's own future.
Career formation framework for recruitment staff (採用担当者のキャリア形成, Figure 019) offers multiple paths from the recruitment practitioner role.
Specialist path: become a recruitment expert (採用の専門家) by diving deeply into specialized domains such as recruiter work and employer branding.
Generalist/HR leadership path: broaden into other HR functions such as HR planning (人事企画) with the aim of becoming an HR manager/responsible person (人事責任者).
Independent path: work as a recruitment consultant, RPO provider, lecturer, freelancer, or independent professional.
HRBP path: apply HR knowledge as a business partner that creates and demonstrates business value.

Competencies acquired through hands-on recruitment practice: dialogue capability with the front line and with management (現場・経営との対話力); empathy for candidates' lives (候補者の人生への共感力); learning ability to adapt to change (変化に対応する学習力); and the ability to convert practical knowledge into formal/explicit knowledge through verbalization (実践知を形式知にする言語化力).
採用実務は組織と人の未来をつなぐ経験の宝庫である。
採用実務は採用担当者の成長に直結する。
A recruiting team must not only hire people in the short term but also continuously deliver value over time by accumulating five types of capital: data, knowledge, process, brand, and network.

Data capital: Continuously record facts in numbers using a consistent format—application counts, screening evaluations, offer-acceptance rates, and post-hire performance. After about three years of data, quantitative trends become visible, such as which recruitment channels lead to high-performing talent and when screening tends to stall. The core principle is to store records in a form that is easy to aggregate later; the specific format does not matter.

Knowledge capital: Organize and share reusable know-how in a common place—effective job-posting copy, interview questions that worked, and tips for post-offer follow-up. After every interview, add what went well and what to improve so the knowledge base is continuously updated. This enables anyone in charge to maintain a consistent quality of work.

Process capital: For each recruiting step, create a shared, always-current table showing who performs the work, who makes the final decision, and who to consult or report to. Evaluation criteria and approval procedures should also be visible at a glance. This keeps quality from fluctuating when personnel change. The ideal is a system in which even a newcomer can be entrusted with interviews after a short period.

Brand capital: Do not let encounters at company information sessions or internships remain one-off events. Maintain ongoing interaction—for example through newsletters or communities that regularly share updates and initiatives—so relationships become lines rather than isolated points. This becomes the soil that grows a future pool of applicants.

Network capital: List external collaborators such as educational institutions, industry associations, alumni, and specialists, and create regular opportunities for information exchange. Even holding a networking or study session once every six months helps cultivate a circle of trust and cooperation.

In hiring, support can be obtained quickly even in difficult situations if relationships have already been built; the key is not to rely on others only when needed, but to cultivate trust in ordinary times (平時から信頼を育む姿勢).
Consciously accumulating five types of capital (5つの資本) makes a recruiting team continue to function even when the person in charge changes.
Start with small, immediately doable systematization (仕組み化), such as unifying and retaining evaluation records (評価の記録を統一して残す).
Repeated small systematization and accumulation of the five capitals is what builds a strong recruiting team.
The next section (Chapter 3) covers hiring requirements (採用要件).
Five types of capital to accumulate (積み上げる): Data (データ), Knowledge (ナレッジ), Process (プロセス), Brand (ブランド), and Network (ネットワーク).
These five capitals are presented as a stacked framework in 図表 020 (Figure 020).
Diagram elements associated with the stacking process include 手順 (procedures/steps), 数字 (numbers/data), 知恵 (wisdom), 評判 (reputation), and 信頼 (trust).
資本 (Capital) とは、将来の価値創出を支える元手のことです。 (Capital is the principal/funds that support the creation of future value.)

Recruitment is an investment in the future (未来への投資), not a cost-reduction activity. Executives who treat it as leverage that creates competitive advantage (競争優位を生むレバレッジ) accelerate and strengthen hiring decisions.

Three executive practices that make a recruiting team's decision-making fast and strong: (1) translate sales and growth targets into talent requirements, (2) personally communicate the vision in one's own words to both candidates and employees, and (3) issue approvals without delay.
The most important executive mission is to get the entire organization to internalize that hiring is competitive-advantage leverage rather than a cost to cut.
Field managers must first specifically verbalize what results they want from a new hire and by when. This language becomes the foundation for selection and onboarding.
In interviews, evaluate professional skills and culture fit at equal weight. Also show candidates the concrete content of post-hire onboarding; doing so sharply reduces mismatch.
An interview is simultaneously an evaluation setting and a stage for conveying attractiveness. A manager's words directly affect a new member's ramp-up speed and the cohesion of the existing team.
Recruitment staff should position themselves as a hub of information and learning (情報と学習のハブ): consistently own process design, data collection, knowledge sharing, and bridging with external partners.
Feed both quantitative metrics and qualitative episodes back to executives and the field. This closed loop upgrades the recruiter from a mere process administrator to a strategic partner.
By connecting people around them and circulating learning, recruiters maximize the organization's hiring-related capital (採用に関する資本).
Members should treat hiring not as “HR-only work” but as “building our own colleagues/team” (仲間づくり).
Internal referrals (社内紹介), cooperating in interviews, and post-hire OJT are chances to turn one’s own knowledge and experience into capital.
If new colleagues become productive quickly, the frontline team’s load decreases and the existing member’s own learning opportunities expand.
Hiring is a collaborative project that simultaneously improves the organization’s future and one’s own future (ツボ 011).
The next section (Chapter 3) covers hiring requirements (採用要件).
Recruitment teams can take several organizational forms: distributed type (分散型), dedicated type (専任型), hybrid type (ハイブリッド型), project type (プロジェクト型), and outsource type (アウトソース型).

In a recruitment team, executives provide direction (方向), field managers handle workplace/job matching, external partners contribute efficiency (効率), and the recruitment staff member acts as the hub (ハブ).
The executive's role in recruitment is to show direction, appear in person (show their face), make rapid decisions, and talk about company culture.
Key activities in the hiring process include language of requirements (要件言語化), assessing fit/suitability, producing candidate experience (CX), supporting adaptation, and verifying results.

External partners play specialized roles: job media for mass outreach/volume, talent introduction agencies for quality guarantee, scouting for direct contact, and RPO (Recruitment Process Outsourcing) for full outsourcing.
A recruitment team continuously demonstrates value by accumulating five types of capital: data, knowledge (ナレッジ), process, brand, and network.

Core principle of personnel strategy: never stop hiring, even when business performance is poor. Stopping recruitment casually is a mistake that creates long-term structural problems in the workforce.

A hiring freeze of even two years produces a conspicuous gap (a 'hole') in the company's age and experience pyramid. That missing cohort later leaves the organization without ready successors for key middle-management roles such as department heads (部長) and section chiefs (課長), especially around the 40-year-old band.

Large-scale hiring during boom periods (for example the bubble-economy generation) later creates its own imbalance once those employees become seniors; the earlier surge and subsequent freeze together distort the talent pipeline.

Workforce planning must therefore treat continuous, even modest, recruitment as a non-negotiable investment in future leadership capacity rather than a discretionary cost that can be cut whenever results weaken.

The speaker, Tsutomu Okamoto (representative director of the Human Capital Innovation Research Institute and supervisor of 'Strategic Management of Executives and Personnel Costs'), emphasizes this as a standing principle he repeats in seminars: 'No matter how bad performance is, absolutely do not stop hiring.'

Even if performance is somewhat poor or voluntary retirement (希望退職) is implemented, companies should continue hiring new people steadily and quietly; this is an important long-term element. Decision-makers should carefully determine a minimum number of people to hire each year rather than abandoning recruitment due to immediate short-term constraints such as 'no budget this year' or 'costs are tight now.'
If personnel costs must be reduced, it is better to solicit voluntary retirements and actively refresh the workforce ('replace the blood') than simply to stop new hiring.

Short-term hiring cost pressures and medium-term productivity plans may indicate that hiring should be stopped, yet from the standpoint of the long-term cycle of corporate metabolism (新陳代謝), new 'cells' (employees) must always continue to be introduced.

Halting recruitment is reputationally damaging. Word that 'that company has stopped hiring' easily mutates into rumors that 'their performance is in trouble,' so that when the company later wants to hire again, candidates may not even apply.

The tension between protecting this year's results and continuing to hire resembles the conflict of ambidextrous management (両利きの経営). Presidents and department heads, focused on current-year performance, tend to order 'stop hiring' as soon as results look bad.

A company's personnel composition (人員構成) and age pyramid (年齢ピラミッド) record history like the annual rings (年輪) of a tree. Years of favorable conditions or aggressive hiring produce wide rings; years of poor climate or performance produce narrow rings. Dents in the pyramid typically correspond to past business slumps when hiring was cut; peaks correspond to periods when aggressive leaders insisted on hiring large numbers.
Personnel planning cannot be driven by business-plan needs alone; candidates who clash with the company's actual brand image will either not join or will be unable to work together if they do.

A common failure pattern is claiming to want people with free thinking to create new businesses, then immediately subjecting them to thorough reviews and nitpicking once they join, often with no internal backing.
Whether the company truly has the resolve (覚悟) to let new talent thrive is more important than simply telling recruiters to hire them.
The organization must invest in the environment that allows new people to succeed, rather than treating hiring as a hand-off to the recruiting function.
Culture and climate (文化や風土) must already support the desired talent; if they do not, forced hiring typically ends in turnover.

Effective 人員計画 (personnel planning) therefore requires simultaneously considering brand-image fit, cultural readiness, environmental investment, and retention risk rather than headcount numbers in isolation.

Okamoto Tsutomu (Deloitte Tohmatsu Consulting, Human Capital Division) emphasizes that human-capital strategy must integrate these organizational conditions, not treat recruitment as an isolated transactional activity.

A common organizational problem in hiring is a 'disconnect' (分断) between the recruiting team and the assignment destination, caused by the pursuit of efficiency; newly hired employees who were recruited with the hope they would thrive can then be neglected in the field, with no one watching over them.

An illustrative case: when discussing how to help a struggling employee grow, the employee's department head said 「私が採用した人じゃないですから」 ('Because I didn't hire that person'), revealing an unwillingness to commit to that person's development.
Corporate Direction Inc. (CDI), an ~80-person consulting firm, uses an apprenticeship system (徒弟制) so that independent consultants can be developed.
Under CDI's system, Managing Directors (経営陣 / 'masters') each set their own hiring criteria and process and personally bring in a small number of elite 'disciples.'

Apprenticeship begins at hiring: a candidate chooses which executive they want as their master and joins the firm only if that master hires them; how the disciple is then developed is left to the master, and involvement styles vary.
Masters are expected to create, with resolve and responsibility, the soil in which disciples can grow, and to watch over them.
The transferable lesson is that someone inside the company must exist who has the resolve and responsibility to personally develop the people they hired (「この採用した人を自分が育てる」).
Hiring criteria ('what kind of person to hire') should be verbalized using structure and logic rather than relying on intuition or sensation.
A 4-axis framework for defining hiring requirements: Skills (スキル), Stance (スタンス), Behavior (行動), and Experience (経験).
Requirements can be classified using Must / Want / Nice categories as immediately usable techniques.
Clear hiring requirements create consistency across selection, candidate experience (CX), and employee development/training.
Organizing requirements internally requires essential dialogue with both frontline operations (現場) and management (経営); reading alone does not complete the process.
Attempting to set perfect hiring requirements carries the risk of conversely making the organization unable to act or move forward.

採用要件 (hiring/recruitment requirements) is defined as the concretization of the candidate profile a company seeks in recruitment activities, expressed in forms such as skills, experience, and personal characteristics. It is not merely a wish list; it is the starting point and standard axis for the entire hiring process, influencing job posting creation, interviews, offer decisions, and even post-hire evaluation.

Clear hiring requirements create consistency in selection and make it easier to prevent mismatches between the company and applicants. Examples of 採用要件 include: 3+ years of sales experience; a flexible attitude toward change; and empathy with the company’s philosophy/mission.

人材要件 (talent requirements) is the overall, medium-to-long-term picture of the talent a company seeks. It is linked to management strategy and organizational culture, and is an abstract, general concept. It is used not only in recruitment but also in transfers and talent development. Examples: people who take on change; people who keep learning.
採用要件 (hiring requirements) are the specific conditions set for each job type or position, based on 人材要件. They are expressed as the behaviors, skills, and stances needed to perform the job.

求人票 (job posting) consists of the publicly disclosed subset of hiring requirements. It is the information job seekers use to decide whether to apply: application qualifications, compensation, work location, etc. It can also include promotional content.

ペルソナ (persona) is a recruitment-marketing concept: a fictional person that concretizes the target job-seeker image. Age, career history, values, and lifestyle are specified so stakeholders can share ‘what kind of person we want to apply.’

選考基準 (selection criteria) are evaluation standards set based on hiring requirements. They are used in selection judgments (e.g., 3+ years of corporate sales experience adds points; no experience deducts points). They are concrete check items for interviews and document screening, and they reduce judgment gaps among interviewers and evaluators.
採用要件は人材要件の一部であり、採用における広報や判断の出発点となる概念である。
採用要件を言語化することは、企業の期待を明示することであり、求職者にとっても自己判断の手がかりになる。
採用要件を言語化すると、後のステージ（募集・選考・内定後フォロー）での整合性を保ちやすくなり、採用活動全体の質が上がる。
採用要件 (recruitment requirements) is a verbalization of the type of person a company wants to hire; it is the standard that runs through the entire recruitment process.
採用要件 is framed from the perspective of what talent is needed to realize management strategy and foster organizational culture, and it includes concrete conditions such as skills.
Related terms in the recruitment pipeline include 人員計画 (workforce/personnel planning), 採用計画 (recruitment plan), 募集 (job posting/recruitment), 選考 (selection), and AMS.

選考基準 (selection criteria) is the measuring stick (ものさし) used to evaluate candidates in document screening and interviews; it is used not only in hiring but also in transfers (異動) and talent development (人材開発).
Items that are disclosed externally include 応募資格 (application qualifications), 待遇 (compensation/treatment), and 勤務地 (work location).
ペルソナ (persona) is used in 採用マーケティング (recruitment marketing) as a concretized image of the target candidate.
The process of putting hiring requirements into words itself activates the organization.
Verbalizing recruitment criteria (adopting requirements in language) is not merely documentation; the act of doing so energizes and activates the organization as a whole.
How to create recruitment requirements (採用要件のつくり方): fill in the appendix “採用要件すりあわせシート” (recruitment-requirements alignment sheet) while reading to deepen understanding.
Step A — Draw the ideal structurally (演繹 / deduction): start by structurally depicting the ideal person expected for the position (details in ツボ 023–024).

Four-axis structure of the ideal: 職務 (organization / objective) = the objective work the organization actually wants done; スキル (individual / objective) = abilities the person needs to perform that work; カルチャー (organization / subjective) = values and behavioral styles each member of the organization subjectively holds dear; スタンス (individual / subjective) = the person’s attitude and way of facing work.

Step B — Extract common points from real examples (帰納 / induction): imagine people who actually thrive on the ground and ideal external talent, then align the requirement image with the field using concrete cases of “this kind of person thrives” vs. “this kind of person did not fit,” to judge which qualities are effective. This is the process of checking the ideal against reality (details in ツボ 025).

Step C — Make the invisible visible with the iceberg model (統合 / integration): stance and skills required for the job and culture cannot be seen directly in interviews, so convert hard-to-see elements (stance, skills) into observable ones (behavior, experience). This structure is explained by the “氷山モデル” (iceberg model; details in ツボ 026).
Iceberg-model example: “a stance of not fearing challenges” is rewritten as “experience of volunteering for a new project,” which makes evaluation at selection time possible.

Step D — Prioritize with intention: demanding someone who meets every requirement leads to “no such person exists in the market.” Therefore assign priority ranks to requirements and organize them (details in later ツボ).
When setting hiring requirements (採用要件), it is important to form consensus with the workplace/field (現場) on what to prioritize, referring to related points 027 and 028.
At this stage of defining hiring requirements, one must confront the gap between ideals and reality (理想と現実のギャップ) while clarifying the judgment axes (判断軸) used for hiring decisions.
A final check is required to confirm that the set requirements do not violate laws or ethics (法令や倫理); details are covered in ツボ 029.
Coordinate with HR (人事) and legal (法務) as needed so that job postings (求人情報) can be published with confidence.
Hiring requirements are constructed through dialogue with the workplace, by finding the intersection (接点) between ideals and reality.
The subsequent section (ツボ 023) addresses verbalizing job duties and skills (職務とスキルの言語化).
A dedicated step labeled WE is to protect law and ethics (法と倫理を守る) when finalizing requirements.

Hiring requirements (採用要件) should be created by: drawing the ideal with structure, extracting common points from real examples, visualizing them, willfully assigning priorities, and complying with law and ethics.
The process combines deduction (構造で理想を描く / drawing the ideal via structure) with induction (実例の共通点を抽出する / extracting commonalities from actual cases).
A useful lens for examples is subjective vs. objective, plus stance vs. skills and culture vs. job content (カルチャー vs 職務).
Culture covers the organization’s values and behavioral style; job content covers the actual work the person is expected to take on.

After visualization, assign priorities with intent using Must (absolutely necessary), Want (desirable if present), and Nice (nice to have), distinguishing more visible experience from less visible factors.

Requirements must be checked so they do not violate law or ethics. Discriminatory or inappropriate criteria include birthplace, family composition, family occupation, living environment, religion or beliefs, supported political party, and marriage plans.
With a hypothesis in mind (仮説をもって), complete the 「採用要件すりあわせシート」 (Recruitment Requirements Alignment Sheet) and then align/coordinate it with the workplace or on-site team (現場).

This is a practical methodology for defining hiring requirements: start from a hypothesis rather than unexamined lists, document it on a dedicated alignment sheet, and verify it against actual field conditions so recruitment criteria match operational reality.

In recruitment, the first things that must be clarified are 職務 (job duties) and スキル (skills): what work will be assigned and what capabilities are required. Accurately verbalizing both makes hiring criteria clear and reduces mismatch.

The first step is 職務分析 (Job Analysis). It is conducted through hearings with field managers and responsible employees, gathering specifics on what tasks exist, what daily actions are required, and what actual difficulties occur.
Job analysis can also draw on existing grade definitions, job requirement definitions, work manuals, past job postings, and evaluation sheets.

Verbalizing 職務 means making concrete the work a hired person will take on, escaping vague states such as a “somehow busy department” or “just not enough people,” and clearly defining roles and responsibilities.
When organizing a job, specify business content, scope of responsibility, required outputs, and involvement with related parties. The resulting document is the 職務記述書 (Job Description).

Once the job is clear, verbalize skills: what capabilities the sought person must have. Skills include 専門スキル (specialized skills such as knowledge and technique) and 汎用スキル (generic skills such as interpersonal coordination and problem-finding ability).

Express which skills are indispensable for producing the results the job requires, referring to characteristics of high performers. The resulting document is the 職能要件書 (competency/skill requirements document).

Job analysis is also important for new-graduate hiring, contrary to the view that it is unnecessary because graduates lack job experience. Observe how young employees actually produce results through their actions.
Extracting required behavioral characteristics (行動特性) and attitudes (姿勢) yields guidelines for potential-based hiring (ポテンシャル採用).

Example behavioral tendencies that can serve as the ideal image for new-graduate hires: proactively asking questions (“自分から質問する”) and quickly building rapport even with people met for the first time (“初対面の人ともすぐ打ち解けられる”).
Verbalizing job duties (職務) and skills (スキル) is the starting point for creating hiring requirements (採用要件づくり).

Whether hiring experienced people or new graduates, being able to clearly state “I want to entrust this job to them” (“この仕事を任せたい”) aligns selection judgment criteria (選考の判断軸) and communication of those criteria (伝え方).
The next tip (ツボ 024) covers verbalizing culture (カルチャー) and stance (スタンス).
Job analysis (職務分析 / Job Analysis) is the foundation for creating two complementary documents: the Job Description (職務記述書) and the Job Requirements Document (職能要件書).
職能要件書 (Job Requirements Document) clarifies what abilities a person needs to perform the job; it focuses on required capabilities rather than the position itself.
職務記述書 (Job Description) clarifies what the position does: its purpose, main duties, reporting line, related departments, and working conditions.

A job–skill framework can be organized along complementary axes such as subjective vs. objective, stance vs. skills, and culture vs. job, so that both hard skills and cultural/attitudinal fit are specified.

Example capability items for a customer-facing SaaS role include basic IT tool operation (Excel, Slack, etc.), customer correspondence, SaaS industry knowledge, and proposing and executing operational improvements.

Example Job Description for Customer Success: job title Customer Success; department Customer Success Team (within Sales); purpose increase retention through usage support and satisfaction; main duties onboarding support and product explanation, regular follow-up, FAQ maintenance; supervisor Customer Success Manager; related departments Sales, Development, Support; location Tokyo HQ with one remote day per week.
Job analysis method — Hearing (ヒアリング): interview incumbents and managers about work content, workflow, required skills, and pain points.
Job analysis method — Observation (観察): watch incumbents at work and record tasks and interactions; especially suitable for visible work such as factory, customer service, or reception roles.

Job analysis method — Document research (文書調査): extract information from existing hiring materials, manuals, grade definitions, job requirement definitions, and goal-management sheets; low effort and useful for quickly grasping an overview.

Job analysis method — Questionnaire (アンケート): employees self-report job content and difficulty; efficient for surveying many people at once, but results are self-evaluations and must be interpreted with caution.

Job analysis method — Workshop (ワークショップ): employees, managers, and HR discuss together questions such as the job’s purpose and the characteristics of high performers; yields diverse perspectives in a short time.
職務記述書は、精緻で厳密なものではなく、現場とズレないものを目指す。

Even when candidates have sufficient skills, they often fail to fit after joining; many such cases are due to a mismatch between the candidate's stance and the organization's culture (lack of culture match).

Stance (スタンス) is the attitude that precedes behavior: how a person approaches work, people, and challenges. It can be observed from past decision-making patterns and behavioral episodes, e.g. 'try acting first,' 'proceed after carefully checking,' or 'consult colleagues before deciding.'

Culture (カルチャー) is the values and judgment tendencies naturally shared inside an organization. It may be written as a philosophy or code of conduct, but it is actually formed by accumulated daily practice: which behaviors have been evaluated and which behaviors have earned trust.
Organizational character shows up in recurring behavioral patterns such as 'emphasize speed,' 'proceed only after everyone agrees,' or 'praise taking on challenges.'

Culture match means the candidate's stance and the organization's culture naturally resonate. A 'try acting first' stance tends to fit organizations that value change and speed; a 'check procedures carefully then act' stance tends to thrive in organizations that value stability.
The key question is not which stance or culture is 'correct,' but whether the candidate fits this particular company.
To assess culture match, the company's culture must first be put into language. This starts by interviewing founders, on-site managers, and others who know the organization's origins.
Unspoken organizational culture can be surfaced by investigating which behaviors have historically been valued/evaluated and which attitudes or postures have historically been trusted.
Making that previously unarticulated culture explicit makes it easier to judge which stances (attitudes, ways of working) will actually match the organization.

When designing hiring requirements, culture-fit stance should be specified with the same seriousness as skills: define requirements from the question “what stance fits our culture?” rather than skills alone.
The following section (ツボ 025) presents the concrete method for designing those stance-based hiring requirements.
To grasp an organization's origins, interview people who know its founding and history and probe the behaviors and postures that have long been valued.
Chart 024 frames organizational culture versus individual stance across several polarities that can be used diagnostically.

Decision-making polarity: obtain sufficient prior consensus before acting versus move first and correct later; treat failure as a credibility-risk versus treat failure as proof of challenge; emphasize intra-team coordination and confirmation versus trust and delegate to individual discretion.

Communication polarity: anyone may speak frankly versus language must match rank; proposals can be made flatly even to superiors versus action is taken by reading the boss's intentions; information is shared with everyone versus information is passed stepwise only to those who need it.

Work-style and time-use polarity: remote / discretionary-labor centered versus office attendance and explicit time control; once results appear the process is left to the individual versus frequent reporting and progress sharing are required; each person optimizes their own way of working versus organizational rules and a sense of unity take priority.

Risk-and-challenge polarity: leaders say 'let's try it first' versus precedents and risks are checked carefully; change is welcomed versus continuity and reliability are prized; important projects are entrusted to people in their twenties versus young talent is developed in staged steps.

A complementary structural lens (labeled A) maps ideals along axes of subjective versus objective, stasis versus skill, and culture versus job duties, allowing culture and stance to be drawn as an explicit architecture rather than left implicit.
Culture (カルチャー) is the unconscious evaluation standard (無意識の評価基準) of what kinds of behaviors and attitudes one naturally prefers or finds desirable (どんな行動や態度を“自然に好ましく思うか”).

To make hiring requirements realistic, do not only draw an ideal image; confirm the gap between reality and ideal using actual field examples of people who are succeeding and people who did not work out.
This process adds reality to abstract requirements and aligns a shared candidate image between the field and HR.

Start by having the field specifically name several currently successful employees. Hear what is excellent about them, which behaviors contribute to the team, and what stance they take. Have them talk through actual episodes rather than evaluations or impressions so that the requirements become more reproducible.

Next, review people who were expected to succeed but did not fully thrive. Carefully explore why they did not work out and what misalignment existed. Examples include sufficient skills but a poor team fit, or discomfort with stance; culture mismatch often becomes visible. This also clarifies elements to avoid in hiring.

Sharing external model cases is also effective: people seen at other companies or in the industry of whom one thinks, 'someone like this person would likely succeed.' Referring to realistic talent images from nearby other departments or partner companies brings diversity and a sense of reality to hiring requirements.
From these real examples, extract skills, stances, and patterns of behavior and experience that are common across multiple people, then reflect those commonalities in the hiring requirements.
Basing hiring requirements on real existing people makes selection interviews more concrete: it becomes easier to ask specific questions and to judge candidates against a clear, lived example.
Input should not come only from the hiring manager. Voices of the people who will actually work with the new hire are equally important.
The same person looks different depending on the observer’s role. Interviewing several people therefore produces more balanced requirements.
Typical complementary viewpoints: managers tend to emphasize results and outcomes; team members tend to emphasize daily communication and working style. These perspectives offset each other.
The next step (tip 026) is to integrate the individual requirement elements defined in tips 023–025 into a single, visible picture of the desired hire.
Realistic hiring requirements (リアリティある採用要件) can be built by inductively extracting common points from actual examples (実例の共通点を抽出する / 帰納), rather than relying only on abstract wish lists.
Compare two internal groups: people who are thriving in the company (活躍している人) versus people for whom things did not go well (うまくいかなかった人).
For successful employees, probe what they excel at, which behaviors contribute to the team, and what stance or attitude they hold.
For unsuccessful cases, investigate why it did not work, what misalignments (ズレ) existed, and make explicit the elements that hiring should avoid.
Alignment among stakeholders is done through sharing concrete “actual episodes” (実際のエピソード), not only generalized traits.
External model cases can be added: people seen at other companies or in the industry of whom one would say “someone like this would likely succeed here,” then treat those as shared reference models.
The method treats hiring criteria as something grounded in observed people (named internal examples plus external ideals) so requirements stay realistic and avoidable failure patterns become visible.
Going back and forth (いったりきたり往復する) between deduction (演繹) and induction (帰納) is a key technique for raising the accuracy/precision of hiring requirements (採用要件の精度を高めるコツ).
Iterative reciprocation between deductive and inductive reasoning is presented as a practical method for refining recruitment criteria.

In hiring requirements, what matters most is how to make those requirements visible. Even if skills and stances are clearly defined, they are meaningless unless they can be confirmed during the selection process.

The iceberg model (氷山モデル), as described in the Personnel Assessment Handbook (人事アセスメントハンドブック by Osawa Takeshi, Shiba Yujun, and Futamura Hideyuki), treats human capability as iceberg-like: what is visible above the water is Behavior (行動); Skills (スキル) and Stance (スタンス) lie hidden below.
The premise of the model is that behind visible behaviors and experiences sit less-visible abilities and attitudes, and those hidden elements support results.

To make defined skills and stances evaluable in selection, they must be verbalized as concrete behaviors—how they actually appear in someone’s actions. Example: the stance “can act autonomously” translates into the behavior “discovered issues before the supervisor’s instructions and proposed them independently.”
Behaviors are easier to confirm directly in interviews and become the starting point for specific questions.

Skills and stances should also be translated into Experience (経験): the situations in which they were exhibited as behavior and accumulated over time. Example: the skill “hypothesis-thinking ability” becomes “experience of forming hypotheses and proposing solutions for multiple issues.” Example: the stance “someone who enjoys change” becomes “experience of volunteering for a project in the launch/startup phase and repeatedly going through trial and error.”
Experience functions as the execution history of skills and stances.

When assessing candidates, go beyond listing experience itself: dig into what actions they actually took and what mindset or consciousness they brought to the work; this raises the precision of selection.

Visualizing hiring requirements (採用要件を見える化する) means translating iceberg-below-the-waterline skills and stances (スキル・スタンス) into concrete, selection-evaluable experiences (経験) and behaviors/actions (行動).

The iceberg metaphor: much of what matters (skills, stance) sits under the waterline and is not directly visible; it must be rendered as observable experience and action so it can be scored in interviews and screening.

Grasping requirements structurally produces consistency in selection criteria and in judgment calls, which in turn produces hiring decisions that feel high in conviction and mutual understanding (納得度の高い採用).
After requirements have been made visible in this way, the next step (ツボ 027) is learning how to assign priority among those visualized requirements.

The iceberg model (氷山モデル) is used in recruitment to translate abstract 'skills' (スキル) and 'stance' (スタンス) into observable 'experience' (経験) and 'behavior' (行動) so hiring requirements can be evaluated more concretely.

In the iceberg model of corporate human capabilities (企業人能力の氷山モデル), the visible above-water portion consists of accumulated work history that can be verified, such as three years of sales experience or team-management experience.
Observable, visible behaviors that sit just above the waterline include reading ahead to structure tasks and involving stakeholders to drive initiatives forward.
Concrete, demonstrable abilities that can be assessed include presentation skills, data analysis, and practical marketing work.

The large invisible portion below the waterline consists of posture, stance, and persistent attitudes, such as taking positive action even in difficult situations and accepting responsibility in order to see work through to completion.
The model is used as an integration tool (C. 氷山モデルで見える化する) to make hiring criteria visible by stacking verifiable history, observable behaviors, actual capabilities, and underlying attitudes.
The corporate-capability iceberg model presented here is adapted by the author from Osawa Takeshi, Shiba Yuujun, and Futamura Hideyuki, Personnel Assessment Handbook (人事アセスメントハンドブック).
適性検査は、スタンスのさらに下にある「性格」を測定する手法として用いられる。
性格はスタンスよりも深層に位置するものとして捉えられる。
It is unrealistic to expect any candidate to satisfy every listed hiring requirement; stacking too many conditions leaves an extremely small talent pool and risks excluding otherwise viable people.

When writing recruitment requirements, keep an ideal profile in mind but always filter through the practical question of whether such a person actually exists in the market, then prune and prioritize accordingly.

Classify every requirement into one of three importance levels: Must (non-negotiable, e.g., a legally required license or a language skill essential to the work), Want (desirable yet substitutable or coachable), and Nice (pleasant extras that should not drive selection decisions).

The Must/Want/Nice split turns requirements into usable evaluation criteria that can be copied directly into interview scorecards and job postings; avoid converting every item into a Must and instead combine the three categories flexibly for realistic hiring.

A job requirement is simultaneously an internal evaluation standard and an external message to candidates, so it must be written in concrete, observable, action-based language rather than abstract traits.

Replace vague phrases such as “has leadership” with verifiable behavioral statements such as “has led or driven work in a team of five or more people,” so both interviewers and applicants interpret the same evidence.

Even identical labels (e.g., “XX ability”) are understood differently by different people; to prevent scoring drift, alignment sessions must explicitly define “what specific behaviors that term actually means.”

When defining hiring requirements, concretization is necessary, such as specifying in what situations a skill or quality was actually demonstrated. Aligning the granularity of expression across requirements is a key to raising their practical effectiveness.
Do not forget to align hiring requirements with the actual recruitment market. No matter how clearly requirements are written, talent that meets those conditions may not actually exist in the market.
Hiring requirements must be examined while matching them against the real talent pool.

Practical verification methods include using databases such as BizReach or LinkedIn to check how many job seekers match the requirements, or consulting recruitment agencies about whether such talent exists, in order to test whether the requirement is actually hireable.
Fact-based confirmation of market availability increases the validity of hiring requirements.
The next section (ツボ 028) addresses skill match versus culture match as important perspectives when prioritizing requirements.
Hiring requirements (採用要件) should have clear priority ranking, expressions that communicate well to candidates, and consistency with the recruitment market.
Job requirements are commonly structured as Must (必須), Want (望ましい), and Nice (あると良い), each covering four dimensions: 経験 (experience), 行動 (behavior/actions), スキル (skills), and スタンス (stance/attitude).

Startup example (30 employees, SaaS development) recruiting Customer Success — Must: experience building customer trust; flexible, proactive work in changing environments; interest in SaaS/IT tools and self-learning; no resistance to customer dialogue and autonomous action. Want: CS or support experience; coordinating internal/external stakeholders; Slack/CRM use; collaborative, proactive stance. Nice: startup work experience or SaaS events; basic HTML/CSS; industry interest and continuous learning.

Established manufacturer example (2,000 employees, food manufacturing) recruiting factory site leader candidate — Must: cooperative work in a team of 5+; understanding and practicing safety/hygiene basics; basic safety/hygiene knowledge; following rules and carefully engaging with the workplace. Want: manufacturing-site experience, junior coaching or manual creation; active involvement in kaizen and efficiency. Nice: ongoing community/volunteer participation; forklift or hygiene-manager qualifications; attachment to products and local contribution.

Growing mid-sized company example (300 employees, BtoB marketing) recruiting new-graduate hiring officer for HR — Must: building internal/external trust; carefully executing tasks with multiple stakeholders; basic business-document and Excel skills; careful interpersonal handling and empathy with company philosophy. Want: HR/recruiting internships or experience; SNS outreach and event planning; HR-tool use; proactive trust-building with candidates and employees. Nice: student-group planning experience; continuous themed posting/recording; storytelling materials and basic design sense; enjoyment of communicating organizational appeal.

Regional SME example (60 employees, construction design office) recruiting general affairs (also accounting support) — Must: daily clerical work with Excel/Word; accurate, deadline-compliant task execution; Excel/Word and document-management basics; high confidentiality awareness and responsibility. Want: accounting, payroll, or social-insurance experience; proposing and implementing daily-work efficiencies; accounting-software use; flexibility toward change and varied tasks. Nice: SME back-office experience; smooth internal/external coordination; bookkeeping level-3+ qualification; valuing company and community connections.
Always have a partner who can inform you about conditions in the recruitment/hiring market (採用市場の状況を知ることができるパートナーを必ず持っておきましょう).

Skill match (スキルマッチ) is a candidate’s job aptitude: how fully they possess the knowledge, experience, and techniques required for the role. Examples: sales experience and customer-management ability for sales jobs; programming skill and development experience for engineering jobs.
Skill match is especially weighted when the organization needs immediate contributors (即戦力). It is comparatively easy to evaluate and to define with clear criteria.
Culture match (カルチャーマッチ) is organizational compatibility: how well a candidate’s values and behavioral style (“stance” / スタンス) align with the organization’s culture.
People whose stance fits the culture more easily build trust with colleagues and are more likely to stay long term. A large stance mismatch creates a risk of isolation even if skills are high.
Culture match is hard to quantify, but it strongly affects long-term contribution and workplace harmony.
Hiring rule of thumb: hire when both skill match and culture match are high; decline when both are low. The hard case is when one is high and the other is low.

“Chaos talent” (カオス人材) means high skill match and low culture match. Short-term results are likely, but internal discord is also likely. Deliberately hiring such people can be valuable when the organization wants to dismantle existing culture or strongly needs diverse perspectives; it is a major risk when unity and cohesion are the priority, so judgment should be cautious.
Regardless of the situation, setting an explicit cultural hiring policy such as “we do not hire people with this kind of stance” reduces hesitation in decisions.
Investment talent (投資人材) describes candidates with high culture match but low skill match; long-term growth and retention can be expected from them.
Developing investment talent requires time and cost, so it is a suitable choice when the organization has spare capacity or for new-graduate and young-talent hiring.
When short-term results are needed, hiring high-culture/low-skill people risks disrupting operations.
Organizations should clearly decide whether to prioritize skills or culture according to their current state and strike an appropriate balance between the two.
Hiring requires strategic judgment of when, why, and how to bring people in.
When hiring, clarify whether to prioritize skill match or culture match based on the current state of the organization.
Skill match (スキルマッチ) is the degree of alignment between the abilities required for the job and the candidate's skills.
Culture match (カルチャーマッチ) is the degree of alignment between organizational culture and the candidate's stance.
Figure 028 maps hiring decisions on two axes: skill match (low to high) and culture match (low to high).

Chaos talent (カオス人材): high skill match, low culture match. Short-term results can be expected. Hire if the goal is to dismantle existing organizational culture. Causes internal discord; high risk if a sense of unity (一体感) is desired.

Investment talent (投資人材): low skill match, high culture match. Long-term growth and retention can be expected. Hire when the organization has spare capacity. Personnel development takes time and cost, and is an obstacle when short-term results are needed.
Candidates with both low skill match and low culture match should be passed over (見送り).
Netflix has issued a hiring policy of not employing 'brilliant jerks' (ブリリアントジャーク).
A brilliant jerk is defined as someone who is excellent or highly talented (優秀) but unpleasant or difficult to work with (嫌な奴).

Hiring requirements (採用要件) make clear what kind of talent an organization wants to hire, but both how they are written and how they are applied must follow laws and ethical rules; setting them without knowing those rules can lead to employment discrimination or legal violations.
Japanese law prohibits setting hiring requirements based on attributes unrelated to a person's own effort, such as gender, age, or place of origin.
The Equal Employment Opportunity Act (男女雇用機会均等法) forbids discrimination in recruitment and hiring on the basis of gender.
The Employment Measures Act (労働施策総合推進法) generally requires that age limits not be imposed.
The Labor Standards Act (労働基準法) and the Constitution prohibit discrimination based on race, creed, social status, and similar grounds.
Requirements that violate these rules (for example, “recruiting men under 35” or “excluding people from origin OO”) can become the object of administrative guidance or sanctions as legal violations.

Even items not clearly banned by statute can be inappropriate under social norms. The Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare’s “Basics of Fair Recruitment Selection” (公正な採用選考の基本) states that the following should not be used as hiring criteria or interview questions: registered domicile or birthplace; family composition or family occupation; housing floor plan or living environment; religion, creed, or supported political party; respected persons or favorite books; views on life or marriage plans.

Those items have no relation to a person’s ability or job aptitude and risk producing discriminatory treatment. For example, asking about marriage plans and then rejecting only women can be judged illegal.
Hiring decisions should be centered on aptitude and ability.
Hiring criteria must be directly related to job duties (職務に直接関連する基準). An example is a standard such as being able to collaborate in a team (チームでの協働ができる).
Job-related selection criteria enable a process that applicants can accept as reasonable (納得感のある選考) and support recruitment that is fair (公平性) and highly reliable (信頼性の高い採用活動).
When defining hiring requirements (採用要件), employers must correctly understand applicable laws and regulations (法令) and simultaneously respect applicants' human rights (人権) and diversity (多様性).
Hiring is the company's entrance (企業の入口); fairness (公正さ) in recruitment builds organizational trust (組織の信頼).
Avoid casual wording (安易な表現) and ambiguous judgments (曖昧な判断). Design hiring requirements carefully and in accordance with the rules (ルールに則した丁寧な設計).
The next topic (ツボ 030) covers the relationship between hiring requirements and the hiring process.
Recruitment requirements in Japan should open doors widely to applicants (応募者に広く門戸を開くこと) and be based solely on the individual's aptitude and abilities (本人のもつ適性・能力に基づいた要件とすること).
図表029 (Chart 029) catalogs elements that must be avoided in recruitment requirements (採用要件で避けるべき要素), citing applicable statutes and giving concrete prohibited examples.
Gender (性別) discrimination is forbidden by 男女雇用機会均等法 第5条; prohibited examples include 男性のみ募集, 女性限定で採用, 35歳以下に限る, and 20代歓迎.
Creed, including religion and political beliefs (信条), is protected by 労働施策総合推進法 第9条 and 日本国憲法 第14条 第1項; examples of unlawful criteria are 特定宗教の信者不可 and 〇〇党支持者は応募不可.
Race and ethnicity (人種・民族) cannot be used as hiring criteria under 日本国憲法 第14条 第1項; examples include 〇〇系民族のみ採用 and 外国人不可.
Nationality (国籍) restrictions violate 労働基準法 第3条; an unlawful example is 日本国籍の方に限る.
Social status (社会的身分) and family origin/lineage (門地) are barred by 日本国憲法 第14条 第1項; examples include 華族など良家の出身者のみ and 〇〇家の親族限定.
Presence or absence of disability (障害の有無) is protected by 障害者雇用促進法 第34条; an unlawful requirement is 心身に障害のない方.
Health condition and medical history (健康状態・病歴) must not be used, per 厚労省「公正な採用選考の基本」; prohibited examples are 心身ともに健康な方 and 持病のない方.
Pregnancy and childbirth (妊娠・出産の有無) cannot be criteria under 男女雇用機会均等法 第5条; unlawful examples include 未婚者に限る, 現在妊娠していない方, 出産予定のない方, and 既婚女性は不可.
Family composition and home environment (家族構成・家庭環境) are likewise barred by 男女雇用機会均等法 第5条; examples include 長男・長女は不可 and 親が一流企業勤務の方歓迎.
Registered domicile and birthplace (本籍・出生地) are restricted by 職安法 第5条の5 and 労働省告示141号; examples include 〇〇県出身者のみ募集 and 本籍地が〇〇の方.
Current address and residential area (現住所・居住地域) cannot be limited under 職安法指針; examples include 〇〇在住の方限定 and 通勤〇分以内の方.
Appearance (容姿) is prohibited by 厚労省指針; an example is 美男美女に限る.
Height, weight, and physical strength (身長・体重・体力) restrictions violate 男女雇用機会均等法施行規則; examples include 身長〇〇cm以上 and 体重〇〇kg以下.
Labor-union membership or activity history (労働組合加入) is protected by 職安法指針 and 憲法 第28条; an unlawful criterion is 労組活動歴がある方は不可.
Sexual orientation and gender identity (性的指向・性自認) must not be used, per 厚労省「公正な採用選考の基本」; an example is 同性愛者は不可.
Criminal record (犯罪歴・前科) is sensitive personal information under 個人情報保護法 第2条3号 and cannot be a hiring barrier; an example is 前科のある方は応募不可.
Debt and credit status (借金・信用状況) cannot be required under 職安法指針; an example is 多額の負債がない方.
In Japanese job advertisements, explicitly stating an age limit such as 「35歳までの方」 (people up to 35 years of age) is NG (not acceptable).
An acceptable alternative phrasing is 「長期的な就業意欲をお持ちの方」 (people who possess long-term employment motivation/desire), which is OK.
This contrast illustrates how to avoid prohibited age-based wording while still signaling preference for candidates oriented toward long-term employment.
Verbalizing hiring requirements (採用要件の言語化) is the starting point of recruitment: if it is not clear 'what kind of person to hire', the entire hiring activity becomes vague.

Verbalizing hiring requirements is not merely drawing an ideal image. It is a dynamic practice in which the workplace (現場) and HR dialogue based on the realities of the job and organization, concretizing the necessary experience (経験), behavior (行動), skills (スキル), and stance (スタンス), thereby forming shared knowledge.

Impact on recruitment (募集): Clear hiring requirements greatly influence the quality of job information. When duties and required behaviors are explicitly documented, job seekers can more easily self-assess their fit, reducing mismatches.

When stance and culture elements are included in job postings, applications from people who empathize with the organization's values are encouraged, enabling approach to intended talent layers rather than mere headcount filling.

Impact on selection (選考): Vague requirements cause interview evaluation axes to vary by person or be swayed by impressions and subjectivity. Verbalized requirements enable designing questions that specifically inquire about candidates' experience and behavior, and aligning evaluation viewpoints for stance and skills.
Especially when multiple interviewers are involved, verbalized hiring requirements maintain evaluation consistency and enable fair, persuasive selection.

Impact on adaptation (適応): Verbalized requirements also support post-hire onboarding and retention. Specific expectations and roles presented before joining reduce the gap after joining, and make it easier for the new hire to envision how they can contribute.
Development staff can share the background of 'we hired this person expecting these qualities', making it easier to create individualized support plans.
Verbalizing hiring requirements (採用要件の言語化) is not mere preparatory work; it is the foundation that raises the quality of the entire hiring process.
Aligning with the workplace/field (現場とのすりあわせ) and deeply exploring job duties and expectations surfaces real, results-connected requirements rather than a superficial person image.
This verbalization becomes a single unifying axis connecting recruitment targeting (募集のターゲティング), selection accuracy (選考の精度), and successful adaptation (適応の成功).
The characteristics of effective human resource management (人材マネジメント) are consistency (一貫性) and adaptability (適応性).
Quote: 効果的な人材マネジメントの特徴は「一貫性」と「適応性」です
Verbalizing hiring requirements (採用要件の言語化) is the starting point that reconnects management strategy with organization building.
Deciding who to hire is a statement of intent about what culture to nurture and what future to build.
To welcome talent who resonate with the company philosophy and can perform autonomously, structurally define jobs, culture, and behaviors (ツボ 022・024).
When requirements become clear, hiring evolves from personal/subjective judgment into an organizational choice (ツボ 030).
Facing the question of who will share daily work with you is the first step of hiring.
To confidently say “I want to entrust this job,” verbalize the actual reality of the job and identify common points among people who succeeded and those who did not (ツボ 023・025).
Hiring requirements are not finished at the point of hiring; they are a shared foundation that also connects to post-joining development and collaboration.
Draw the design blueprint together through dialogue with HR (ツボ 026・027).
Hiring requirements are a “common language” that unifies job understanding, recruitment design, and selection evaluation.
Through alignment with the workplace, translate necessary skills and stances into specific behaviors and experiences (ツボ 026).
Organizing priorities with Must / Want / Nice prevents variation in candidate evaluation and enables realistic requirement design (ツボ 027).
As the starting point of hiring, nurture criteria that run through the entire process (ツボ 022・030).
Chapter 3 summary targets distinct messages to executives, field managers (management), hiring staff, and all working members.
Considering hiring requirements (採用要件) is also a way of re-examining the question of 'who do you want to work with.'
Recalling colleagues who felt comfortable to work with, versus those who created a sense of discomfort (違和感), makes the team's culture (カルチャー) and the stance it wants to cherish visible.
People-to-people compatibility (相性) cannot be measured by skills alone; the ability to put that compatibility into words comes from the lived sense of those who actually work together.
Hiring is not someone else's job; it is the team's own practice of creating the future of the workplace (現場).
The next chapter covers recruitment (募集).

Sowa Toshimitsu (曽和利光), author of 『人事と採用のセオリー』 (The Theory of HR and Recruitment) and former Recruit recruitment lead, now president of BAAR Co. Human Resources Research Institute, discusses practical hiring methods.
In recruitment, personas should be treated as 「みずみずしい人物像」 (vivid/fresh person images) rather than dry profiles; this vividness is described as the core (肝) of effective targeting.

Scout-media (direct-approach recruiting platforms) reply rates have been falling sharply; a few years earlier 30–40 % response rates were common and were likened to 「入れ食い」 (easy fishing / fish jumping on the bait).
The interview frames the practical question as how to move from abstract personas to concrete, living talent images that still elicit responses in a cooling market.
Recruitment has shifted into a contest of search ability (検索力); scout/response rates that were once higher are now commonly below 10%.
Scout media platforms may contain 200,000–250,000 student profiles, yet scout emails concentrate on a small subset of people because most recruiters lack search skill.
When asked what kind of person they want, recruiters typically give an overly vague persona: high communication ability, good 地頭 (natural intelligence), and high stress tolerance.
Communication ability is not one skill: expression, logical speaking, reading the atmosphere (空気を読む), and getting along with people are distinct capacities.
Even “challenge spirit” is ambiguous—it may mean curiosity that jumps at new things or goal-achievement motivation.
The abstraction level of the “desired person image” (求める人物像) is typically too high, so recruiters cannot picture a real person or generate useful search keywords.

A vivid (みずみずしい) persona is built by a team collectively imagining concrete examples (“what kind of person actually meets those conditions?”). Concrete details then yield searchable keywords (e.g., shogi, Starbucks vs. self-sourced tutoring vs. working at Try).
Free-word search on scout media is almost unused because recruiters cannot answer “who is that person?” when the persona remains abstract.

True grasp of the desired persona is shown by being able to hypothesize specific, even “trivial,” details—for example, that such a person might avoid ubiquitous Starbucks and instead go to Ueshima Coffee.
Recruiters should maintain a personal “person database” (人物データベース) by meeting many people and learning what kinds of people actually exist.

An imaginary vivid persona is powerful precisely because it is not a factual record: it stimulates imagination. Once a candidate is characterized, the character begins to “move” automatically in the mind (example: predicting how Nobita would behave if he found 1,000 yen on the street).

When building a character (persona) image, create one that stands as a coherent character so impressions arise spontaneously; this enables active imagination of how the person would behave if a given measure or policy were applied, and gradually clarifies many related issues.
Character creation fails when it combines elements that do not actually coexist in real people.

After decades of life experience, people already hold many real human patterns in mind (including types they are good at reading); combinations that prompt the reaction “do such people really exist?” are the so-called “god specs” (unrealistically perfect or contradictory specifications).
The discussion occurs in the context of personnel planning and HR practice, emphasizing realistic rather than idealized employee images.

A company president's sudden hiring preference such as 'we should hire athletic/sports-club types (体育会系)' often sounds like an unfounded whim, but is frequently backed by a large body of lived experience and observation.

Founders and executives who regularly deal with many clients and employees necessarily hold a large amount of implicit data in their heads; they may simply not have verbalized why they want people with soccer experience, yet they have already formed a sense of which types tend to fit the company.

Hiring staff often react with 'the president is saying something weird again' mainly because the president's vast experiential database has never been put into language, so a statement like 'sports types are good' arrives without evidence and looks like personal taste being imposed.

The recruiter's real skill is to dig into the intuition and elicit the 'why': behind '体育会系' there may be concrete qualities such as having experienced proper hierarchy and possessing the perseverance to see goals through.
Once those underlying reasons are extracted, the preference stops looking like 'just likes club activities' and becomes a practical clue for judging the qualities that actually fit the organization.

A president's intuition can be understood as unconscious insight (無意識の洞察) generated from past observations of both successes and failures; it should not be ignored but unpacked, turned into shared language, and used to align hiring staff with management so the organization can identify the talent it truly needs.
Recruitment (募集) is a 'technology of delivering' (届ける技術); this framing organizes the premises for forming a candidate pool (候補者群の形成).
The chapter supplies a logical design perspective for job postings (求人票) and channel selection (チャネル選定).
Readers become able to design outreach that follows job seekers' behavior and psychology (求職者の行動や心理).
The chapter does not cover channel-specific operational know-how or techniques of linguistic expression.
Serious execution still requires redefining the company's own attractiveness (自社の魅力) and target persona (ターゲット像).
Hiring (採用) does not start with the company selecting talent; it starts when a job seeker becomes aware of the company and feels interest in it.

Even expensive selection processes or well-designed interviews are meaningless if no candidates apply in the first place. Before a company chooses job seekers, job seekers choose companies (Hattori Yasuhiro, 『採用学』).

In recent labor markets, a higher effective job-opening ratio and the spread of remote work have expanded job seekers’ options and reduced geographic constraints, so companies must first obtain awareness and interest.
求職者 (job seekers) = everyone considering employment or a job change; they typically have many alternatives, so a company cannot even begin recruiting unless it is widely known to them.
候補者 (candidates) = those among job seekers who actually take application action and apply.
募集 (recruitment) = outreach to the broad job-seeker population in order to convert interested people into candidates.
Without job-seeker awareness, the hiring process never starts.
The relationship with a candidate is first established through the action of applying (応募).
Recruitment activities (募集活動) have discrete steps that are covered in detail in the following section (ツボ 032).

まず、求職者から企業が選ばれないと何も始まりません: First of all, nothing can begin unless companies are chosen/selected by job seekers. This is a core principle in recruitment and employer branding: the hiring process is initiated by candidate interest and choice, so firms must first become attractive options in the talent market before any subsequent steps (screening, interviews, offers) can occur.
募集 (the act of soliciting applications itself) is distinct from 募集活動, which is the broader process of planning, implementing, and verifying recruitment to make it successful.

The first step in recruitment activities is creating a 求人票 (job posting) based on hiring requirements. It should clearly organize and communicate recruitment background, required skills and experience, compensation (待遇), and benefits (福利厚生) so that job seekers get the information they want and mismatch is greatly reduced.

The second step is choosing recruitment channels: deciding which media and methods will be used to distribute the completed job posting. Representative channels include job sites, talent introduction agencies (人材紹介), scouting, referrals (リファラル / employee introductions), and internships.

Optimal channel selection should not be based on gut feeling. First grasp two preconditions: scale of hiring budget (採用単価 × 採用人数) and scale of human resources (担当者数 × 時間). Combining these two factors yields four quadrants for choosing channels.

Quadrant strategies: (1) abundant budget and abundant human resources → use all channels together; (2) budget available but insufficient manpower → leverage external expertise; (3) limited budget but available manpower → run company-led recruitment; (4) both limited → re-examine the urgency of hiring.

Once the job posting and channels are ready, start actual recruitment, proceed with selection, and continuously review results. Because recruitment faces the market, many things cannot be known until executed; reviewing and adjusting is the most important factor for achieving results.
If the number of job applications is low, review the job posting wording and the recruitment channels used.
If too many applications come from a different candidate pool than the one sought, review and revise the hiring requirements.
When reflecting on a recruitment process, it is essential to examine both quantity (number of applications) and quality (number of hires/offers made).
Looking at only quantity or only quality does not allow an appropriate judgment of the recruitment effort.
The next topic (Tsubo 033) covers how to create a job posting, which is the first step of the process.
Recruitment (募集) follows a four-step process (募集の4ステップ), presented as Figure 032.
Step 1: Create a job posting / job requisition (求人票を作成する).
Step 2: Choose recruitment channels (募集チャネルを選ぶ).
Step 3: Execute the recruitment activities (実行する).
Step 4: Review and reflect on the process (振り返る).
Listen to the voices of the recruitment market (採用市場の声を聞きましょう).
Personnel introduction / recruitment agencies (人材紹介会社) know the real voices of the market.

A job posting (求人票) is an indispensable unified communication tool in recruitment because many stakeholders are involved: job seekers, internal interviewers, field managers, and external partners such as recruitment agencies and scout agencies. It must clearly show what position is being filled and what skills and mindset are sought.

A well-prepared job posting helps job seekers imagine whether they are a fit and what career they could build at the company. External partners can clearly grasp the criteria for proposing candidates, reducing the risk of introducing mismatched people and thus reducing waste for both company and candidates. Internal interviewers referring to the same information also makes selection criteria more consistent and decision-making smoother.
An effective job posting must appropriately include both what the company wants to convey and what the job seeker wants to know. Missing information can prevent a valuable encounter from happening.

Four key elements to include in a job posting: (1) 職務 (duties/position) — concisely explain why this position is needed now, including organizational or business changes and direction, so candidates can concretely imagine what they could contribute (see ツボ 023).

(2) スキル (skills) — state required vs. preferred abilities and ways of thinking separately, so candidates can judge whether they meet the requirements and so internal teams and agencies share the same understanding (see ツボ 023).

(3) カルチャー・スタンス (culture/stance) — go beyond listing philosophies; show what social issues the company wants to solve and what future it wants to create, so candidates can see whether their own values overlap and feel stronger motivation to apply.

(4) 待遇・働く条件 (compensation and working conditions) — provide information essential for life planning such as salary range, work location, remote-work possibility, and benefits, answering how secure the candidate’s daily life would be in this role.
If items in a job posting (求人情報) are left vague, candidates are more likely to drop out before applying (応募前に離脱), raising the risk of lost applications.
Simply making those items more complete and detailed can often raise the candidate pool's conversion rate into actual applications (応募に至る割合).
The following section (ツボ 034) covers representative recruitment channels (募集チャネル) for effectively delivering job information.

Hiring requirements (採用要件) form a structured framework for defining a role, covering why the position is needed now, required abilities/culture/stance, the organization's aimed worldview, and compensation/working conditions that provide life security for the candidate.
Core question in the framework: なぜ今、このポジションが必要なのか (Why is this position necessary at this time?).
Requirements specify どの能力・カルチャー・スタンス (which abilities, culture, and stance) the candidate must bring.
The organization must communicate どんな世界観を目指しているのか (what worldview or vision it is aiming for).
待遇・働く条件 must address この仕事で生活面はどう安心できるのか (how the job enables a sense of security in daily life).
