Practical checkpoints beyond test quality include usability in operations: (1) Scope of application — whether it is for managers or new graduates, general-purpose or highly specialized; (2) Cost (cost-effectiveness) — evaluate not only per-examinee unit price but also effort for aggregation, analysis, and operation; (3) Burden on examinees — difficult content or long duration affects concentration and motivation; for web-based tests, communication environment and device effects must also be considered.
Before introducing aptitude tests (適性検査), clearly define who, what, and why you are measuring, then choose a test that matches those criteria.
Do not select an aptitude test merely because it is commonly used or famous; examine whether it aligns with the company's talent philosophy (人材観) and selection process.

Select tests using three quality standards—reliability (信頼性), validity (妥当性), and standardization (標準性)—plus practical checkpoints, so aptitude tests become more effective tools for selection and development.
Aptitude tests are tools; outcomes depend on how they are used. Choosing a purpose-fit test that matches the company (“自社にフィットする検査”) is the first step toward successful hiring.
Related sections: various aptitude tests are introduced in ツボ 059; tool limitations are discussed in ツボ 053.
Aptitude tests (適性検査) are judged along three quality criteria (品質基準): Reliability (信頼性), Validity (妥当性), and Standardization (標準性).

Reliability (信頼性) asks how effective and accurate what appears as the test result actually is. A reliability coefficient of 0.8 or above is considered quite high; even if lower, around 0.7 should preferably be secured.

Validity (妥当性) asks whether the test results feel convincing and whether the test truly measures what it intends to measure. A test with low reliability cannot have high validity, but a test with high reliability can still have low validity. Validity is confirmed by analyzing actual employee data or by judging from validity-verification results published by the testing company.

Standardization (標準性) asks whether one can tell at what level the examinee stands within a reference group (example: deviation value / T-score). Even if only one person’s test result is available, it should still be possible to judge that person’s level.
Disclosing inspection quality standards (検査の品質基準を開示すること) is usual/common practice in America (アメリカでは通常です).
In Japan, disclosing inspection quality standards is still rare or uncommon (日本ではまだ珍しいようです).

Aptitude test results are only one indicator of a candidate's personality tendencies and abilities; they are not the entirety of the person and do not necessarily correlate directly with actual job performance.
Work adaptability and on-the-job behavior can change substantially depending on environment, experience, and the individual's own effort.
Treat aptitude-test results as hypotheses and make a comprehensive judgment by combining them with interviews and actual work experience.
Results can be influenced by the test-taker's psychological state and testing environment (e.g., illness or strong tension), so original traits may not be accurately reflected.
Online testing can also be affected by differences in communication environment and devices.
A test captures only a snapshot at that moment in time and must therefore be interpreted flexibly.
Most aptitude tests are self-report instruments, so candidates can deliberately control answers to look favorable to the company (self-report / social-desirability bias).

Example of bias: if a candidate knows the company emphasizes teamwork, they may consciously choose high-cooperativeness responses, creating a gap between scores and actual behavior ("performative answering" or faking).
To detect performative answers, elicit concrete behavioral episodes in interviews and use them as verification.
Aptitude tests measure personal tendencies; they cannot fully predict job-specific skill fit or task-execution ability.
Example: a high score on logical thinking does not automatically imply strong presentation skill or fast decision-making.
Even within the same occupation, the traits required differ according to company culture and management style.
To compensate for the limitations of aptitude tests (適性検査), multiple information sources must be combined rather than relying on tests alone.
Candidates should be understood from multiple angles by combining aptitude tests with specific interview interactions, past job experience, behavioral observation, and reference checks (リファレンスチェック).
Even after hiring, aptitude-test results should be revisited and applied to employee development (育成) and job placement (配置).
Aptitude tests are not omnipotent; they are merely 'one of the tools' (道具のひとつ).
True value comes from not over-relying on aptitude tests and instead devising effective ways to use them.
The following section (ツボ054) addresses combining aptitude tests with interviews for hiring decisions.
Aptitude tests (適性検査) are subject to situational influences and self-report errors, so they must not be treated as absolute; comprehensive judgment is required.
Figure 053 covers the limits of aptitude tests and complementary methods (適性検査の限界と補完手段).
Complementary methods to aptitude testing include interview exchanges (面接のやり取り), behavioral observation (行動観察), and references (リファレンス).
Do not overtrust aptitude/suitability test (適性検査) results in isolation; combine them with other information when forming a judgment.

Aptitude tests (適性検査) should not be used in isolation for hiring decisions; they must be combined with other methods, especially interviews, so each compensates for the other's weaknesses (mutual complementarity).
Aptitude tests provide an objective picture of a candidate's personality tendencies and abilities, but deciding hire/no-hire on the test alone raises the risk of misjudgment.
Interviews enable direct evaluation of a candidate's actual expressions and attitudes, yet they readily admit evaluator subjectivity and bias.
When interview results and aptitude-test results agree, judgment is relatively easy; discrepancies (ズレ) are common and should not be resolved by simply choosing which source is 'correct.'

Investigate the origin of any discrepancy: the candidate may have been unable to display true traits because of tension or environmental factors, or may have been deliberately performing to create a favorable impression.

Share aptitude-test results with interviewers in advance and fold them into question design. Example: if the test flags weak logical thinking, pose a case-study or hypothesis-thinking question and observe the live response.
Example: if the test rates leadership high, probe specific past episodes in depth to verify credibility of the result.
Adopt a dialogic stance ('How do you yourself feel about this?') so that gaps between the candidate's self-perception and the test scores can be explored, yielding deeper person understanding.
Assign complementary roles to the test and the interview and then integrate both sources into a single, holistic hiring judgment.
Aptitude tests (適性検査) and interviews (面接) serve complementary, not opposing, roles in hiring: tests reveal tendencies (傾向を見るもの) while interviews reveal actual/real-world behavior (現実の行動を見るもの).
Tests yield static data (静的データ); interviews yield dynamic observation (動的観察).
Do not treat aptitude-test results as the 'correct answer' from the start. Instead, use them to set specific points to verify in the interview.
Do not be overly swayed by interview impressions; return to the test results and think objectively.
The back-and-forth process between test data and interview observation is what produces higher-accuracy hiring decisions (精度の高い採用判断).
The following section (ツボ 055) addresses how aptitude-test results should be shared internally within the company.
Aptitude tests (適性検査) and interviews (面接) should be combined and used as complementary tools that make up for each other's weaknesses rather than relying on either method in isolation.
Do not overly trust either aptitude-test results or interview impressions alone; integrate both sources of information when making hiring judgments.
Avoid the error of hiring someone solely because their aptitude-test scores indicated high ability.
Avoid the error of hiring someone solely because of what the interviewer personally 'saw through' or discerned during the interview.
The recommended process is to confirm findings thoroughly in the interview and then reach an integrated judgment that combines both the test data and the interview observations.
This combined approach is presented as a practical methodology for more reliable personnel selection in recruitment.
Discrepancies or misalignments (ズレ) and feelings of discomfort or incongruity (違和感) should not be treated as problems.
Such ズレ or 違和感 instead become a chance (チャンス) for dialogue (対話) aimed at understanding the other person.
Key framing: discomfort in interaction is an opening for 対話 rather than a defect to be eliminated.
Aptitude test (適性検査) value is not limited to hiring judgments; results can also be used after joining for development (育成), placement (配置), management, and team building.
To use results beyond hiring, share them with necessary stakeholders and build a system for continuous utilization.
The purpose of sharing aptitude-test results is not 'to judge people' but 'to understand people and help them thrive' (人を理解し、生かすこと).

When sharing, clearly communicate 'why we share' to both related parties and the individual, using positive purposes (e.g., interviews: deeper understanding; assignment: mutual understanding and team building; development: supporting growth).
Information handling must be careful: obtain the person's consent and share only necessary information aligned with the purpose (see related point ツボ 056).

How results are communicated and used should change by role: hiring/interview staff use them to clarify interview checkpoints and raise selection accuracy; assignment managers use personality tendencies, strengths, and cautions for guidance and follow-up; team members use them for mutual understanding and collaboration; HR and executives use them for company-wide talent management, right-person-right-place placement, and development policy.
Share and reinterpret results by stage: before interviews, use results to design questions; after interviews, use them for comprehensive interpretation.
Onboarding (入社時): share key points from aptitude-test data with supervisors and the team to support early adaptation.
Regular evaluations and interviews: keep using the data as ongoing reference material for career development and training.
How aptitude-test data is handled can produce either distrust (不信感) or growth support (成長支援); sharing must therefore be careful and thorough.
Information should be used to free people, not to bind them.
Sharing is not mere data transmission but communication that builds trust (信頼づくり); treating it that way helps aptitude tests take root as a living organizational tool.
The following section (ツボ 056) covers risks and considerations when sharing the data.
Aptitude test (適性検査) results should be shared carefully according to the recipient's role, so they can be utilized in recruitment (採用), assignment/placement (配属), and development/training (育成).
Sharing of aptitude test results is done in order to deeply understand the individual (個を深く理解して) and to 'utilize' or bring them to life (「生かす」).
When sharing aptitude test results, consider who the sharing targets are (だれに / 共有対象者) and why / the main purpose (なぜ / 主な目的).
Figure 055 (図表 055) presents a framework for sharing aptitude tests, structured around sharing targets and main purposes.
Sharing aptitude test (適性検査) results is not for evaluation (評価) but a means of deepening mutual understanding (相互理解) and trust (信頼).
Key statement: 適性検査結果の共有は、評価ではなく相互理解と信頼を深める手段です

When sharing aptitude test (適性検査) results inside an organization, four main risks must be managed: personal information leakage, incorrect interpretation and use, decline in morale and distrust, and bias/discrimination.

Personal information leakage: aptitude tests contain personality and behavioral tendencies, so oversharing can violate privacy. Define handling rules for paper, email, and internal systems; strictly limit access; disclose only to defined roles (hiring staff, interviewers, supervisors, HR); and enforce log management and security controls.

Incorrect interpretation and use: non-experts can misread results and cause mismatched evaluations or placements. Share measurement items and proper usage through internal training, verify results from multiple angles, and never treat the test as the whole of a person’s ability—combine it with interviews and actual performance, using results only as a complement, because people grow and situations change.

Decline in morale and distrust: if sharing scope or purpose is opaque, the person may fear that only their weaknesses will spread. Explain in advance who will see the results and why, and obtain consent before sharing.

Bias and discrimination: data bias or algorithmic problems in the test itself can disadvantage certain attributes. Do not uniformly conclude that a given type is unsuited for management; periodically verify and correct the instrument to ensure fairness, and select high-quality aptitude tests.

Core principle: thorough information-management rules plus a clearly stated purpose of use let both the organization and the individual use aptitude tests with confidence. Relationship management (関係性のマネジメント) is part of this process.
Sharing aptitude test results (適性検査結果の共有) is simultaneously information management (情報の管理) and relationship management (関係性のマネジメント).
Practitioners must maintain the awareness that they are handling people, not data, and therefore operate with care and respect (丁寧な運用).
Always keep the perspective of bringing out the best in people / making people thrive (人を生かす).
The next section (ツボ 057) covers methods for giving feedback to the individual themselves.

Four main risks of using aptitude/personality test (適性検査) results in HR and personnel decisions: (1) personal information leakage, (2) incorrect interpretation and utilization, (3) decline in morale and distrust, and (4) bias and discrimination.

Risk of personal information leakage: Test results contain sensitive information such as personality tendencies and behavioral characteristics. Sharing too much detail can cause privacy violations and information leaks.

Countermeasures for information leakage include limiting sharing to the minimum necessary people (hiring staff, interviewers, supervisors, HR); sharing only key-point summaries rather than detailed results; strengthening system controls (access rights, logging, encryption); and setting clear internal handling rules and guidelines.

Risk of incorrect interpretation and utilization: Treating test results as if they equal a person's entire ability leads to mismatches in assignment and evaluation and distorts the original purpose of aptitude testing.

Countermeasures for misinterpretation include combining tests with interviews, work performance, and the person's own wishes (comprehensive judgment); training supervisors and interviewers on correct interpretation; using checklists to prevent misuse; and later re-interviews or re-evaluations to check whether judgments remain valid.
Risk of morale decline and distrust: If examinees worry about how results are used and who sees them, they may feel that only their weaknesses are known, damaging trust and motivation.

Countermeasures for morale and distrust include explaining purpose, usage scope, and sharing destinations in advance and obtaining consent; giving the person feedback on key results to increase acceptance; framing results around strengths and how to use them; and building a team culture of confidentiality and ethics around personal data.

Risk of bias and discrimination: Bias in the test itself or in how it is used can produce unfavorable judgments against attributes such as gender, age, or personality type, promoting unfair discrimination and stereotypes.

Countermeasures for bias include selecting tests that have been bias-checked and are reliable; banning blanket rules such as 'XX type = unsuitable'; periodically comparing test results with actual performance to reassess validity; and using tests supportively to leverage diverse personalities rather than to exclude.

Core operating principle: aptitude-test results should never be used in isolation; they are one input among interviews, performance, and individual preference, and must be handled with privacy minimization, informed consent, and ongoing validity checks.
Any tool always has inherent risks associated with it.
Tools should be utilized only after implementing correct operational practices and appropriate countermeasures.
Quote: どんなツールにも必ずリスクがあります。正しい運用と対策を講じて活用しましょう

Feedbacking aptitude test (適性検査) results to the examinee themselves deepens their self-understanding (自己理解) and can connect to future work styles and growth, but it can feel abrupt in cultures where such feedback is not common, and incorrect delivery can backfire.

Promote self-understanding through dialogue rather than one-way judgment: instead of telling someone 'You are like this,' ask 'How do you feel about this?' Treat test results not as a fixed evaluation but as 'seeds of awareness' (気づきの種).

Start by asking what insights the person themselves had from taking the test, to grasp their interpretation and underlying assumptions; then compare those with the results using comments such as 'this matches' or 'there is a bit of a gap here' so awareness deepens naturally.

Focus first on strengths even when results also contain challenging traits; use positive phrasing (e.g., ability to carefully build relationships, ability to work steadily at one's own pace) so the person can gain confidence.

Connect strengths to concrete work contexts by jointly considering in which workplaces or situations they come alive; relating results to actual duties and behavior (e.g., a cautious tendency as a strength in quality-control work that requires detailed checking) helps the person specifically imagine the value their tendencies create.
Deepen the conversation by drawing out the person's own work experiences and episodes so the feedback feels convincing and owned.

Close feedback by jointly considering how the person will use the insights going forward, with questions such as in what future situations a given trait could be utilized or how it could support growth.
Through questions such as 「取り組んでみたいことはありますか？」 (Is there something you would like to try/work on?), it is important that the person themselves leaves with seeds of action (アクションの種).
Do not become bound by or overly focused on inspection/test results (検査結果にとらわれるのではなく).
The essence of feedback is the process of thinking 「ここから自分をどう伸ばしていくか」 (how to grow/develop yourself from here).
The next tip (ツボ 058) covers points that require caution when giving this kind of feedback.
When giving feedback on examination/assessment results, communicate with a focus on the person's strengths (強みを中心に伝え).
The goal of such feedback is to create dialogue that becomes a trigger for self-understanding (自己理解) and growth (成長).
Practitioners should keep in mind conducting dialogue that supports self-understanding and growth rather than one-way reporting of scores.
Figure 057 outlines a method for feeding back examination results (検査結果のフィードバック方法).

Core elements of the feedback method include: conducting it through dialogue; conveying results with strengths at the center; linking results to practical/work experience (実務経験と結びつける); and jointly considering future actions (今後の行動を一緒に考える).
Rather than explaining results, it is more effective to use questions that promote awareness or insight (気づき).
Key principle: 結果を「説明」するのではなく、気づきを促す「問い」が効果的です

When feeding back aptitude test (適性検査) results, avoid giving a negative impression; mentioning issues or cautions can cause examinees to lose confidence or become defensive depending on how it is phrased.
Rephrase negatives into constructive, forward-looking language: instead of saying 'you have low leadership,' say something like 'you tend to proceed while cooperating with those around you.'

Aptitude tests indicate tendencies (傾向), not definitive identity statements such as 'you are this kind of person.' Do not apply fixed labels (e.g., 'introverted person,' 'person weak to stress') because they can restrict the examinee's perceived potential for growth.
Use flexible wording such as 'there is a tendency to…' or 'seems able to demonstrate strength in … situations' rather than categorical descriptions.

If results differ from the examinee's self-recognition, do not communicate unilaterally; ask 'How did you feel about this result?' to draw out their perspective and real experiences, then jointly interpret the meaning of the results through dialogue.

Abstract diagnoses are hard for examinees to internalize; explicitly link results to actual work (実務) so they feel relevant. Example: 'A cautious tendency can be a strength in quality-control work.' This increases conviction and a concrete image of how to use the result.
Clarify the purpose of the feedback itself so the session has a clear aim.
When giving feedback on aptitude-test (適性検査) results, clearly tell the person that the feedback is not for evaluating them but for supporting their growth.
Key message to state: 「このフィードバックはあなたを評価するためではなく、成長を支援するためのものです」 (This feedback is not to evaluate you, but to support your growth).
If the purpose is clear, examinees (受検者) find it easier to accept results in a positive, forward-looking way.
Treat the test not as a “決めつける道具” (a tool for labeling or judging people) but as a “気づきのきっかけ” (a trigger for awareness/insight).
How you communicate (伝え方) can change the meaning of the same test results.
Value dialogue that respects the other person and shines a light on the possibility of change and growth.
The next key point (ツボ 059) covers how to choose aptitude tests.

When communicating assessment or test results, avoid creating a negative impression; instead, convey information in a way that values the examinee's sense of conviction (納得感) and motivation for growth (成長意欲).
Avoid labeling (レッテル貼り): do not attach fixed, limiting trait names that close off possibilities for the person.
Principle: avoid labeling and use expressions that open up possibilities rather than shutting them down.
Example of harmful labeling to avoid: 'Because you are introverted, sales work is impossible.'
Example of harmful labeling to avoid: 'You have low stress tolerance.'
Constructive alternative phrasing: describe a tendency as 'You have a tendency to be sensitive to change and careful' rather than a fixed negative label.
Constructive alternative phrasing: highlight capability as 'You have the ability to concentrate and respond carefully' instead of implying a deficit.
Peter F. Drucker, in The Effective Executive (経営者の条件), states the principle 「強みの上に築け」 (Build on strengths / Build upon strengths).
The core idea is that effective executives and managers should concentrate effort on existing strengths rather than trying to remediate weaknesses as the primary strategy.
Aptitude tests (適性検査) are not a single type; they differ by what they measure, design philosophy, target job types, and applicant groups, and each has distinct strengths and purposes.
Companies should not default to famous tests; they must select tests that match their own hiring strategy and job requirements.
SPI3 (Recruit Management Solutions) combines an ability test and a personality test and is the most widely used general-purpose aptitude test among Japanese companies.
Tamatebako / GAB (Japan SHL) has high adoption at large firms, especially foreign-affiliated companies and comprehensive-job hiring, and emphasizes thinking ability and processing speed.
I-Dats (Diamond) diagnoses motivational factors and behavioral characteristics and is used mainly for potential evaluation of mid-level and more senior employees.
Caliper Profile (Human Strategies Japan) supports 24 languages and is suited to globally expanding companies and multinational projects.
CUBIC (DDL) analyzes job aptitude and organizational adaptability from multiple angles and is also useful for interview support and post-placement use.
TG-WEB (Humanage) is a fully web-based ability test that can be customized per company and measures logical ability and reading comprehension.
Mitsukari is a cloud-based aptitude test focused on organizational culture and team compatibility, with a strength in culture-fit judgment.
Attel is an AI- and psychology-based talent-analysis platform featuring job-suitability prediction and matching functions.
No aptitude test is universal: SPI3 is broadly general-purpose, while CUBIC and Mitsukari are chosen to match organizational characteristics.
Selection should be driven by what the company wants to emphasize in hiring and which job types the test will be used for.
A practical approach is to review vendor comparison materials and user-company feedback, then trial the test internally to confirm fit.
Aptitude tests embody a company’s view of talent (人材観).
Assessment tests (検査) function as a “translation device” (翻訳装置) for hiring strategy, converting organizational values into selection criteria.
They are tools for answering the core question: 「何を大切にして人を選びたいのか」 (“What do we want to value when selecting people?”).
Organizations should identify the assessment that best fits those values rather than treating tests as generic filters.
Subsequent section ツボ 060 will examine how such tests are expected to evolve.
Japanese recruitment uses a variety of aptitude tests (適性検査), including SPI, 玉手箱 (Tamatesbako), and CUBIC; the appropriate test is chosen according to the hiring purpose.

図表 059 is a comparative list of major commercial aptitude tests used in Japan, covering providers, annual/cumulative usage (companies and test-takers), and quality notes on reliability (信頼性) and validity (妥当性).
Quality notation in the list: tests with sufficient verification of quality, those with supporting evidence, those that mainly present a conceptual framework, or blank when no information was found.
SPI3 (Recruit Management Solutions) is among the largest, used by about 14,400 companies per year and 2.15 million people per year.

Other high-volume tools include GAB (SHL Japan / 日本エス・エイチ・エル), tests from Diamond, CUBIC, 3Eテスト (en Japan), ミツカリ, Compass, SCOA, ミキワメ, TG-WEB, アッテル, 内田クレペリン検査 (Uchida-Kraepelin test), BRIDGE, eF-1G, Advantage Insight, MARCO POLO, TAP, CPAG/CPAB, HCi-ab, and GROW採用.
The Uchida-Kraepelin inspection (内田クレペリン検査, 日本・精神技術研究所) remains a listed major aptitude measure, with usage on the order of hundreds of thousands of people per year.
The compiled comparison draws on Yoshida Yosuke’s “主要採用適性検査一覧” spreadsheet as source material.
If you become lost or confused by a large quantity (of data, options, or variables), first clearly define what you actually want to measure.
Recent initial screening of aptitude tests has rapidly expanded use of AI and big data.

Yokohama Bank uses the AI engine KIBIT to score enthusiasm and aspiration from entry sheets, cutting document screening time by about 70 percent; correlation with highly rated field employees has been confirmed.

SoftBank trained AI on internship videos and evaluation data so that AI performs pass/fail judgments for new-graduate first interviews, while retaining an HR confirmation process and achieving large efficiency gains.
Key concerns include the black-box problem (opaque AI decision criteria) and bias arising from skewed training data.
HireVue discontinued facial-recognition interview evaluation in 2020 after concluding it did not improve predictive accuracy.
Companies that introduce AI are expected to conduct internal audits and third-party verification to meet fairness and accountability obligations.

Personalized test design according to individual characteristics is advancing; computer adaptive testing (CAT) adjusts item difficulty based on the examinee's right or wrong answers, enabling high-precision ability measurement in a short time.
Services such as Mikiwame (Reading Mark) learn the profiles of currently successful employees and score applicant similarity, allowing evaluation of culture fit that generic tests often miss.
Telework and international talent acquisition have made remote delivery of aptitude tests essential.
Akitafuzu introduced Japan's first AI interview, substantially lowering application barriers for candidates from rural or distant locations.
Online testing raises cheating risk, prompting adoption of remote proctoring (distant monitoring).
HirePro reports that AI monitoring of voice, video, and screen activity achieves a fraud-detection rate of 98 percent.
Future aptitude tests (適性検査) are expected to evolve toward enhancing three core elements: efficiency (効率性), accuracy (正確性), and flexibility (柔軟性).
As testing technology becomes more advanced, governance (ガバナンス) is indispensable and must cover personal information protection (個人情報保護), accountability (説明責任), and ethics (倫理性).
Aptitude tests should not be used merely as pass/fail judgment material; they should function as infrastructure for “adaptation” (適応) that nurtures the relationship between people and organizations.
To make effective use of test results, it will become increasingly important to prepare an environment defined by purpose (目的), dialogue (対話), and trust relationships (信頼関係).
The subsequent chapter (Chapter 7) addresses the topic of adaptation (適応).
While utilizing technology, it is important to carefully cultivate human sensibility and the ability to truly see people (技術を活用しつつ、人を見る感性を大切に育てましょう).
Technology should be applied as a tool without replacing or diminishing interpersonal awareness and human-centered observation.
Chapter 6 of this material summarizes aptitude testing (適性検査) with role-specific messages for executives, field managers, hiring staff, and all working members, plus a Q&A overview of points 051–060.

For executives: aptitude tests must be judged by how they contribute to strategy, not treated as a cost. Understand the role and selection criteria of tests (points 051–052) and grasp their evolution and ethical risks in the AI era (point 060).

Hiring decisions—who to recruit—are strategic choices that define the future organization. Tests should be positioned as a “value-creation device” (価値創出装置) and given a clear place in the organization.

For field managers: the priority is understanding and leveraging subordinates’ characteristics. Combine test results with interviews (point 054), share results in ways that support management (point 055), and practice feedback methods (points 057–058).
Managers should read aptitude-test results as growth support rather than as evaluation; the sensibility to interpret results for development is more important than using them only to rate people.

Hiring staff are responsible for how tests are chosen and used. Master basic selection axes (051–052), limitations and complementary methods (053), concrete interview linkage (054), and tool comparison/selection viewpoints (059).
Hiring quality depends on “middle-ground” discernment (目利き力): neither over-reliance on tools nor purely personal judgment.
For all working people, aptitude tests (適性検査) are 'hints to know yourself and make the most of yourself' (自分を知り、自分を活かすヒント).
Tip 057 (ツボ057) covers how to receive interactive/dialogical feedback that deepens self-understanding (自己理解を深める対話的なフィードバックの受け取り方).
Tip 058 (ツボ058) covers a reading method that is not bound by labels (レッテル) and that opens up one's own possibilities.
Aptitude tests are not 'evaluations' (評価) but 'questions' (問い).
Changing how one reads aptitude-test results can change one's way of working and even one's confidence.
Aptitude tests should be engaged with carefully as an aid to self-growth (自己成長の一助).
The following Chapter 7 addresses adaptation (適応).
Aptitude tests (適性検査) are numerous and hard for hiring managers to differentiate; many therefore adopt heavily advertised or cheaper products under the assumption that they are essentially the same.
The quality of an aptitude test is judged by its validity (妥当性)—the correspondence between test results and the intended criterion.

Naito Jun (Recruit Management Solutions, Personnel Measurement Research Institute) researches psychological assessment, organizational-diagnosis tools, and HR-data analysis; he identifies validity as the primary check for whether an aptitude test is good or bad.
The conversation frames three judgment axes for selecting aptitude tests, beginning with validity as the first and most fundamental criterion.
The most important criterion when choosing an aptitude test (適性検査) is confirming how valid and accurate the traits that appear in the results actually are.
If a company already has a track record of using aptitude tests, accumulated employee data should be used first: analyze those results and confirm validity before selecting or continuing with a test.

Validation method with existing data: exclude people who have already left the company; among remaining employees, compare average scores of the high-performing group versus the non-high-performing group.

Examine whether high performers share common features in their aptitude-test results and whether those tendencies are intuitively convincing (examples: people with very high motivation succeeding, or people with good agility/footwork succeeding).

The observed differences between high- and low-performer groups should be something one can agree represents the real characteristics of people who succeed in that company; alignment between lived experience and statistical results is the most important check.

For companies with little internal data (e.g., those just starting to hire at scale), Recruit Management Solutions recommends three judgment axes for aptitude-test quality: reliability (信頼性), validity (妥当性), and standardness (標準性).
Reliability (信頼性) means stability of the test as a measuring instrument: repeated measurements of the same person should yield nearly the same scores.

A practical reliability check is to have the same person take the test twice; the closer the two scores, the higher the reliability. Perfect identity is rare, but large score swings from one administration to the next should not occur.
Reliability is expressed by the reliability coefficient (信頼性係数). Test publishers normally disclose it; for the SPI series it is typically 0.8–0.9.

A coefficient of 1.0 would mean identical results every time, which is unrealistic; no real test reaches 1.0. A coefficient of 0.8 or higher is considered quite high; at least around 0.7 is desirable, otherwise score fluctuation across sittings becomes too large.

When selecting a test, prefer those that disclose a reliability coefficient calculated from a large sample and whose value is sufficiently high; tests that do not publish the coefficient should be treated with caution.
Attention should also be paid to the relationship between reliability and validity when evaluating aptitude tests.

Validity (妥当性) in aptitude/psychological testing means whether one can be convinced by or accept the test results—for example, whether a convincing, sensible relationship exists between employees’ actual performance/success and their scores on the test.

Reliability (信頼性) and validity (妥当性) are related but distinct: a test with low reliability cannot have high validity. However, even a test with very high reliability can still have low validity, so this distinction requires caution.

Classic analogy: a weighing scale (体重計) has extremely high reliability (near 1) because two consecutive measurements produce almost identical values. If that same scale were used as an aptitude test claiming to measure ‘job-performance ability’ (職務遂行能力), its validity would be extremely low.
These points come from HR/psychometric discussion of aptitude tests (適性検査) used in corporate hiring and personnel assessment.

Aptitude-test (適性検査) development for series such as PT and SPI pursued two conflicting goals at once: scientific backing (科学的な裏付け) required because the tools support important personnel decisions, and practical usability so that HR staff without specialist psychological-test expertise can still apply them; this dual aim was pursued over roughly 60 years of practice.

SPI-series reports include verbalized ‘person-characteristic comments’ so that users who lack skill or experience in reading raw scores and profiles can still understand results; the comments are not mere automatic output.

Comment development process: actual individuals’ test results are read, manuscripts are written on the basis of personality theory, accuracy is checked via feedback from the person and those around them, and the wording is repeatedly revised while reviewing employees’ results—a grounded, iterative craft rather than a purely algorithmic dump.
The weight placed on the reaction ‘当たっている!’ (‘It’s accurate!’) and the founding philosophy of ‘個をあるがままに生かす’ (letting each individual live as they are) guided the work.

Inside Recruit, personality-test results were once used openly as culture: types appeared in the company newsletter, were printed on the backs of business cards, and were used to form sports-day teams; the stated reason was simply that it was interesting (面白い).

Aptitude tests are not only instruments for hiring and evaluation; they function as triggers for mutual understanding. In interviews, development, and education, results generate dialogue that expands the process of knowing oneself and knowing others; that usage is where the tests’ original power is realized.
The ‘面白さ’ (interestingness) of mutual understanding through aptitude-test results is presented as something worth spreading beyond specialist HR use.
Recruitment activities should be designed not only up to the job offer (内定) but to include post-joining retention and active contribution (入社後の定着と活躍).
Onboarding design should be based on the psychology and behavior of new hires (入社者の心理・行動).
A connecting perspective between CX (Candidate Experience / 候補者体験) and EX (Employee Experience / 従業員体験) is essential.
Even an ideal support model is hard to execute without collaboration with the workplace/field (現場との連携).
Treating extensive onboarding support as 'just normal/expected' can increase the sense of burden.
Chapter 7 theme is 'adaptation' (適応) in corporate organizations, covering two levels: an organization's adaptation to society/external environment, and an individual's adaptation to the organization.

Organizational Adaptation (組織適応 / Organizational Adaptation) is when an organization (e.g., a company) adapts to social and external conditions such as market changes, customer needs, technological innovation, and laws/institutions.

Definition of organizational adaptation (Sarta, Durand, & Vergne, 2021, Journal of Management): it is intentional decision-making by organizational members that leads to observable actions aimed at reducing the distance between the organization and its economic and institutional environment.

When a firm perceives a 'gap' or misalignment with the external environment, it adjusts strategy, structure, products, and talent so that it can 'connect well' with that environment—this self-changing process is organizational adaptation.

Individual adaptation to a new workplace is Organizational Socialization (組織社会化 / Organizational Socialization): not only learning tasks, but acquiring the attitudes, knowledge, skills, and behaviors needed to function as an organizational member.

Definition of organizational socialization (Bauer & Erdogan, 2011, APA Handbook of Industrial and Organizational Psychology): the process by which newcomers learn the attitudes, knowledge, skills, and behaviors necessary to function effectively within an organization.

Socialization includes understanding the organization's 'way of doing things' and culture, building relationships with supervisors and colleagues, handling implicit workplace rules, and gradually becoming able to produce results.
Organizational socialization (組織社会化) refers to the adaptation of individuals to organizations (個人の組織への適応).
Subsequent discussion focuses mainly on organizational socialization.
Individuals adapt to organizations along three aspects, which are to be confirmed next (ツボ 062).
Two-stage model of adaptation in organizations consists of Organizational Socialization (組織社会化) followed by Organizational Adaptation (組織適応).
The process involves both the organization and the individual as interacting parties.
Organizational socialization is the earlier stage in which a person learns to function within the organization; organizational adaptation is the subsequent stage of fitting in more fully.
A practical self-reflection prompt associated with the model: recall the specific moment when you first felt “I can make it / I can go on in this organization” (「この組織でやっていける」と感じた瞬間).

The International Adjustment Model (Black, Mendenhall, & Oddou, 1991) describes how individuals adapt to a new organizational environment. Originally developed with cross-cultural adjustment in mind, it is now widely applied to the adaptation processes of new hires, transferees, and newcomers within organizations.
Individuals adapt along three interrelated aspects: work adjustment, interaction adjustment, and general environment (organizational culture) adjustment.

Work adjustment means understanding the content and methods of a new job and becoming able to fulfill required roles. It includes grasping tools, procedures, and evaluation criteria so work can proceed without mistakes. The core is rapidly acquiring necessary skills and knowledge in order to work independently.

Interaction adjustment means building trust with supervisors, colleagues, and people in other departments so that communication can occur with a sense of security. It also includes becoming accustomed to the hard-to-verbalize workplace “atmosphere,” such as conversation style within the team, timing of reports, and the mood of casual talk. Smooth interpersonal relations strongly affect how easily work can be carried out.

General environment adjustment (organizational-culture adjustment) means becoming accustomed to the organization’s unique values, climate, and customs. Examples include judgment criteria such as “speed-focused” versus “caution-focused,” as well as dress, working style, and meeting procedures that form the background of daily work. In some cases it also includes getting used to the local region or lifestyle of the workplace.

The three aspects appear independent but are closely interconnected. Memorizing job content while interpersonal relations remain awkward makes it hard to produce results; conversely, a sense of security in relationships makes it easier to consult about work problems. Failure in any one aspect can delay overall adaptation.
To work with peace of mind in a new workplace, it is important to consciously identify, across these three viewpoints, where one already feels comfortable and where anxiety remains.
Finding an adaptation approach that fits the individual is the first step toward suitable adaptation.
The next section (point 063) covers onboarding (オンボーディング) as a method that supports adaptation.
Individuals must become accustomed to all three aspects of a new organization: work/business (業務), human relationships (人間関係), and organizational culture (組織文化).

Work adjustment (業務への適応 / Work adjustment) means becoming able to fulfill expected roles in a new organization or job by getting used to the content, methods, and required skills of the work. This includes understanding job procedures and tools; grasping performance goals and KPIs and taking actions toward them; and understanding decision-making processes and role divisions so as to follow the flow of work.

Interaction adjustment (人間関係への適応 / Interaction adjustment) means reaching a state in which one can interact and collaborate with confidence with supervisors, colleagues, other departments, customers, and similar parties. This includes getting used to communication styles (honorific language, small talk, meeting styles); understanding one's standing within the team and non-verbal rules (the 'air' or atmosphere); and becoming able to build relationships of trust and psychological safety.

General environment / organizational-culture adjustment (組織文化への適応 / General environment adjustment) means fitting into implicit environmental elements such as values, climate, ways of working, and daily habits so that one can spend time without a sense of discomfort. This includes understanding organizational culture and values (for example speed-emphasis vs. deliberation-emphasis, top-down vs. bottom-up) and understanding plus adapting to elements that affect daily life, such as morning assemblies, attendance customs, dress codes, and the nature of after-work drinking gatherings.
Anxiety (不安) often conceals an underlying 'expectation' or hope (期待) in its depths.
A useful practice is to deliberately turn awareness toward that hidden expectation, not only toward the anxiety itself.
Key statement: 「不安の奥にある『期待』にも意識を向けてみましょう」 (Let's also try directing our awareness toward the 'expectation' that lies deep within the anxiety.)

Onboarding is a series of processes that support newly joined employees so they can smoothly adapt to the workplace and their duties and become productive early. It is not limited to joining procedures or training; it is strategic, continuous support until the newcomer can safely thrive as a member of the organization.

Academic definition (Talya N. Bauer, 2010): Onboarding is the mechanism by which new employees acquire the knowledge, skills, and behaviors needed to become effective members of the organization. Source: Onboarding New Employees: Maximizing Success, SHRM Foundation. The key idea is that it is a systematic, planned mechanism companies should prepare.

Bauer's 4C model of onboarding consists of four pillars that should be supported in balance: Compliance (understanding employment rules, internal rules, and basic systems); Clarification (clarifying assigned work and expected roles); Connection (forming networks with colleagues, supervisors, and related departments); Culture (understanding and embodying organizational values and behavioral norms). Note: the source text misspells Culture as Caulture.

When the four areas of the 4C model are supported in a balanced way, newcomers can work with confidence earlier, turnover risk decreases, and engagement and productivity increase. The 4C model can be related to three aspects of individual adaptation.
Common onboarding challenges in many companies include stopping after a joining-day explanation meeting only, or leaving the process entirely to the workplace without standardization.
Onboarding (オンボーディング) should be viewed as an integral part of strategic human resource management (戦略的な人的資源管理), not as an isolated administrative task.
Onboarding is a mechanism/system designed to help new employees take root in the organization and become able to fully demonstrate their abilities.

Onboarding is not merely an initial-response or orientation process; it is a critical organizational investment that directly affects employee engagement, retention (定着率), and performance, and thus the future of the organization.
Companies must strategically design the onboarding process in order to raise the experiential value of starting work (働きはじめの体験価値) for new hires.
The book next introduces specific 4C initiatives for onboarding; the first (ツボ 064) is Compliance, defined as understanding of rules (規則理解).
Individual adaptation in organizations has three aspects: work adjustment (業務への適応), interaction adjustment (人間関係への適応), and general environment adjustment (組織文化への適応).
Companies support individual adaptation through organizational mechanisms, mapped to the onboarding 4C model.
The onboarding 4C model (Bauer 2010) consists of Compliance, Clarification, Connection, and Culture.
Compliance supports rule understanding: employment regulations, internal rules, and basic institutional systems (就業規則・社内ルールなど基本的な制度の理解).
Clarification supports work adjustment via role clarification: making assigned duties and expected roles clear (担当業務や期待される役割の明確化).
Connection supports interaction adjustment via relationship building: forming networks with colleagues, supervisors, and related departments (同僚・上司・関係部署とのネットワーク形成).
Culture supports general environment adjustment via culture sharing: understanding and embodying organizational values and behavioral norms (組織の価値観・行動規範の理解と体現).
Original Bauer (2010) orders the model as Culture then Connection; this source reorders to Connection then Culture to emphasize the individual's adaptation process and improve understandability.

New employees' voices (新入社員の声) should be regarded as a treasure trove (宝庫) of improvement (改善); organizations should actively listen to and value the fresh perspectives of newcomers as a source of kaizen and process betterment.

Compliance (規則理解) is the first element of onboarding. Its purpose is for new employees to correctly understand the company's basic rules, systems, employment regulations, and compliance-related knowledge so they can work with peace of mind. This is the 'foundation building' for functioning as a member of the organization.

If Compliance is insufficient, anxieties easily arise such as 'I don't know what I am allowed to do' or 'I am afraid of violating rules.' Conversely, if items such as employment regulations, information security, and harassment prevention are properly communicated, new employees can act with confidence, which also connects to preventing early turnover and improving engagement.

Oracle Japan implements a 5-week onboarding training especially for experienced (mid-career) hires. In the first week, in addition to company history and business explanation, there are sessions that carefully explain employment regulations, internal systems, and basic Compliance matters. Practical content such as expense reimbursement and attendance rules is also included so that new hires can approach work with peace of mind.

At Oracle Japan, each new employee is assigned a senior employee called a 'Navigator' who provides practical follow-up during work. Navigators serve as someone new hires can casually consult about judgments in gray-area situations and how to apply the rules, thereby supporting the establishment of Compliance.

Oracle Japan's onboarding system is operated by a specialized Employee Engagement Office team that consistently handles design, implementation, and follow-up. This structure contributes to resolving anxiety in the early joining period, enabling early productivity, and improving retention rates.

LINE Yahoo provides a mechanism, regardless of new-graduate or mid-career status, for new joiners to learn about information security, harassment prevention, and internal systems through orientation and e-learning at the time of joining.
LINE Yahoo has also prepared a 'Welcome Guide' (受け入れの手引き) for departmental OJT staff and mentors, so that 'preparation on the receiving side' is rooted as part of the culture.
Compliance is supported not by unilaterally teaching people, but by a mechanism that lets them confirm things themselves and put them into practice.
Whether a company verbalizes and shares its rules and designs an appropriate way of communicating them greatly influences the success or failure of onboarding.
The next section (ツボ 065) covers specific initiatives for Clarification (役割明確化 / role clarification).

Compliance (規則理解 / rule understanding) support should target not only comprehension (“わかる”) but a usable (“使える”) state in actual work; delivery and support must enable practice inside real tasks rather than explanation alone (e.g., live demonstration of expense reimbursement / 経費精算, exercises for attendance input / 勤怠入力).
Work adjustment (業務への適応) is a core compliance-support pillar: rules must be taught so they can be applied on the job without remaining abstract knowledge.

Consultation destinations must be explicit: when staff are unsure about the *operation* of a rule, they need a named navigator or mentor they can ask immediately; that presence creates psychological safety.

On-site / receiving-side readiness (現場体制の整備) is required, not only newcomer training: the workplace itself must correctly understand systems and policies so explanations and responses stay consistent (e.g., prepare an acceptance / onboarding manual / 受け入れマニュアル).
Three interlocking points for compliance support: (1) make rules actually usable in work, (2) make who-to-ask crystal clear, (3) prepare the host organization so it can give aligned guidance.
The establishment and maintenance of employment regulations (就業規則) and workplace rules is directly connected to protecting both individuals and the organization.
Properly developed work rules serve a dual protective function: they safeguard employees and they safeguard the organization itself.
Clarification (役割明確化) is the second pillar of onboarding: new employees clearly understand their job content, area of responsibility, expected results, and behavioral standards.

The core point of role-clarification support is sharing what is expected so the newcomer understands with conviction what role they play in the organization and where they should contribute—not merely assigning tasks.
Insufficient Clarification leaves newcomers unsure what to do and how far their responsibility extends, producing anxiety and hesitation.
When one’s role is clear, proactive action becomes easier and supports early results and retention.

Connehito (operator of the parenting app Mamari) shares a Mission Letter at the job-offer stage (before joining) stating 90-day expectations, including expected behaviors and desired relationships with others; the document is shared among the newcomer, the workplace, and HR.

After joining, Connehito uses regular interviews and reviews to align expectations with actual behavior, creating a state in which surroundings share the same expectations, which reduces isolation and misunderstanding and enables action with peace of mind.
i-plug (operator of OfferBox) aligns goals and evaluation: the evaluation system is used as a growth-support tool via 1-on-1 meetings every two months rather than as a mere assessment device.

In i-plug’s 1-on-1s, the direct team leader checks how much has been achieved and what support is needed, with communication that values the newcomer’s motivation and sense of buy-in; meeting results feed directly into formal evaluation so that ‘what should be done’ is clearly ‘what is evaluated,’ which is a source of security for newcomers.

What matters in newcomer–supervisor relationships is not eliminating ambiguity, but including ambiguous matters and having regular dialogue so that both parties raise the resolution (clarity) of roles and expectations over time.
Not everything becomes clear immediately after a new employee joins; therefore continuous alignment (すりあわせ) and confirmation between newcomer and supervisor are required.
Clarification (役割明確化 / role clarification) is a distinct practice whose specific initiatives are treated as a follow-on topic.

Clarification (役割明確化 / role clarification) is a core support process for work adjustment of new employees. It has three linked points: verbalizing expectations, alignment through dialogue, and linkage with evaluation.

Verbalize expectations concretely rather than abstractly. Phrases such as “I want you to work hard” or “I want you to grow” are insufficient. Instead, state specific behaviors and outcome goals and share them in the early stage around joining. Clarify what to do, how much, with whom, and why. This reduces new-hire anxiety and creates a foundation for acting with confidence. Examples: 90-day goals, mission letters, role description documents.

Roles are not fixed. They must be adjusted as business understanding and team conditions change. Repeat confirmation dialogues such as “This is how I understand it—is that correct?” with supervisors or buddies so the “resolution” of the role increases. In the first month especially, provide high-frequency feedback and an environment that makes questions easy. Examples: 1on1s, weekly check-ins, buddy meetings.

Clear roles only translate into action if people understand how the work will be evaluated. Do not treat the evaluation system as a mere appraisal tool. Use 1on1s and similar conversations so it supports the new hire’s goal understanding and growth. Examples: goal-management sheets, 1on1s, OKRs.
制度や人の支援は「見える化」すると効果があがります: Institutional systems and human support become more effective when they are visualized or made visible (見える化).
オンボーディングの3つ目の柱であるConnection（人間関係構築）は、新入社員が上司・同僚・他部門のメンバーと信頼関係を築き、安心して相談・協働できる環境に馴染んでいくプロセスを指す。
「誰に聞けるか」「誰とつながっているか」は、早期の適応や活躍に直結する。新入社員が孤立すると不安や焦りから成果が出づらくなる一方、些細なことでも話せる相手がいることでミスの早期発見、学びの加速、自信の形成が促される。

ホワイトプラス（宅配クリーニング「Lenet」）の事例：新入社員の“歓迎体験”をデザインする仕組みとして、入社初日に会社ロゴ入りTシャツやステッカーなどのグッズが入った「ウェルカムボックス」を渡し、「あなたを歓迎しています」というメッセージを視覚的に伝える。さらに「ウェルカムランチ制度」で部署を越えて様々な社員とランチに行けるよう10回分のランチ費用を会社が負担し、短期間で多様なつながり、質問しやすい関係性、社内の非正式なナレッジへのアクセスを可能にする。

GMOペパボの事例：「新しい人を全員で歓迎する文化」が根づいており、中途入社者が加わると社内チャットの「カクテルチャンネル」に自動追加され、既存社員が即座にコメントを送りランチに誘う・雑談を始めるなどのアクションが活発に起こる。金曜日の勉強会「ペパボテックフライデー」や社内キッチンカーイベント「ランチワゴン」などを通じ部署を越えた交流が促進され、新人が自らつながりを築きにいかなくても自然と対話が生まれる“接点の設計”として機能する。
人間関係構築の支援は人事主導ではなく、組織全体で支えることがポイントである。
The essence of Connection is not making people get along with each other, but preventing isolation and creating an environment where people can speak up with peace of mind.
For Connection to work, receiving-side employees must be prepared as people it is okay to approach and speak to.
The quality of Connection is determined not by relying on systems or programs alone, but by all employees having a welcoming culture.
Culture (sharing of culture) and its specific initiatives are covered in the next section (ツボ 067).
Connection (人間関係構築) support for new employees has three points: (1) intentionally creating contact points, (2) clarifying who to consult, and (3) preparing the receiving side's mindset.
New employees face a psychological hurdle when initiating conversation themselves, so organizations should prepare mechanisms in which they are spoken to rather than requiring them to speak first.

Effective early contact includes automatic introduction within the company right after joining and creating situations where people naturally talk to the newcomer. Welcome lunch programs and a culture of casual chat (雑談OKなチャット文化) create light contact points.
Examples of intentional contact points: buddy system (バディ制度), welcome lunch (ウェルカムランチ), Slack channel invitations.

Not knowing whom to ask is a cause of isolation. A useful design is to clearly separate a Navigator (業務面 / work-related support) from a Success Manager (メンタル面 / mental support) to lower the hurdle of seeking advice.
Support structures must be designed beyond formality: specify when, what, and how support is provided.
Examples of consultation roles: buddy, navigator, success manager.
Building workplace relationships is not solely the new employee's responsibility. Success depends on how prepared the receiving side is.
Companies that prepare guides for OJT trainers and mentors tend to have more stable quality of new-employee support.
Teams should check whether a welcoming culture exists and whether people speak up regardless of rank or role.
Examples for preparing the receiving side: acceptance manuals (受け入れマニュアル), onboarding guides, culture sessions.
This content addresses interaction adjustment (人間関係への適応) as part of Connection support in onboarding.
「慣れること」は段階的です。焦らず一歩ずつ進みましょう
Getting used to something (慣れること) is a gradual/stepwise process (段階的).
Do not rush (焦らず); proceed one step at a time (一歩ずつ進みましょう).

Culture (文化の共有) is the final pillar of onboarding: conveying the values the company cherishes, behavioral norms, and decision-making criteria so new employees understand the 'way of being' as an organizational member. It is not mere explanation of systems or transfer of job knowledge, but a process of internalizing the atmosphere and distinctive 'likeness' (らしさ) of the organization.
Job competence alone is insufficient. Misalignment with organizational values produces personal discomfort and friction with others, and does not lead to long-term retention or high performance.

LayerX case: they prioritize 'understanding culture and sharing language.' The symbol is the 'LayerX Compass' (LayerX 羅針盤), a culture book that systematically compiles strategy, values, and behavioral standards. It is periodically updated at management retreats and shared by the CEO speaking directly to all employees. It records past decisions, the thinking behind them, and the postures the organization has valued, together with real episodes. Newcomers thereby receive 'what LayerX-ness is' and 'why the company made those choices' as stories they can overlay on their own judgment and actions.

White Plus case: new employees receive the 'White Book,' a booklet of the company's journey from founding to the present, including the backstory of management decisions and how difficult periods were overcome. Recruits learn not just a company overview but 'what values this company has operated on' as narrative. Episodes from the book become conversation topics with seniors, creating a shared language that crosses generations and departments.

Culture is transmitted through 'ba' (場, everyday settings), not a single lecture. It lives in daily practice: a word at morning assembly, the background of a decision, a supervisor's behavior, and similar ordinary moments.
During the onboarding period, it is important to consciously design a 'place where one can encounter culture' (文化と出会える場).
Rather than unilaterally imposing culture on newcomers, organizations should connect past and present and nurture culture together toward the future.
Culture is both something that should be protected (守るべきもの) and something that is created together (共につくっていくもの).
The next key point (tsubo 068) covers the design of onboarding.
Culture-sharing support for organizational onboarding has three core points: (1) convey through stories, (2) show scenes of practice, and (3) welcome newcomers with a co-creating stance.

Corporate philosophy and values transmitted only as words do not produce empathy unless the background (why they became that way) is also conveyed. Storytelling sessions covering history from founding to the present are highly effective for internalizing values.

Culture is felt, not merely documented: talking about why a judgment was made and what conflicts existed creates an experiential sense of culture. Examples include sharing the founding story, a representative’s message, and culture workshops.

Many newcomers know the stated philosophy and values but do not know how to behave. Making culture visible in daily work—so they can feel “this is what is considered good here”—promotes natural penetration. Examples include sharing behavioral-norm practice cases, internal awards, and morning-meeting storytelling.

Do not unilaterally impose culture on newcomers. Welcome them as companions who will grow the culture together. Beyond distributing history/thinking materials, create opportunities for newcomers to verbalize how they felt after reading them; this generates dialogue.

Shift the view of culture from something to “protect” to something to “evolve.” This makes the organization–newcomer relationship more proactive. Examples include participating in culture-book updates and a reflection-sharing session three months after joining.
These practices support adaptation to organizational culture (組織文化への適応) by treating culture sharing (文化の共有) as an interactive, experiential process rather than one-way information delivery.
A company (企業) can be understood as a narrative or 'story' (物語).
New employees / new hires (新入社員) function as newly appearing characters (新しい登場人物) within that corporate story.
Key statement: 新入社員は企業という「物語」の新しい登場人物です

Organizational behavior scholar Dr. Talya Bauer, in the SHRM Foundation report "Onboarding New Employees: Maximizing Success" (2010), states that research and general consensus indicate new employees need about 90 days to prove themselves in a new workplace. The sooner they feel welcomed and prepared for work, the more successfully they can contribute to the company's mission.

The "90-day rule" is widely adopted in practice and is highly effective as the axis of onboarding design. It is not mere initial training but staged design until new hires reach a state of feeling secure, confident, and able to contribute.
Dr. Bauer emphasizes that onboarding success or failure is determined by designed experiences, not by chance.

Pre-boarding (before joining) aims to reduce the gap between expectations and anxiety. At offer notification, explicitly state expected results after 90 days (quick wins) and provide pre-guidebooks and system explanations so newcomers do not suffer anxiety from lack of information.

Days 1–7 (introduction phase): Keys are a felt sense of being welcomed and an encounter with organizational culture. Beyond rules explanation and buddy introduction, sharing company vision and history as stories builds trust in the organization.

Days 8–30 (work and relationship-building phase): Focus on role understanding and relationship support. Weekly 1-on-1 meetings and welcome lunches with other departments help new hires feel their position and connections.

Days 31–90 (culture internalization phase): Support deep settlement and cultural understanding. Reading founding stories together and dialogue-based workshops connect values with behavior. On day 90, a joint meeting of HR and supervisor bridges to the next growth stage.

After day 90 of onboarding is the settlement and self-running phase (定着・自走フェーズ): regularly check status via surveys, use HR interviews to promote mid- to long-term career autonomy, and visualize contributions in order to drive organizational settlement and self-propulsion.

Consciously design each onboarding phase by reverse-engineering from the desired feeling at each timing and then putting the corresponding support in place; this reverse-calculation of “what you want people to feel when” is the key to onboarding success.
The subsequent key point (ツボ 069) covers measurement of adaptation and onboarding.

Onboarding can be designed around a 90-day rule with distinct phases: pre-boarding (before join date), introduction (days 1–7), work and relationship building (days 8–30), culture and reflection (days 31–90), and settlement/self-running (after day 90).
The 4Cs of onboarding (Compliance, Connection, Culture, Clarification) can be mapped onto specific activities in each phase rather than treated as a single orientation event.

Pre-boarding (pre-join): share expected 90-day outcomes or ‘quick wins’ at the same time as the offer; send a pre-join guidebook and internal systems manuals; have the supervisor, buddy, and HR contact the new hire in advance and introduce the assigned department.

Introduction phase (days 1–7): day-1 company-wide orientation focused on Compliance; introduce a buddy and schedule lunch with team members (Connection); deliver culture through company intro video, CEO message, history, business vision, and behavioral guidelines; reduce anxiety with a concrete ‘things not to do’ list and FAQ (4C).

Work and relationship-building phase (days 8–30): explain assigned work and share a detailed 90-day plan (Clarification); hold weekly 1-on-1s with supervisor or buddy to check progress (Clarification); run welcome lunches and intro meetings with other departments (Connection); provide guidance and hands-on practice with internal tools such as Slack (Connection).

Culture and reflection phase (days 31–90): founding-story training and joint reading of a company-history booklet (‘White Book’) (Culture); dialogue-style workshops on organizational code of conduct and values (Culture); a 90-day review meeting with supervisor plus HR and setting of the next goals (Clarification).

Post-90-day settlement/self-running phase: regular follow-up surveys checking psychological safety and understanding of systems; HR career interviews to build mid- to long-term career perspective; team presentations or light results-sharing sessions to make contributions visible.
A buddy, supervisor, and HR share responsibility across phases; weekly 1-on-1s and a formal 90-day review are used to keep clarification and goal-setting continuous rather than one-off.
When designing, refer to existing design examples as a guide rather than copying them directly.
Always adapt ("translate") those examples to fit your own company's specific business operations and corporate culture.
Key statement: 設計例を参考にしつつ、自社の業務・カルチャーへの翻訳を忘れずに設計しましょう (Design while referring to the examples, without forgetting to adapt them to your company's work and culture).
To continuously improve onboarding, measure new employees' adaptation state and onboarding effectiveness using surveys.

New-employee adaptation until they can work confidently depends not only on personal effort but also heavily on the organization's support system; judging whether support functions adequately by vague impression is dangerous. Objective visualization of adaptation status and support effectiveness through measurement is the key to raising the quality of HR measures.
The purpose of measurement is not to judge what is being done versus not being done. It should be used as a trigger to notice gaps the person feels and misalignments in support design.
Anxieties and confusion that HR and supervisors find hard to notice surface through numbers and verbalization.
Recommended survey structure is the Result × Factor model: separately measure the person's adaptation state (result) and the organization's supporting situation (factor).

Advantage of the Result × Factor structure: measuring items separately (e.g., 'Have you gotten used to the work?' as result vs. 'Was the job content clearly explained?' as factor) makes it possible to consider which support shortage delayed adaptation is attributable to.
Result measurement uses the 3-aspect model covering work/business, human relations, and organizational culture.
Factor measurement uses the 4C model: understanding of rules, role clarification, building human relationships, and sharing of culture.
Conduct surveys with 5-point evaluation plus free-text comments at milestones such as 1 month and 3 months after joining.
Use results not only by HR but as dialogue material in 1-on-1s with supervisors or buddies, and review onboarding design as needed.
The essence of measuring is not to blame new employees but to jointly look back on and adjust the adaptation process; visualization also changes the organization. Measuring is nurturing.
To continuously improve onboarding quality, treat measurement not as a formal system or institution (制度) but as part of organizational culture (文化), and make it a habitual practice.
Key principle: 測定を「制度」ではなく「文化」の一部であると捉えて習慣にしていきましょう (Treat measurement as culture rather than a system and turn it into a habit).
The next section (ツボ 070) covers mandatory actions at the starting point of employee adaptation, specifically the period from job-offer issuance (内定出し) through company joining (入社).

An adaptive survey (適応サーベイ) for employee onboarding/adaptation uses categories covering work independence, interpersonal relationships, organizational culture, rule/compliance understanding, role clarification, connection/support contacts, and culture sharing.

Work adaptation (業務の適応 / Work) measures whether the person can independently proceed with assigned work; example items: 'Are you able to proceed smoothly with your assigned duties?' and 'Are situations increasing where you judge and advance work on your own?'

Interpersonal adaptation (人間関係への適応 / Interaction) measures trust and ease of consultation; example items: 'Do you have a relationship where you can consult immediately when in trouble?' and 'Do you feel accepted by the team?'

Organizational culture adaptation (組織文化への適応 / General environment) measures familiarity with work styles and values; example items: 'Have you adapted to the organization's atmosphere and judgment criteria without discomfort?' and 'Is there no confusion about daily work styles and how decisions are made?'

Rule understanding (規則理解 / Compliance) checks whether support existed for learning rules and systems; example items: 'Were there materials or explanations to understand internal rules and systems?' and 'Is there no confusion about security, attendance, etc.?'

Role clarification (役割明確化 / Clarification) checks whether expected outcomes were clearly shared; example items: 'Were your role and expected results clearly explained?' and 'Are materials for judging work priorities being shared?'

Connection measures visualization of consultation destinations and designed contact points; example items: 'Is it clear who you should consult?' and 'Was there sufficient contact with your buddy or OJT person in charge?'

Culture sharing (文化の共有 / Culture) checks whether values and behavioral norms were communicated; example items: 'Were the values this organization holds dear explained?' and 'Can those values also be felt from everyday words and actions?'
Closed items typically use a 5-point Likert scale: 5 = strongly agree, 4 = somewhat agree, 3 = neither, 2 = somewhat disagree, 1 = strongly disagree.

Open-ended follow-ups include: recent points of confusion or things that made the person happy; what additional support would currently be welcome; and free comments on requests or insights for the organization.
The key to creating an adaptive organization is to firmly observe (「観て」) and continuously improve: しっかりと「観て」改善し続けることが「適応」する組織をつくる鍵です.
This principle emphasizes ongoing visual observation and kaizen-style improvement as the foundation for organizational adaptation (適応する組織).
New employee adaptation does not begin on the first day of joining the company; the first step toward adaptation starts the moment the informal job offer (naitei / 内定通知) is issued.
The period from job offer to joining should be designed as a 'run-up period' (助走期間) that builds trust and a sense of security (安心感), which is the premise of successful adaptation.

At the job-offer stage, use a welcoming and expectant tone rather than purely bureaucratic language, and enclose materials that convey the organization's philosophy and atmosphere so the candidate feels they were specifically chosen.
Practical ways to ease first-day tension include introducing a buddy, sharing the team's faces/members in advance, and allowing loose pre-joining connection via internal tools such as Slack.
Documenting and sharing in advance 'what is expected in the first 90 days after joining' clarifies the direction of adaptation.

Proper adaptation also requires a solid labor/HR administrative foundation: the job-offer letter (内定通知書) and labor-conditions notification (労働条件通知書) must be issued in writing to ensure transparency of terms.
Employers must understand the legal character of a naitei (informal job offer) to avoid unilateral cancellation or related disputes.

Immediately before joining, complete employment-contract signing (雇用契約書), social-insurance procedures, and advance notice of work rules (就業規則); incomplete administrative tasks create first-day confusion and hinder adaptation.

Adaptation support is not solely the responsibility of the workplace or recruiting team; it should be co-designed with labor/HR so that 'correctness of systems' (制度の正しさ) and 'comfort of the experience' (体験の心地よさ) are both achieved, forming the starting point of trust.
Effective combined designs include sending a culture book (カルチャーブック) together with the job-offer notice, and sharing expected roles at the same time as explaining the employment contract.

Essential onboarding support is not only about helping people smoothly get used to the work, but also about enabling them to feel secure enough to actually join (“enter”). That psychological safety is what creates the first step of adaptation.
The design of the period from job offer (内定出し) through the first day of work is the contact point between recruitment CX (候補者体験 / candidate experience) and adaptation (オンボーディング / onboarding).
Improvement points for the “offer and joining” (内定・入社) phase of recruitment CX are covered in ツボ 077.
The 'foundation of peace of mind' (安心の土台) is cultivated through collaboration among the workplace/site (現場), recruitment staff (採用担当), and labor affairs staff (労務担当).
Chart 070 covers actions from job offer issuance (内定出し) through joining the company (入社).

Workplace / accepting department and supervisor (現場・受け入れ部署・上司) responsibilities: acceptance preparation and building the foundation of work and relationships; assign a buddy/OJT person; prepare the work environment (PC, accounts, seating, etc.); organize post-joining work content and goals; give advance notice and introduction preparation to team members; plan welcome lunch and how the first day will be spent; invite the newcomer in advance to Slack groups or chats; plan messages and greetings directed at the newcomer.

Recruitment staff (採用担当) responsibilities: build a trust relationship with the candidate; provide information and adjust expectations; send the offer notification and labor-conditions notice (in coordination with labor affairs); confirm the schedule for creating and concluding the employment contract; conduct an offer interview to share expected roles; initially present a 90-day post-joining plan; send a pre-joining guidebook and internal introduction materials; provide guidance on belongings and documents to submit before day one; maintain regular contact with the candidate (email, phone, Slack, etc.); share culture books, representative messages, and similar materials; request and collect pre-joining questionnaires and submitted documents.

Labor affairs staff (労務担当) responsibilities: handle legal procedures and system setup; provide a labor environment in which the person can feel at ease; prepare enrollment in social insurance and employment insurance; set up methods for advance sharing of work rules and internal rules; confirm necessary documents such as My Number and resident certificate; establish labor-related FAQ and an inquiry-response system.
Growth that lies beyond adaptation (適応の先にある成長) should be articulated and put into words through dialogue (対話を通じて言葉にする).
The core invitation is to use conversation as the means of naming and making conscious the developmental growth that follows a period of adaptation.

Chapter 7 on 適応 (adaptation/onboarding) emphasizes that even highly capable hires will not perform unless they empathize with corporate culture; culture sharing (文化共有, ツボ 067) is therefore critical for executives.

Philosophy and values should be conveyed not only as words but as 物語 (stories): founding background, decision criteria, and conflicts the organization has overcome. Leaders should deliberately create forums to share these stories.
Corporate culture is not something to merely protect; it is something to grow together with people (文化は守るものではなく、共に育てていくもの).
For field managers, 役割の明確化 (role clarification, ツボ 065) is essential in adaptation. If “what is expected” remains ambiguous, behavioral standards never form and confusion and dead ends result.
