Roles and expectations must be clearly communicated and continuously aligned through dialogue. A role is not unilaterally assigned; it is shaped together. The manager is both a 設計者 (designer) who raises the resolution of the role and a 支援者 (supporter).
For recruiters, the period from 内定通知 (offer) to 入社 (joining) must be designed as more than paperwork (ツボ 070). It is time to foster 信頼と安心 (trust and peace of mind).

Designing the message “we welcome you” changes a new hire’s first day. Information excess and shortage should be balanced, and culture and expectations delivered carefully. The first step of adaptation is how the 迎える体験 (welcoming experience) is designed.
Individuals adapt to an organization along three aspects (個人が組織に適応する3つの側面): work/tasks (業務), human relationships (人間関係), and culture (文化).
Confusion in a new workplace is something everyone experiences.
The important step is to examine where you yourself are stumbling (自分がどこでつまずいているのか)—whether in work, relationships, or culture.
Once you identify the area of difficulty, you can seek the necessary support.
Adaptation is a process of trial and error for everyone.
Organizational adaptation (組織適応) means an individual fitting well into the organization across all three aspects: work/duties (業務), human relationships (人間関係), and organizational culture (組織文化).
Onboarding (オンボーディング) is a company's structured mechanism/system to support an individual's adaptation to the organization.
Support for understanding rules (規則理解): make rules actually usable in practice, make consultation contacts clear, and develop on-site systems and structure.
Support for role clarification (役割明確化): verbalize expectations, align through dialogue, and link roles with evaluation.
Support for building human relationships (人間関係構築): create opportunities (relatively/comparatively), clarify who to consult, and raise awareness on the receiving/accepting side.
Support for sharing culture (文化の共有): communicate through words and stories, show scenes of actual practice, and welcome people with an attitude of creating culture together.
Design the onboarding experience by reverse-calculating from a 20-day rule: decide at which timing what the person should feel or experience.
Measure both results and causal factors, then use dialogue around those measurements.
From job offer (内定出し) through joining: recruiting staff and labor/HR staff should collaborate to foster a foundation of security and peace of mind (安心の土台).
Companies that fail are those that take a wait-and-see (お手並み拝見) approach rather than committing.
Kazuki Tsuboi of JAFCO Group (HRBP and Executive Coach Principal) has supported HR at numerous startup companies in his role with a venture capital firm; the discussion focuses on adaptation (適応).
In recruitment screening, three types of fit should be examined (採用選考で見る3つのフィット).
Besides yarigai (やりがい, sense of purpose/fulfillment) and hatarakigai (働きがい, work satisfaction), harigai (張りがい) is important: it means betting one’s own life and time on something that matters.
In recruitment selection there are three judgment perspectives: Skill Fit, Culture Fit, and Career Fit.

Skill Fit corresponds to a first-screening image. Company side: whether the closest future colleagues on the floor actually want to work together. Candidate side: aligning on the 'やりがい' (meaning/satisfaction) of the actual work to be done.

Culture Fit splits into Mission/Vision and Values. Values ask whether the person matches the company's cherished values and thus is likely to thrive (a performance criterion). Many companies judge Culture Fit mainly on Values, but Mission/Vision Culture Fit also matters: whether the person can become absorbed together with colleagues, which is mutual alignment on '働きがい' (meaning of working at this company with these people).
Possessing only job-level 'やりがい' (expertise or interest in the work itself) without '働きがい' is risky: if job content later changes, the person's hopes no longer match.

Career Fit must be mutual. The interviewer judges as the hiring side, yet an offer is useless if the candidate does not choose the company. Both sides must therefore check Career Fit: what each is betting their life on, what benefits the company can actually provide, how strong the candidate's passion is, and (especially at a startup) whether they can overcome the many difficulties together. Alignment at this level produces the highest engagement.

Getting Career-Fit people to join requires agreement at the '張りがい' level—what they are staking their life and time on. Without that, they may later leave for more obvious values such as higher salary elsewhere.

HR should know in advance which fit (Skill, Culture, or Career) the person joined for, because it changes how the company relates to them. Even if they later leave (e.g., after a pivot, when they originally came for Skill Fit), the company can still support them rather than feel betrayed.
After an offer is accepted ('handshake'), every stakeholder should share the intent to make that handshake turn out to have been the right decision.

Personal illustration of Career Fit / '張りがい': committing one's time (the real bet, not money) to creating new value in the world together with people who start and accomplish things, which is why venture capital feels like a life one can bet on.

In HR and recruitment contexts, unsuccessful employee adaptation (適応) often occurs at companies that take an 「お手並み拝見」 (ote-nami haiken / “let’s see what you’ve got” or wait-and-see) stance rather than actively supporting the person.
Expert comment from the dialogue: companies that fail at adaptation are those that end up 「お手並み拝見」してしまう.

The discussion appears in an excerpt from a conversation with Tsuboi Kazuki (坪井一樹), HRBP and Executive Coach Principal at JAFCO Group, on the topic of 適応 within a work on recruitment theory and practice.

Workplace adaptation when joining a new organization can be analyzed along three dimensions: adaptation to the work/tasks themselves (業務への適応), adaptation to organizational culture (組織文化への適応), and adaptation to human relationships (人間関係への適応).

A professional may join a company they initially dislike or feel pressure from (e.g., aggressive sales culture) specifically as rigorous self-training (武者修行) to develop expertise in their field, such as moving from internal HR to HR consulting at a market-leading firm.

Consulting work differs substantially from internal HR operations; a core struggle can be failing to grasp the fundamental requirement of delivering value to external customers and producing measurable results.
Pre-existing negative impressions of a company can block cultural adaptation by making it difficult to empathize with or accept the organization's values and ways of working.

Human-relationship adaptation can succeed even when task and cultural adaptation fail: veteran colleagues who show genuine interest, give continuous feedback, and extend informal invitations (e.g., lunch) gradually integrate a newcomer into the team.
A close-knit team atmosphere, including veterans who are busy yet still make time for social connection, helps newcomers feel they belong; such closeness can even be joked about by other staff.

Informal, repeated conversations with a long-tenured senior (over lunches, drinks, and business trips) about company history and values can produce a turning point: the newcomer realizes the organization actually embodies what they personally consider most important in life, leading to strong resonance and cultural buy-in.

Key insight from the case: interpersonal interest, ongoing feedback, and storytelling about organizational history/values by veterans can convert initial aversion into genuine alignment with the company.
Every contact point in the recruitment process constitutes candidate experience (候補者体験) and is a brand touchpoint (ブランド接点) that shapes impressions of the company.
Recruitment processes should be designed from the candidate's perspective rather than solely from the employer's internal viewpoint.
Sloppy or careless responses to candidates risk damaging the employer brand; concrete measures exist to reduce that risk.
Being told to act 'politely and sincerely' (丁寧で誠実に) does not prescribe universal actions; how that principle is implemented depends on each company's own context.
Chasing an idealized candidate experience too far can turn into pressure that CX must be perfect, which itself becomes a risk.
採用CX (Candidate Experience) とは、候補者が企業の採用活動に接するすべての場面で感じる体験全体を指す。求人票を見たとき、応募フォームを入力したとき、面接を受けたとき、内定の連絡を受けたときなど、すべてがCXの一部である。
候補者が採用過程で「この会社の対応は丁寧だった」「誠実に向き合ってくれた」と感じるか、「雑な扱いを受けた」と感じるかで、企業の印象は大きく左右される。
近年の採用活動は、企業が人を「選ぶ」場ではなく、候補者から「選ばれる」場へと変化している。背景には労働人口の減少、転職の一般化、SNSなどを通じた情報共有の活発化があり、採用競争が激化している。
企業がどれほど優れた待遇や職場環境を用意していても、採用プロセスでの印象が悪ければ候補者はその企業を選ばない。悪い体験の例：面接担当者の態度が高圧的だった、連絡が遅かった、選考結果の通知が雑だった、といった体験は候補者の志望度を著しく下げる。
スムーズで配慮のある対応がなされると「この会社に入りたい」という気持ちが高まり、辞退や内定辞退のリスクも下がる。
採用CXは応募数や歩留まり、内定承諾率といった採用KPIに直結する。応募者対応を丁寧にすることで面接辞退が減り、結果的に内定まで進む候補者が増える可能性がある。
「選考を受けて良い経験だった」と感じた候補者は、たとえ不採用だったとしても企業のファンになることがあり、こうした企業との良好な関係性は将来の再応募や知人紹介にもつながる。
Recruitment activities (採用活動) are the first point of contact between candidates (候補者) and the company; the CX experienced there directly shapes the company's image (企業イメージ).
Candidates can include existing users of the company's own services as well as future customers, so a poor impression during hiring can damage the brand as a whole (ブランド全体の毀損).
Sincere, honest handling of candidates during recruitment increases corporate trust and contributes to building good relationships with employees, customers, and society.
The subsequent key point (ツボ 072) covers the candidate journey (候補者ジャーニー).
図表071は採用CX（候補者体験 / Candidate Experience）を示す図である。
採用CXにおける候補者ジャーニーの主なタッチポイントは、WEBで発見 → 説明会参加 → カジュアル面談 → 面接である。
候補者は各接点で「こんな会社が」「CEOが熱いね」「話が合うかも」といった印象を形成する。
採用CXでは候補者のすべての体験が重要であり、プロセス全体を通じた体験設計が求められる。
採用CX (Recruitment CX) is an application of Human-Centered Design (HCD / 人間中心デザイン) from product and service development.
Key statement: 採用 CX は 商品 ・ サービス 開発 の 「 人間 中心 デザイン (HCD )」 を 応用 したもの です

When designing recruitment CX, the most fundamental concept is the Candidate Journey: treating the entire flow from a candidate encountering the company, applying, going through selection, to receiving an offer and joining as a single 'journey.'
Candidate Journey is analogous to Customer Journey in marketing. Structurally grasping what candidates see, how they feel, and how they act at each touchpoint clarifies opportunities to improve CX.

The Candidate Journey has four phases: (1) Awareness/Interest — learning about the company and becoming interested; (2) Application — actually applying (including events or internships); (3) Selection — document screening and interviews; (4) Offer/Onboarding — receiving an offer and joining.

Candidate psychology and behavior change at each stage. In Awareness, key touchpoints include the company website, SNS, and employee word-of-mouth. In Application, form usability and reply speed matter.
Different touchpoints exist at each stage; the experience provided at those points determines CX.
The first step is to inventory and visualize the current candidate journey in your recruiting: list where you contact candidates, what guidance you give, and how you respond.

Arrange the materials, emails, and web screens candidates actually see in chronological order. Interviewer behavior, waiting time during selection, and post-offer follow-up are all part of the journey.
Recruiters often focus only on efficiently running recruitment operations, but what matters is thinking from the candidate's standpoint (候補者の立場で考える).
Small misalignments—such as briefing-session information being hard to find, slow replies, or interviewers being blunt—can have a large impact on candidates' emotions.
When designing the candidate journey (候補者ジャーニー), the perspective of what kind of talent to target is essential; this is persona (ペルソナ) setting.
Persona setting for the candidate journey is referenced as ツボ 084; the next tip (ツボ 073) covers the relationship with the recruitment process.
The candidate journey (候補者ジャーニー) is a framework describing the stages a job candidate experiences in the recruitment process.
The candidate journey consists of four sequential stages: Awareness/Interest (認知・関心), Application (応募), Selection (選考), and Offer/Onboarding (内定・入社).
Awareness/Interest is the initial stage in which potential candidates become aware of and develop interest in an opportunity or employer.
Application is the stage in which candidates formally apply for a role.
Selection is the stage covering evaluation, screening, and hiring decisions.
Offer/Onboarding is the final stage covering job offer, acceptance, and joining the organization.
Break down a company's recruitment (hiring) process to the smallest possible units in order to identify every contact/touchpoint with candidates.
Key statement: 自社の採用プロセスを最小単位まで分解してどんな接点があるかを見ていきましょう (Let's decompose our company's recruitment process to the smallest units and examine what contact points exist).

To improve recruitment CX (candidate experience), focus on the entire hiring process: what candidates feel at each step and where they drop off. Improvement points should be mapped to each phase of the candidate journey.

Awareness and interest phase: the first impression is everything. This is the stage where job seekers learn about the company and become interested. Every channel—company homepage, recruitment site, SNS, job postings, employee interview articles—is a first contact point. The key is whether messaging is attractive enough to make people want to apply. Enrich content that shows real employees, values, and workplace atmosphere.

Application phase: ease of applying is the candidate’s first real step. Poor form usability or tedious input causes drop-off. Keep the path to application completion as simple as possible and fully completable without stress on a smartphone. Post-application auto-reply emails should not be cold templates; they should thank the applicant and briefly explain next steps to increase a sense of security.

Selection phase: interviews become the company’s “face.” Document screening through interviews is the deepest contact between candidate and company. Interviews are a rare chance for candidates to experience culture and people; impressions here strongly affect desire to join. Basics matter: start on time, polite ice-breaking, two-way dialogue. Interviewer attitude, clarity of explanations, and handling of questions all reflect CX quality. Frequent contact during selection plus polite feedback regardless of pass/fail greatly raises candidate satisfaction.
Cross-phase principle: candidate experience quality is determined by details across awareness, application, and selection—not only by job content or offer terms.
After an offer (内定) is extended, candidate experience (CX) still continues through the joining (入社) phase; recruiters must continue engaging candidates carefully and thoroughly until the end.
An offer notification is not merely a pass/fail contact; it is a critical moment for making the candidate genuinely feel welcomed.
Beyond phone or email, adding genuine enthusiasm and a personal message to the offer letter (オファーレター) helps the message resonate with the candidate.

Post-offer follow-up (e.g., social gatherings/懇親会 or introducing a mentor) should be used to resolve pre-joining anxiety and strengthen the candidate’s desire to work at the company. Details are covered in ツボ 077.
ツボ 074–077 examine recruitment CX improvement points phase by phase; the next section (ツボ 074) addresses the awareness/interest (認知・関心) phase.

The more earnest or serious a hiring/recruiting manager (真面目な採用担当者) is, the more they tend to think only from their own company's internal perspective (自社側の視点だけ) rather than considering other viewpoints.

Recruitment CX (candidate experience) does not start at the application; it starts at the earlier awareness/interest (認知・関心) stage. The experience already begins the moment a job seeker first learns about the company.

Every first-contact channel is an 'entrance' for the candidate: job-site listings, the company homepage, SNS posts, employee referrals, news, and word-of-mouth. Unconscious judgments such as 'this company seems interesting' or 'it doesn't feel like a fit' already occur here and form the first branching point of CX.
After interest is sparked, candidates first check official information. Experiences that make desired information hard to find, use difficult language, or fail to convey atmosphere reduce interest.
Improving awareness/interest-stage CX requires imagining who looks at what information in what state, then designing information that is easy to find and easy to understand.

Practical design tactics: mobile-readable UI/UX; first-view photos and copy that immediately convey company atmosphere; content featuring real employee voices (interviews, a day-in-the-life); and clear navigation paths to briefing sessions and events.
The critical shift is from mere awareness to empathy: the candidate thinking 'this might fit me' and 'I can imagine myself working here.'

Publishing employees' failure stories and inner conflicts on the recruiting site conveys authentic culture, lowers the psychological hurdle, and lets candidates feel that an ordinary person like themselves could still take on the challenge.

Explicitly stating what the company aims for and what kind of people one would work with supplies candidates with concrete 'selection material.' This stage is described as the entrance of the employer brand (see Chapter 9).
Candidates routinely consult third-party word-of-mouth and employees' own SNS in addition to official company messaging. Platforms cited include OpenWork, YouTube, and X (formerly Twitter).
Job seekers naturally try to sense a company's actual working style and atmosphere through information exchange in communities.

Reputation generated by candidates who went through the selection process—such as saying the process was thorough, that their desire to join increased, or even if rejected that it was a good company—is incorporated into corporate value.
Whether job seekers are attracted to a company is strongly influenced by how they first encounter it.
Companies should deliberately design the first step of recruitment CX (candidate experience).
The next key point (075) covers improvement points in the application phase.

The awareness/interest phase (認知・関心フェーズ) of recruitment can be improved by combining official information sources with empathy-building content such as employees’ failure stories and internal conflicts (社員の失敗談や葛藤).
Accumulating CX (candidate/customer experience) enables a cyclical loop that continuously improves word-of-mouth (口コミ) and employee-generated communications (社員の発信).
Organizations should broadcast information and values that are easy to find (探しやすく) and easy to convey (伝わりやすい).
The recruitment funnel after the awareness/interest phase proceeds through Application (応募), Selection (選考), and Offer/Joining (内定・入社).
Recruit Co., Ltd. (リクルート社) states its mission as 「まだ、ここにない、出会い。」
The mission phrase 「まだ、ここにない、出会い。」 translates as encounters/meetings that do not yet exist here (yet-to-be-found encounters).

Application (応募) is the first milestone of trust-building in recruitment CX. Candidates rarely apply immediately after viewing a careers page; the desire to work at the company accumulates gradually until the action of applying occurs.

Job seekers deepen understanding by interpreting company atmosphere, job content, and career prospects in their own way. They also perform internal checks such as whether the company seems like a fit and whether they could work there with peace of mind.

Companies should not merely publish information but answer candidates' interests in stages. Useful formats include published Q&A, employee interviews, video content, information sessions, events, and internships, aiming to create a state in which 'what they want to know becomes naturally clear.'

Casual interviews (カジュアル面談) serve as an effective bridge before formal selection. The company frankly explains work content and culture while the candidate freely discusses career aspirations and values, deepening mutual understanding. Treat the meeting as dialogue rather than evaluation to generate candidate security and conviction.

Many reasons candidates hesitate to apply stem from insufficient or ambiguous information. Explicitly disclose basics needed for application—salary, benefits, evaluation systems, working styles, and growth opportunities—so anxiety is not left unresolved.

Do not hide company challenges or areas currently undergoing change; honest communication is a shortcut to trust. Job seekers do not seek a perfect company; they want an environment in which they can make decisions with peace of mind.
The first hurdle for job seekers who have decided to apply is the design of the application form.
Usability problems such as too many input fields, difficulty operating on smartphones, and lack of a save function lower application rates.
Application forms should be limited to the minimum necessary items and designed so they can be completed within 3 minutes.
Immediately after an application is completed, send an email that thanks the candidate and explains the next steps, in order to reduce anxiety.
Delayed responses can create distrust and become a trigger for candidates to withdraw.
Applying for a job is a decision in which the job seeker takes a step toward their own future.
Recruiters should design the process from the job seeker's standpoint, carefully considering where the candidate currently feels hesitation.
The next key point (076) addresses improvements in the selection phase.

The application phase (応募フェーズ) in recruitment can be improved by creating gradual understanding (段階的な理解) and opportunities for dialogue (対話の機会) so that job seekers reach a state of conviction or consent (求職者の納得のため).
Casual interviews (カジュアル面談) are used to resolve candidate anxiety (不安の解消) before or during the application process.

Elements that make candidates hesitate to apply (応募をためらわせる) include poor comfort of procedures (手続きの快適さ); the process should allow smooth operation (スムーズに操作できる) and naturally surface the information candidates want (知りたいことが自然に).
The goal is to deepen mutual understanding between company and candidate (双方の理解を深める) and create a clear state of understanding (分かる状態をつくる).
Information gaps and ambiguity should be filled in order to eliminate anxiety (情報の不足と曖昧さを埋めて不安を消す).
Practical tactics include preparing an application form and responding immediately after an application is submitted (応募フォームを用意し応募後は即対応する).

The broader recruitment funnel stages shown are: 認知・関心 (Awareness/Interest), 応募 (Application), 選考 (Selection), and 内定・入社 (Offer/Onboarding), aligned with English labels Interest, Application, Selection, Offer, and Onboarding.

Design principle for conversion/application UX: after a user has already overcome a psychological hurdle (心理的ハードル), the subsequent flow must be designed so it does not obstruct their formed intention to apply (応募する).
Key statement: 心理的ハードルを越えて「応募する」という意志を邪魔しないように設計しましょう (Design so as not to interfere with the will to apply once the psychological barrier has been crossed).
Context marker HINT $2 appears with this guideline, suggesting it is presented as a numbered design hint in a book on forms, recruitment, or conversion optimization.
Selection (選考) is not merely a process for evaluating candidates but a process in which candidates and the company deepen mutual understanding.
From a recruitment CX (candidate experience) perspective, the selection stage should be designed as a place to accumulate trust and raise the accuracy of final decision-making.
Candidates use interview time to discern whether they truly want to work at the company and whether it is a place to which they can entrust their future.
Psychological contract (心理的契約): unwritten, implicit expectations and trust exchanged during selection, beyond what is stated on paper.

Sensory aspects that job postings and briefing sessions cannot fully convey—expectations behind phrases such as “growth opportunities,” team atmosphere, and work-style flexibility—are felt and judged in interviews.
Candidates read the company’s true image (実像) through the interviewer’s speaking style, facial expressions, quality of questions, and overall atmosphere.
Consistency (一貫性) between the company’s stated vision/culture and the atmosphere and behavior candidates actually experience in interviews generates trust; any gap immediately undermines it.

Example of inconsistency: introducing the company as a “flat organization” while the interviewer speaks one-sidedly and does not welcome questions makes the claim ring hollow. Candidates are more sensitive to attitude and consistency than to words.
What is said during selection must be continuously checked against actual behavior so that they do not contradict each other.
A good interview is an opportunity for both sides to confirm each other’s expectations and values.
Creating an atmosphere in which candidates can easily ask questions and carefully explaining actual job content and required stance enables transparent dialogue.
Questions that help candidates notice their own potential turn the interview into a learning experience that goes beyond mere selection.

Sincere, specific feedback regardless of pass/fail is highly effective for building trust: stating what was evaluated and what raised concerns helps candidates understand their market value and improvement points.
Even a rejected candidate can leave with a positive impression (“this company seriously engaged with me”) when feedback is concrete and respectful.
As the selection process nears its end, companies must confront and align candidates' expectations with the actual job content (期待と実際の仕事内容のすりあわせ).
Honest sharing of the current situation (誠実な現状共有) reduces risk by preventing gaps in the psychological contract (心理的契約).
Example: Honestly communicating that a job is rewarding (やりがいがある) while also involving periods of high workload (業務量が多い場面) lowers the risk of discrepancy in the psychological contract after hire.
誠実な現状共有 is the key to raising post-joining satisfaction (入社後の満足度) and retention (定着).
The next point (ツボ 077) addresses improvement areas in the offer and joining phase (内定・入社フェーズ).

The selection (選考) phase of recruitment can be improved by addressing the psychological contract (心理的契約), which is implicit, not written down, and consists of exchanged unspoken expectations and trust between company and candidate.
Consistency (一貫性) requires checking whether the company’s prior claims match the reality the candidate actually experiences in interviews.
Mutual understanding (相互理解) is built through questions that surface possibilities plus sincere sharing of the current situation, including harsh realities.
Sincere feedback (誠実なフィードバック) is used to verify alignment and thereby reduce discrepancy (誤差) in the psychological contract.
The candidate journey stages shown are Awareness/Interest (認知・関心), Application (応募), Selection (選考), and Offer/Onboarding (内定・入社).

The final stage of candidate experience (CX) in recruitment is the period from job-offer notification through joining the company; treating it as mere paperwork can cause unexpected declines or post-join mismatches.

This phase is the most delicate and important timing because candidates mix expectation with anxiety; company consideration determines whether security or doubt is created. Completeness of recruitment CX is decided by offer-phase design.

When delivering an offer, do more than announce pass/fail: communicate what was evaluated in the candidate and what performance is expected. Avoid template emails; add personalized messages that reference interview impressions and specific episodes so the candidate feels ‘they saw me as an individual.’ Direct phone contact to convey warmth is also effective.
After the offer, emotions easily waver through comparison with other firms or anxiety, often leading to decline; regular follow-up is therefore required.
Follow-up examples that shorten psychological distance: social gatherings with current team members, events for offer-holders, and individual consultation opportunities.
Administrative contacts (document submission, training notices) remain candidate touchpoints; timing, clarity, and politeness of every response form part of the experience.

Pre-joining workplace tours or lunch opportunities deepen understanding of the work environment and reduce post-join gaps. Move beyond formal procedures and prepare to welcome the person as a colleague.

The first day of joining is the culmination of CX and the decisive moment for whether the new hire feels ‘I’m glad I chose this company.’ Fully prepare basic reception: welcome words, desk and PC setup, and a well-organized first-day schedule.
Involvement of not only HR but also the assigned supervisor and colleagues produces a warmer experience; the impression formed that day directly affects future engagement and retention motivation.
The period from job offer (内定) to joining the company (入社) is a process that involves more individuality and emotion than the selection process itself.
The more carefully this phase is designed, the more candidates can take their new step with peace of mind and confidence.
Hiring is not the goal but the beginning of a relationship; aim for consistent experience design (体験づくり) all the way through to joining.
After candidates become employees, their onboarding/adaptation experience is covered in Chapter 7 (適応).
The next section (ツボ 078) introduces practical examples of recruitment CX (Candidate Experience).

In the offer/joining (内定・入社) phase, the job-offer notification should go beyond a simple pass/fail result and provide a sense of security (安心感) by directly communicating the evaluation of the candidate and the expectations of the company.
After the offer is issued, regular follow-up contact is used to shorten psychological distance (心理的距離) and to support and reinforce the candidate’s intention to join the company.

On the first day of employment, the receiving organization must have a complete welcome/acceptance system in place so that the new hire is warmly received together with their supervisor and colleagues.
The recruitment funnel illustrated on the page proceeds through the stages 認知・関心 (awareness/interest) → 応募 (application) → 選考 (selection) → 内定・入社 (offer/joining).
Having interest or concern (関心を持つ) toward new companions or colleagues (新しい仲間) is a basic principle that is actually the most important stance or attitude (最重要のスタンス).
This fundamental approach of showing genuine interest in new members of a group is presented as the core, highest-priority posture one should take.

Recruitment CX (candidate experience) should not stop at subjective impressions such as 'it felt somehow good' or 'it felt bad.' Visualize where candidates were satisfied and where they felt dissatisfaction as measurable indicators so that specific improvement actions become possible.

Five basic quantitative indicators for measuring recruitment CX: (1) Application completion rate — the percentage of people who visited a job page who actually applied; it drops when forms are hard to use or have too many input fields. (2) Selection dropout/withdrawal rate — the percentage of candidates who decline during the selection process; slow communication and interviewer attitude surface as CX problems. (3) Offer acceptance rate — the percentage of candidates who received an offer who actually decided to join; it indicates aspiration level and sense of conviction. (4) Time-to-hire (average days from application to offer); speed is directly linked to candidate satisfaction. (5) Candidate satisfaction and NPS (Net Promoter Score) — quantified via surveys; NPS is measured by asking whether the person would recommend applying to this company to others.
Regularly monitoring these five CX indicators reveals the company's recruitment CX strengths and weaknesses.

Qualitative information is essential to capture 'feelings' that numbers alone cannot show. Free-text survey comments and verbal post-interview feedback contain improvement hints (e.g., 'the explanation was thorough' vs. 'the response felt mechanical'). Opinions from candidates who ultimately do not join are especially valuable because they tend to be unbiased and frank.

Everyone who has contact with candidates (interviewers, hiring managers, executives) is a designer of recruitment CX. Build a team habit of regular reflection and reporting so the entire recruiting team shares the importance of CX, discusses survey results and metrics together, and decides what went well and what to change.
Improvements to recruitment CX (採用CX / candidate experience) do not have to be large-scale initiatives; small changes are sufficient and effective.
Identify and carefully review small points of friction or discomfort (小さな違和感) one by one rather than only pursuing big measures.
Example of friction: requiring photo attachments on an application form can cause high candidate dropout.
Example of friction: blunt or unfriendly wording in reminder emails can harm the candidate experience.
The accumulation of these small, careful revisions is what drives overall improvement in recruitment CX.
This incremental approach of picking up and fixing minor discomforts is presented as more effective than relying solely on major overhauls.
Recruitment CX (candidate experience) review should combine quantitative metrics (定量数値) with qualitative information (定性情報) and be reflected on by the hiring team.
Rising selection dropout rate (選考離脱率) is a warning signal that may be caused by slow communication (連絡の遅さ) with candidates.
Candidate feedback that a reminder email's wording felt blunt or impersonal (「リマインドメールの文面がそっけなかった」) should trigger a review of the actual email content.

Core quantitative CX metrics include: (1) application completion rate (応募完了率), (2) selection dropout rate (選考離脱率), (3/4) offer acceptance rate (内定承諾率), (4) time-to-hire / days until hiring (採用までの所要日数), and (5) candidate satisfaction / NPS (候補者満足度・NPS).
Qualitative sources that complement the numbers are surveys (アンケート) and unfiltered candidate voices (生の声).

Recruitment CX (candidate experience) is a strategic practice: how candidates are treated during hiring affects not only talent attraction but also brand reputation, referrals, retention, and even existing customers.
Nitori ranked #1 for two consecutive years in the Mynavi/Nikkei 2025 humanities popularity ranking among Japanese undergraduates, making it a leading case of strong recruitment CX.

Nitori frames internships as a chance to confront 'what work means,' not as a sales pitch. Design focuses on students examining their own values and asking what they want to achieve in society, rather than on conventional application motives.
Nitori changed internship surveys from 'Do you want to join the company?' to 'Could you see a future vision?' This shift increased empathy and trust; many students later arrived via friend referrals.

Nitori prioritizes a selection experience with conviction over speed. Interviews include dialogue with management so candidate and company jointly imagine a future; offers are delivered by a direct phone call from the HR director rather than email, creating a memorable 'story' candidates can later narrate themselves ('why I chose Nitori').

Nitori's 'recruiter 1-year guarantee' keeps the hiring contact following the new hire after assignment, visiting the workplace and offering consultation as needed. Interview insights are shared with the receiving team to strengthen onboarding.

Nitori's premise for retention: many early quits are caused by the receiving side, not the hire. Therefore they involve the workplace and management in onboarding reform rather than treating hiring as finished at offer.

Virgin Media found that 6% of candidates who had a negative recruitment experience later cancelled existing service contracts with the company. Poor process (delayed contact, high-handed interviewers, silence after rejection) spilled from hiring into customer churn.

Virgin Media's estimated annual opportunity loss from deteriorated recruitment CX was about £4.4 million (approximately 540 million yen), illustrating that neglecting candidate experience can have large, measurable commercial costs beyond unfilled roles.
The impression a candidate forms throughout the selection process affects the company's reputation regardless of whether the candidate is hired or not.
This principle is a core element of 採用CX (recruitment/candidate experience).
Subsequent content (ツボ 080) addresses the future of recruitment CX.
Nitori’s internship is framed as a stage for students to discover what they want to do and to think about why they work in society, not only as a hiring funnel.
The program treats both outcomes as valuable: people who become interested in Nitori (which can lead to hiring) and people who become interested in other companies.
Students who do not join Nitori can still strengthen long-term relationships by bringing juniors to Nitori internships.
Internships are positioned as a junction point (結節点) between students and society.
Recruitment CX here means cherishing both groups—those who convert to Nitori interest and those who do not—rather than optimizing only for immediate hires.
People do not forget being treated roughly or carelessly at important moments in their own lives. (自分の人生にとって大切な瞬間に、粗雑に扱われたことを人は忘れません)

Recruitment CX is shifting from a one-way process to a mutual “handshake” relationship: neither purely the company selecting talent nor purely the job seeker selecting the company, but individuals and organizations understanding each other and agreeing to join with genuine consent.
The essential ingredient for that handshake is trust (信頼).
Candidates judge whether they can trust a company less by the words themselves than by whether those words match actual behavior (主張と実態の一貫性).
Inconsistency example: claiming a “flat organizational culture” on the careers page while interviewers emphasize titles, seniority, and take an authoritarian stance creates dissonance.
Inconsistency example: claiming a “challenge-friendly environment” while interviews allow no questions and unilaterally criticize skill gaps makes the company’s words sound empty.

People evaluate not only the content of messages but how they are delivered—facial expression, tone, timing, and the atmosphere of the room—and form a sensory judgment of whether company people truly believe what they say.

Impressions formed over a few days of selection are stored strongly and deeply in memory; consistency of claims and reality functions as the candidate’s criterion for the company’s “trust balance” (信頼残高).

If claims and reality align, even difficult pay or job content can still produce the feeling of an honest company; if they diverge, even good conditions can trigger the fear of being betrayed after joining.
That wariness can lead to dropping out of selection, declining offers, or early turnover after joining.
What is said in recruitment PR, info sessions, and interviews must be carefully aligned with actual field conditions (現場の実態).
It is valuable for leadership and HR to describe ideals, but trust is built by honestly stating how things are now, how far they have been realized, and what is still ahead.
Candidates do not seek a “perfect company”; they empathize with a “company without lies” (嘘のない会社).
The starting point of generating trust is making claims and behavior consistent—across reality vs. ideal, and across the field, management, and HR.
Hiring is shifting beyond a one-sided ‘selecting / being selected’ relationship into a setting where the individual and the organization face each other as equals.
That setting is used to mutually confirm the intention to walk together on the basis of trust.
Recruitment CX (candidate-experience) design is the work of creating that ‘handshake’ moment between person and organization.
The work of recruitment CX design is described as quiet yet powerful.
The next topic (Chapter 9) is recruitment marketing that builds trust over the long term.
Chapter 8 of the book summarizes Recruitment CX Design (採用 CX デザイン), presenting Q&A for tips (ツボ) 071–080 plus role-specific messages for executives, field managers, recruiters, and all employees.

For executives: consistency between stated ideals and actual interviews/explanations is essential for candidate trust. Recruitment is neither merely “selecting” nor “being selected,” but a handshake of mutual consent between individual and organization (Tip 080). Aligning words and behaviors across management, the field, PR, and reality is the starting point for sincerely engaging future colleagues.

For field managers: interviews are a precious encounter in which the manager is the “face of the company.” Candidates infer the company’s essence from facial expression, attitude, questioning style, and word choice. Any gap between the company’s stated values and actual field behavior creates discomfort that severs trust (Tip 076). Treat interviews as both evaluation and mutual understanding, and face the candidate’s life milestone with sincerity.

For recruiters: prioritize improving the CX of the application process itself (Tip 075). Candidate impressions form from the accumulation of small experiences—application-form usability, reply speed, and the tone of messages. Applying is a decision that crosses a psychological hurdle; design that removes hesitation and provides careful guidance, so information flows naturally and candidates can apply with peace of mind, is the first step toward trusted recruitment.
Members (employees) should understand the CX of 「認知・関心」 (awareness and interest), referred to as ツボ074.
「働いている人がどんな人か」 (what kind of people work there) is a major deciding factor for candidates when choosing a company.
Through word of mouth, SNS, and employee referrals, an employee's words and behavior create the company's impression.
Attractive recruitment starts from the employee's own behavior (魅力的な採用は、あなた自身のふるまいから始まっている).

By being conscious of words and attitudes that are easy to convey and that others can empathize with, one can create an entry point for encounters where people think 「この人たちと働きたい」 (I want to work with these people).
The following Chapter 9 covers 採用マーケティング (recruitment marketing).
採用CX (Candidate Experience / Recruitment CX) is defined as the experience candidates feel in every situation where they interact with a company's recruitment activities.
The first step in working on recruitment CX is to inventory the company's own hiring journey and identify all candidate touchpoints.
To improve recruitment CX, review the entire hiring process from the candidate's perspective.
Improvement points for the 'interest/awareness' experience: make information easy to find and easy to understand; communicate employees' real struggles and values.

Improvement points for the 'application' experience: staged understanding, opportunities for dialogue, reducing anxiety, comfortable procedures, psychological contract, consistency between the company's claims and reality, mutual understanding, and feedback.
Improvement points for the 'selection' experience: frank and honest sharing of the current situation.
Improvement points for the 'offer and onboarding' experience: an offer notification that provides a sense of security, follow-up that shortens psychological distance, and a welcoming first day.

How to proceed with reviewing recruitment CX: based on quantitative metrics and qualitative information, the hiring team reflects together and continuously makes small improvements to eliminate even slight discomfort.
What to learn from real recruitment CX case studies: success comes not from short-term hire/no-hire decisions but from building long-term relationships.

The future of recruitment CX: it will evolve from a 'selecting / being selected' model to 'hiring as a handshake between the individual and the organization,' in which trust becomes the most important factor.
Recruitment (採用) is conceptualized as relationship-building (関係性づくり) between individuals and companies, rather than a one-sided selection process.
Recruitment CX (candidate experience) is discussed by Hiroyuki Nagashima, representative of Toitoi LLC and former Head of Organization Development / recruitment lead at Nitori Holdings.
A key interview theme is the 'meaning of work' (働く意味) that cannot be fully conveyed even in a final interview.
Nitori’s internship program is frequently cited as the most popular among students in Japan, and the conversation examines the actual initiatives behind that popularity.

Nagashima Hiroyuki left Sony and spent about two years as a Nitori store manager before being suddenly transferred in 2014 to become the company-wide recruitment manager; days after leaving the store he was already conducting final interviews.
After one year of recruitment work, Nagashima observed that few candidates at the final-interview stage had seriously thought about “the meaning of working in society” or “why Nitori.”

Students typically deliver manufactured self-PR rather than genuine reflections on entering society; initially they seemed impressive, but it became clear that everyone was saying essentially the same things.

Because the existing recruitment flow could not be changed, Nagashima placed the question “What is the meaning of working in society?” at the center of 45-minute final interviews and, when a candidate seemed promising, abandoned conventional motivation and gakuchika (student-experience) talk in favor of genuine dialogue.

Serious goal-oriented dialogue in only 45 minutes often leaves much unsaid; deciding by impression after hearing similar stories is easier, which led Nagashima to conclude that such conversations should occur much earlier in the process and therefore to invest fully in internships.
The internship emphasis was a way of front-loading relationship-building time spent jointly considering “the meaning of work.”
Asking “Are we your first-choice company?” is described as the worst possible recruiting move.

Effective company–individual relationship building in recruitment should focus on making candidates like the company’s 10- or 20-year-future image and want to “create it together,” rather than merely liking the present company; recruitment ought to be such a relationship-building space.
Many firms suffer low offer-acceptance rates, joining rates and early turnover because they issue offers before any real relationship has been constructed, a symptom of weak interview processes.

A genuine relationship requires (1) some overlap between the organization’s mission/vision (its values) and the candidate’s values, (2) the candidate’s ability to imagine enjoying a future at that company, and (3) a shared picture of that future.

Interviewers need proper training: desperately describing the company’s current state does not help future-oriented students see growth potential; a better question is “The future will look like this—what could you do there?” yet most interviewers cannot conduct that dialogue, revealing a problem both of individual interviewers and of the entire recruitment process.
Asking candidates whether the company is their first choice (第1志望ですか?) before any relationship has been built is considered the worst possible interview move.
This question is especially common among interviewers who are executives or management-layer people at large companies that built the current organization.
Asking in the form “You’re here because we’re your first choice, right?” is already a failure (“chin”) at that point in the process.
The question is analogous to asking someone “You’re dating with the intention of getting married, right?”
Some students volunteer that the company is their first choice; those who are pressured into saying it are pitiable.
Hiroyuki Nagashima (永島寛之) studied marketing and industrial organization theory, then worked at Toray and Sony on overseas new-market development (including a U.S. posting at Sony USA).
At Nitori Holdings, under Chairman Akio Nitori, he led organization and HR as talent-management owner, directing hiring, development, and HR-system reform.

At Renova (TSE Prime renewable-energy developer) he served as Executive Officer CHRO, linking mid- to long-term business strategy with organization and talent strategy and focusing on developing “green talent” (leaders of global energy transformation).
In February 2023 he founded Qrious LLC (now Toytoy LLC) to support future organization development starting from individual growth, working with multiple company executives.

The excerpt is from a logmiBusiness dialogue on recruiting CX (candidate experience) titled “Asking Hiroyuki Nagashima about Recruiting CX,” from the book Illustrated Recruiting Primer: Theory and Practice 100 Tips (dated 25 January 2025).
At Recruit Management Solutions (RMS), a cultural practice exists of calling a departure that is supported and celebrated by colleagues 'graduation' (卒業) rather than mere resignation.

Graduation (卒業) is defined as completing what one ought to do in the organization, thoroughly discussing the move with superiors and colleagues, and leaving for the next step while remaining in a mutually supportive relationship.
Not every departure qualifies as graduation: sudden unexplained exits, or leaving without finishing one's tasks and without others' support, are simply unfortunate 'resignations' (退職).

The author 'graduated' from RMS, receiving congratulations and three booklets of messages showing that colleagues had noticed his work and sincerely expected his future success; rereading them still moves him to tears.

The author previously only 'resigned' from another firm: after he announced his departure the superior stopped listening, possibly feeling betrayed; the memory remains painful despite the author's respect for that person.
Someone who has only known resignation may dismiss talk of 'graduation' as empty rhetoric or corporate branding, yet mutually happy graduation is realistically possible.
Recruitment activity can be designed as a funnel: 認知 (awareness) → 関心 (interest) → 応募 (application) → 選考 (selection) → 入社 (joining).
Marketing techniques such as target design and EVP (Employee Value Proposition) can be applied to recruitment.
A core shift is from 「待つ採用」 (waiting/passive hiring) to 「育てる採用」 (nurturing/growing talent through hiring).
The chapter uses many katakana and abstract terms, which can feel difficult for readers who resist that style.
Even when the ideas are understood, resource-poor companies often feel a gap of 「結局できない」 (we still cannot do this in practice).

Traditional recruitment was reactive: companies posted job ads, received applications, interviewed for fit, and made offers. Pre-application contact between company and candidate was limited; awareness and interest were left to advertising and word of mouth.
That model mainly competed for active job seekers (people who already want to change jobs now). Firms with weaker brand awareness or lower pay struggled to attract a candidate pool.

With a shrinking workforce due to population aging and more diverse worker values, posting ads and waiting is no longer enough to reach needed talent. Recruitment marketing (採用マーケティング) emerged to address this.

Marketing (the parent concept) means delivering the value customers want ahead of time and building a system so products/services are chosen naturally without hard selling. Peter Drucker described it as making selling unnecessary; Philip Kotler as meeting needs and generating profit. In short, marketing is the overall design that aligns the interests of seller and buyer.

Recruitment marketing applies that idea to hiring. Companies want talent that will grow the firm; candidates want a workplace that fits them and where they can grow. The goal is to create a situation in which those hopes naturally overlap.

Recruitment marketing starts before applications: it nurtures relationships with candidates. Practitioners define a desired persona (求める人物像), then reach those people earlier with the company’s existence and appeal.
Recruitment marketing (採用マーケティング) actively delivers a company's appeal by transmitting corporate culture and employee voices through SNS and owned media.
It creates bidirectional contact points via events and casual interviews (カジュアル面談).
During the selection process, rapid feedback is used to foster a sense of security (安心感).
After application, support continues through offer follow-up (内定フォロー) and onboarding so candidates can become active, connecting to long-term retention and referrals.
Traditional recruitment takes a waiting stance (待ちの姿勢), whereas recruitment marketing designs contact points from before application and focuses on nurturing relationships (関係性を育てる).
The next topic (ツボ 082) covers the relationship among recruitment marketing, recruitment CX, and the recruitment process.
Recruitment marketing (採用マーケティング) is presented as the counterpart to general marketing, with the goal of growing/nurturing the relationship between job candidates (候補者) and the company (企業).
General marketing is characterized as aligning the interests of both parties (両者の利害を一致させる).

Figure 081 (図表 081) conceptually links marketing and recruitment marketing as related practices that manage stakeholder relationships, substituting customer-interest alignment with candidate-company relationship development.

Peter Drucker stated that marketing is an activity that concerns the entire business (マーケティングは全事業にかかわる活動である). This frames marketing not as a specialized departmental function but as a company-wide activity viewed from the customer's (final-result) perspective.

Recruitment activities consist of three complementary layers, analogized to building a house: the blueprint (設計図) = recruitment marketing (採用マーケティング); quality standards (品質基準) = recruitment CX design (採用CXデザイン); and actual construction/execution (実務) = the recruitment process (採用プロセス).

Recruitment marketing is the overall design of 'who, when, where, and what to communicate.' It decides at which stage to meet candidates, which media to use, and what Employer Value Proposition (EVP) to send. Channels and messages are placed along the funnel: awareness (認知) → interest (興味) → application (応募) → selection (選考) → joining (入社) → contribution/active work (活躍), so effects can be verified with numbers.

Recruitment CX design is the planned 'quality of experience' candidates should feel during hiring. Examples of designed impressions: fast email replies; interviews that are dialogic rather than one-way; offer meetings that make the image of working style concrete. These experiences are designed, measured, and improved systematically.

The recruitment process is day-to-day operational work: requirements definition (要件定義), sourcing/posting (募集), selection (選考), and onboarding/adaptation support (適応支援 / オンボーディング). HR and the business cooperate to execute according to the marketing blueprint, e.g. writing job ads based on personas and conducting interviews that meet CX standards.

The three layers must interlock: marketing supplies the master plan, CX design sets the quality bar for candidate experience, and the process is the daily execution. Alignment among them is what connects the company and the candidate.
When the interests of the parties naturally align, a relationship develops in which applicants feel they want to work at the company (応募者が「ここで働きたい」と感じる関係性が育っていく).
The next section (ツボ 083) covers how to design recruitment marketing (採用マーケティングの設計方法).
採用マーケティングは設計図、採用CXデザインは品質基準、採用プロセスは実務である。
採用マーケティングは、候補者と企業の関係性を育てる。認知から入社後活躍までの全工程をデザインし、長期における採用活動全体の骨格となる。家づくりに例えると設計図に相当する。
採用CXデザインは、候補者が魅力的に感じているかを測る品質基準である。接点ごとに設計し、チェックし、改善し続ける。家づくりに例えると品質基準に相当する。
採用プロセスは実際の採用の実務である。採用要件設定、募集、選考、適応支援を実行する。家づくりに例えると大工さんの実務に相当する。
Building a house without a blueprint (設計図) is not only inefficient but also very dangerous.

Recruitment marketing (採用マーケティング) is designed in three sequential parts: (1) who to reach — the recruitment target (採用ターゲット); (2) when and where to meet them — the recruitment funnel (採用ファネル); (3) what value they should feel — recruitment branding (採用ブランディング).

Recruitment target (採用ターゲット): Go beyond job type and years of experience. Imagine what the person values at work and what working style they prefer, then create a single-person persona. A concrete example: “a 30s engineer who wants to try new technology in a small team.” Specific personas naturally determine later wording and media choices. A clear target produces more accurate applications and reduces mismatch.

Recruitment funnel (採用ファネル): Map contact timing and place, then deepen the relationship stage by stage. The flow is: awareness (認知) → interest (興味) → application (応募) → selection (選考) → joining (入社) → thriving (活躍). Place the optimal channel at each stage — e.g., SNS for awareness, tech blogs or study groups for interest, job sites or casual interviews for application. Counting how many people sit at each stage reveals where to improve.

Recruitment branding (採用ブランディング): Use employee surveys and competitor comparison to identify unique company points such as “an environment where you can take on challenges,” “work that contributes to society,” or “flexible working style.” Explicitly state the attractiveness that makes the target think “I want to work here” (EVP). Narrow the message to 4–5 points. Deliver the same message consistently in every article, video, and briefing slide so an impression (brand) is formed.
Recruitment marketing begins by clarifying who should feel value, when and where they should feel it, and what they should value.
Execute the recruitment process first from a design blueprint assembled as a hypothesis, then verify effects with actual numbers.
Repeat the cycle of hypothesis → execution → improvement on a monthly basis.
Success in recruitment marketing requires continuously adjusting three elements at the same time: target, funnel, and branding.
The next section (point 084) covers specific methods for defining the optimal target.
Recruitment marketing (採用マーケティング) is structured around a framework that answers who to target and what value to offer.
The 'who' question is answered by defining the recruitment target (採用ターゲット), using demographic attributes on an objective/external axis.
The process uses a recruitment funnel (採用ファネル) as a core component of attracting and converting candidates.
The 'what value' question is answered through recruitment branding (採用ブランディング).
EVP (Employee Value Proposition) is the value of working at this company (この会社で働くことの価値).
The EVP must be communicated consistently (一貫して伝える) as part of recruitment branding.
Do not use currently popular katakana loanword terms vaguely or without thought; instead, firmly grasp and understand their actual meaning.
In recruitment marketing, the starting point is clearly defining who you are communicating to. Even the best messages and attractions lose effectiveness if the intended audience is vague or blurred.
Articulate in words what kind of person the company wants to hire and what kind of person is likely to thrive there. This character image is called a persona (ペルソナ).
Segmentation (セグメンテーション) means dividing the recruitment market into groups rather than treating all candidates as one, because they have different values and needs.

Two main segmentation axes exist: demographic (objective/external factors such as age, occupation, industry experience, education, and language skills that can appear on a resume) and psychographic (subjective/internal factors such as values, career orientation, preferred work style, and life stage).

Combining demographic and psychographic axes produces a more realistic group portrait. Example: early 30s, from a small-to-medium IT company, field-oriented, values discretion/autonomy, wants full remote work.

Targeting (ターゲティング) is deciding which segmented group to concentrate on. Approaching every layer is unrealistic given limits of resources, brand power, and budget; find where the company can win more easily.
Competing with large companies on identical skills and conditions is intense. Layers that want discretion or cultural empathy can be easier to hire because of value alignment.
Companies without name value and startups are often more effective focusing on values and work-style compatibility rather than high skills or experience.

Example orientations to target include wanting to turn one's own ideas into reality, wanting to be involved in everything in a small team, and wanting to work autonomously; show that the company enables those things.
When communicating in recruitment, phrasing that highlights a 'meaningful difference' versus other companies makes that difference stand out.

When choosing a recruitment target, three viewpoints are useful: (1) whether the company's strengths will resonate (whether candidates will find the company's strengths attractive), (2) whether competition is low (whether the target does not overlap with other companies), (3) whether they are likely to thrive after hiring (whether retention and results after joining can be expected).
Prioritize targets using these three viewpoints and concentrate recruitment activities on them.
The following section (ツボ 085) explains the recruitment funnel (採用ファネル).
Recruitment strategy involves segmenting the hiring market (採用市場を切り分け) and deciding which specific layer or segment to concentrate on.
Target setting (ターゲット設定) is framed using demographic (デモグラフィック) attributes plotted on an external/objective axis (外面 (客観) 軸).
The recommended approach is to focus resources on one chosen layer and actively approach it (この層に集中してアプローチしよう).

Two evaluation questions for selecting the focus segment: (1) Do the company’s own strengths resonate with that layer? (自社の強みが響くか？); (2) Are people in that layer likely to thrive and perform well after they are hired? (採用後に活躍しやすいか？).
The page presents this targeting logic as a visual framework (図表 084).
To segment or divide a market (市場を「分ける」), one must first thoroughly understand the market (市場をよく「分かる」必要がある).

Japanese marketing insight uses wordplay on 分ける (wakeru, to divide/segment) and 分かる (wakaru, to understand), both sharing the kanji 分, to stress that effective market segmentation depends on deep market comprehension.
In recruitment marketing, the goal is not merely to increase touchpoints with candidates, but to design the overall flow of when, where, and how those touchpoints connect.

A recruitment funnel (採用ファネル) diagrams the stages from awareness through to post-hire performance. It is named because candidate numbers are successively narrowed at each stage, resembling a funnel (じょうご / 漏斗).

Treat the funnel as the candidate journey. For each stage, organize what information to deliver and what experience to provide. Example: awareness via SNS or event speaking so people learn the company exists; interest via employee interview articles or owned media that convey culture and the actual work.

After designing the funnel, set KPIs at each stage to measure how many people advance. Examples: awareness = site visitors; interest = article views or information-session attendees; application = actual applicants. Numbers make drop-off points visible.

Interpreting funnel metrics: many applications but many interview no-shows may indicate a gap between expectations at application and the selection experience. Few information-session attendees may mean announcement channels or content do not match the audience.

Optimize channel and touchpoint placement by stage. Typical mapping: awareness on X (Twitter) or YouTube; interest on note or tech blogs; application on Wantedly or the company careers site; selection via Zoom or in-person interviews.

Choose channels that match the information sources the target already uses. Segment examples: students on Instagram; new-graduate STEM talent via university labs; mid-career engineers on Qiita or connpass.
A recruitment funnel (採用ファネル) is not something you draw once and then finish; it must be continuously monitored and refined.
Use actual data to keep checking which stages of the funnel are weak and which channels are strong, then make adjustments while nurturing the funnel over time.
Think in numbers about where to improve in order to increase better encounters/matches; this shifts recruitment from ad-hoc activity to planned work that actually produces results.
The next topic (ツボ 086) covers recruitment branding (採用ブランディング).
The origin (源流) of funnel thinking (ファネル思考) is the AIDA model proposed by Elmo Lewis in the United States at the end of the 1890s (1890年代末).
AIDA is a foundational marketing/sales model from which later funnel-based thinking developed.

Branding means conveying unique value in a form that is easy to understand and memorable. In marketing, a brand is not merely a logo or slogan but the impression itself that exists in the customer's mind.
When people choose among similar products because they feel they can trust this company's offering, that is the brand at work.
Brand theory emphasizes three key elements: consistency, differentiation, and being memorable (Keller, 1993).
Recruitment branding applies the same thinking: it is the work of designing how a company is perceived as a place to work.
To make candidates want to work there, companies must communicate not only pay and conditions but also the company's values, the kinds of people who work there, and what employees can gain.

Recruitment branding has become more important for two reasons. First, it is now an era of being chosen: with declining birthrates and an aging population, candidates routinely select companies rather than only being selected by them. Second, it is an era in which information travels widely and quickly; SNS and word-of-mouth transmit company images beyond official recruiting materials, so a clear message is needed for candidates to feel the company might fit them.

The core of recruitment branding is the EVP (Employee Value Proposition): a concise 'promise' that states what people gain by working at the company. Examples include being able to do work that benefits society, growing at one's own pace, or a culture of taking on challenges as a team. The EVP must express value unique to that company.
EVP (Employee Value Proposition) is the starting point for making candidates feel the value of working at this company.
After deciding on the EVP, it is critical to determine where and how it will be communicated.
Key communication channels for EVP include the recruitment website, SNS, job postings, information sessions, and interviews.
The same message flowing through every touchpoint builds candidate trust.
If the content communicated varies by channel or location, candidates become anxious.
The foundation of branding is to repeatedly communicate using consistent language.
Consistent wording across all recruitment scenes is essential for employer branding credibility.
Recruitment branding (採用ブランディング) is an initiative that consistently delivers 'the value of working at this company' to candidates and imprints an impression on them.
EVP (Employee Value Proposition) expresses 'the value of working at this company'.
Figure 086 diagrams recruitment branding as linking impression, EVP, and candidates (with communication indicated between them).
In branding (ブランディング), the most important principle is to consistently 'point to' or indicate (指し示す) something.

Recruitment branding is made more effective by five methods; the first four emphasized here are: keep messages consistent, deliver real voices from the field, talk honestly about challenges as well as strengths, and make outbound communication a habit.

Consistency is central to recruitment branding. The same message should be repeated across SNS, the careers site, information sessions, interviews, and other touchpoints so that what the company values is naturally understood by candidates.
Share the EVP (Employee Value Proposition) with interviewers and recruiters so the same language appears everywhere; this consistency builds candidate trust.

Field (frontline employee) voices are essential. HR and leadership messages alone are harder to convey and less appealing; the same points become much more persuasive when expressed in employees' own words.
Practical method: interview employees about why they joined and what they actually feel at work, then publish those stories. Unadorned, unpolished language reaches candidates more effectively.
Honesty about challenges is required. Overstating attractiveness or stating things that are not true causes post-hire mismatch.
Example of mismatch: claiming 'you can work freely' while detailed rules actually constrain work erodes trust and can drive early turnover.
Communicate not only strengths but also current challenges. A sincere stance itself becomes a strong brand.
Branding works through continuity. Starting with even one post per month is acceptable: employee introductions, event reports, or small initiatives.
Manage content on a calendar that makes visible who posts what and when, so communication can continue without strain. Perfect articles are not required.
It is acceptable to gradually reveal one's current authentic self or appearance rather than presenting everything at once.
Step 5 of the process is to reflect on the effects of outreach: review how much the disseminated content actually reached people.
Use indicators such as article view counts, SNS reactions, and the content of questions at information sessions to determine what information reached candidates' hearts.
Qualitative feedback is as important as numbers; comments like 'I applied after reading this article' are valuable clues.
Regular reflection on these results clarifies what to communicate next.
The following key point (ツボ 088) addresses who delivers this value and how.
メッセージを一貫させる (keep messages consistent)
現場の声を届ける (deliver voices from the field/front line)
課題も正直に語る (speak honestly about issues/challenges as well)
発信を習慣にする (make communication/outreach a habit)
効果を振り返る (reflect on the effects/results)
These appear as numbered or listed principles associated with 図表 087 (Figure 087)
「伝える」(tsutaeru: to convey/tell) and 「伝わる」(tsutawaru: to be transmitted/get through) are different concepts in communication.
Always verify that a message has actually reached the intended recipient (候補者 / candidate), rather than assuming that sending it is sufficient.
Recruitment branding depends not only on message content but on who delivers it; the communicator strongly changes the impression candidates receive.
Hiring involves many types of narrators (語り手), each with a distinct role that should be designed deliberately.
Executives should put into words why this talent is needed now and communicate the purpose and significance of hiring.
Frontline managers should describe the actual work and which skills will be used, setting realistic expectations in interviews.
Frontline employees can most authentically convey daily life at the company; their words carry persuasion and reduce candidate anxiety.
External narrators include recruitment agencies, university career centers, and industry media.
Treat recruitment agencies as partners who convey the company’s appeal on its behalf, not mere introducers; share information regularly so they understand business, culture, and working style.
Former employees (OB/OG) and even declined or rejected candidates are important narrators; a single SNS comment from them can affect new candidates’ application motivation.
To stop treating hiring as HR-only work, circulate information inside and outside the company and clarify role division.

Practical mechanisms include opening employee-interview schedules company-wide, distributing shared materials to interviewers, and sending weekly hiring topics via Slack or email; small repeated actions build a cooperative system.
Key principle: how a message lands changes depending on who tells it (「誰が語るか」で伝わり方は変わる).
Even the same words create a different impression depending on who speaks them.

Example: HR saying “裁量がある会社です” (this is a company with discretion/autonomy) is less persuasive than a talent employee who actually leads projects saying “自分の意見が通る場面が多いです” (there are many situations where my opinions get through). See ツボ 040.
Enabling many different people to speak in their own words is the key to successful 採用ブランディング (recruitment branding).
The value of recruitment is determined as much by “誰がどう伝えるか” (who communicates how) as by “何を伝えるか” (what is communicated).

Stakeholders to involve include 経営 (management), 現場 (the field/front line), 社員 (employees), 採用パートナー (recruitment partners), and even past candidates; grow recruitment as a company-wide activity (“会社全体の活動”).
The next section (ツボ 089) introduces case studies of companies succeeding at 採用マーケティング (recruitment marketing).
採用ブランディングの語り手には、社内の経営者、現場マネージャー、タレント社員が含まれる。
社外の語り手として人材紹介会社、学校、OB・OG、辞退・不採用の方が挙げられる。
図表088は採用ブランディングの語り手を示し、人材紹介会社、社内、OB/OG、現場マネージャー、社員、採用担当者などの関係者を位置づけている。
Full commitment from management (経営者が全面的にコミットしていること) is a prerequisite condition (前提条件) for successful recruitment/hiring (採用成功).
Successful recruitment marketing is illustrated by two companies: Yumemi (app development) and Nitori (furniture/interior retail). Their shared traits are sincerity (誠実さ) and systematization (仕組み化).
Yumemi has no dedicated recruitment HR staff yet stably hires 30–40 people per year by combining “topic creation” (話題づくり) with “all-employee recruiting” (全員採用).

Yumemi concentrates resources on high-visibility rankings to create “illusion assets” (錯覚資産) so outsiders feel “this company might be amazing,” then backs that up with technical articles and speaking appearances to convert awareness into trust.

About 60% of Yumemi employees take part in recruiting; interviews and scout messages are handled by frontline staff. Evaluation criteria and manuals are published in Notion so anyone can act as an interviewer.

Yumemi interviews are designed to start after only 30 minutes of training, preventing person-dependency (属人化). Broader candidate contact also makes employees treat hiring as “their own job,” which naturally supports post-hire retention.

Nitori shifted from “offer and done” to accompanying candidates from the start of their careers. Internships emphasize jointly exploring “what I want to do in society” rather than company understanding, and are not premised on joining.
Nitori’s internships aim to create a setting where students can speak honestly with peace of mind.
Nitori’s “recruiter 1-year guarantee” assigns the same person as counselor from offer notice through one year after joining, enabling early resolution of anxiety and questions and raising retention.
Even when assignment cannot be guaranteed, Nitori thoroughly explains career options from the selection stage and dialogues about “what can be expected” and “what if it differs from hopes.”
Yumemi and Nitori share a recruitment approach of building systems that continue sincere, ongoing dialogue with candidates rather than treating the relationship as a one-time/temporary exchange.
Both companies embed recruitment into internal systems and corporate culture instead of relying only on the efforts of some hiring managers.
The two companies' cases show that, regardless of company size or industry, what matters is how sincerely and how long the organization engages with candidates.
The next section (Tsubo 090) addresses the future of recruitment marketing.
Yumemi builds candidate relationships through continued sincere dialogue and operates recruitment as a company-wide system rather than a siloed HR function.

Yumemi practices thorough information disclosure on recruitment: everything from recruitment philosophy to final-interview pass rates is verbalized, reviewed, and published internally and externally, which preserves message consistency and enables cooperation from many stakeholders.
Business-model constraint at Yumemi: management-department ratio about 29%, sales about 3–4%, combined indirect departments kept under 10% as a productivity target.

Until the organization reaches roughly 1,000 people, Yumemi does not place dedicated full-time recruiters; the president personally leads recruitment operations. This gives the CEO higher-resolution understanding of the hiring market than typical executives and enables faster, bolder management decisions to raise hiring power—framed as “recruitment-driven management” (採用ドリブン経営).
Yumemi Compass (owner-oriented resource-allocation ranking) places recruitment as the highest priority among all work; current employee involvement rate in hiring is about 60%.

Recruitment philosophy: recruiters easily fall into “hire people who are good for Yumemi.” They must also ask whether Yumemi is a good company for the applicant, and continuously question and embody socially proper hiring so that mismatch and social distortion decrease. That social role is part of Yumemi’s reason for existing.
Example of the philosophy in action: aggressive use of RJP (Realistic Job Preview) so that honest previews of the job and company become normal practice and mismatch declines.
Yumemi recruiters’ work is therefore not limited to company and candidate; they must approach hiring as socially meaningful activity.
Recruitment attitude (background value): hiring is not the goal; the priority is whether the applicant can thrive and achieve self-actualization after joining.
Recruitment attitude 1: in interviews, recruiters should behave as their ordinary selves rather than adopting an evaluating/judging posture.
Recruitment attitude 2: use Realistic Job Preview to close the post-hire gap by communicating real company challenges and conditions.

Recruitment attitude 3: the interview is valuable time for the recruiter as well as the candidate. Feedback and service attitude should develop both the candidate’s growth and the recruiter’s own feedback skill and customer-service quality.
Yumemi Inc. (ゆめみ社) is cited as an example of thorough/radical information disclosure (徹底的な情報公開).
Such exhaustive corporate transparency is framed rhetorically as possibly the ultimate expression of sincerity (誠実の究極の形).

In recruitment marketing (採用マーケティング), the emphasis is shifting from 'showing the company well' or 'standing out' (うまく見せる / どう目立つか) to 'communicating correctly' (正しく伝える). In an era of information overflow, candidates independently research, compare, and see through companies' actual conditions, so firms should convey accurate information rather than information designed merely to look good.
The essence of recruitment marketing is alignment of interests (利害の一致) between the company and candidates. This requires a genuinely sincere stance rather than exaggeration or staging.

Three reasons a more sincere stance is increasingly required: (1) Spread of SNS and review/word-of-mouth sites, so that even company internals and interview treatment are shared among candidates; (2) AI-driven information comparison, in which job postings and company pages are instantly compared with competitors and exaggeration or contradictions are quickly detected; (3) Structural labor-market change from population decline, shifting from 'companies choose talent' to 'companies are chosen by talent,' strengthening workers' position.
