Sincere information disclosure is not merely impression management; it produces measurable outcomes such as more applications and lower offer-decline rates. Openly communicating company values attracts people who culturally fit, reducing post-hire mismatch.

The importance of sincerity in recruitment is supported by multiple theories and empirical studies (referenced as Figure 090). Communicating reality as-is builds a foundation of trust with candidates.
Future recruitment gains strength not from making things look good, but from communicating reality 'as it is' (ありのまま).
A sincere attitude (誠実な姿勢) is a message that reaches candidates' hearts and is the starting point for nurturing trust (信頼を育む起点).

In recruitment marketing (採用マーケティング), no matter how well systems and mechanisms are organized, the most important foundation of trust (信頼の土台) is the ongoing practice of asking whether there is any lie or concealment.
In an era of advancing technologies such as AI, sincerity is increasingly demanded.
Sincere attitude (誠実な姿勢) is presented as the foundation of trust and is increasingly required, especially in recruitment and employer communication.

Signaling theory (Spence, 1973): In situations of information asymmetry (e.g., job seekers cannot fully know a company's reality), information that is costly to disclose (e.g., turnover rates or workplace challenges) functions as a credible, trustworthy signal.

Social exchange theory (Blau, 1964): Explains the principle of reciprocity in human relationships—when one is trusted, one wants to return trust. In hiring, if candidates feel the company was sincere toward them, they tend to respond positively after joining, raising engagement and retention intention.

Employer brand research (Lievens & Highhouse, 2003 and others): Candidates are attracted not only by attractiveness but strongly by credibility/reliability. Mere 'looking good' does not lead to applications; whether the company can actually be believed drives behavior. Consistent, fact-based corporate communication increases application intent and offer-acceptance rates.

Person-organization fit theory (Kristof, 1996): Greater alignment between candidate and company values is associated with higher post-hire satisfaction and retention. By conveying culture and values without exaggeration (as they actually are), mismatched people self-select out early and only truly fitting people remain, which also reduces recruitment costs.
Theories are built from the accumulated work of predecessors (理論は先人たちの積み重ねからできています).
Such theories should be actively applied and utilized in practice (実践に活用していきましょう).

Recruitment marketing (採用マーケティング) is the starting point for building long-term relationships with candidates; companies should deliver messages aligned with corporate philosophy about who they are promising what to.
Executives must personally communicate, in their own words, why particular talent is needed rather than delegating that narrative.
Recruitment branding (採用ブランディング) is the practice of consistently conveying corporate culture and values to candidates.
Trust with candidates requires sincere dialogue that includes not only attractions but also real challenges and issues.
Field managers have a critical role in delivering workplace reality to candidates so they can form an accurate picture of the job.
During selection, managers should verbalize specific job content and expected skills so candidates can imagine the actual work.
Words used in interviews and casual conversations become part of recruitment branding and must be treated as such.
Recruitment should not be treated as solely HR’s job; proactive field involvement reduces post-hire mismatch and improves retention.
Recruitment marketing design rests on three questions: who to target, where in the funnel to reach them, and what branding message to convey.
Measures should be improved through a cycle of hypothesis and verification, with candidate flow made visible through numbers.
Messages must be consistent and must not contradict the actual experience of selection and post-joining work.
Fostering a company-wide recruitment culture requires increasing internal storytellers and coordinating among the field, management, and recruiting functions.
An employee's everyday work itself becomes the company image that job candidates perceive.
Real voices of employees have greater persuasive power than HR messaging and raise conviction both at the application stage and after joining (ツボ 088).
Recruitment branding does not require perfect communication; speaking in one's own words about the appeal and the worries of the job is what supports it (ツボ 087).

Even employees not directly involved in hiring can contribute through posting, referrals, encouragement, and other forms of involvement; a culture in which everyone participates in recruitment is what builds trust (ツボ 089).

Recruitment branding (採用ブランディング) is presented as important advice from consultants to small and medium-sized enterprises (around 100 employees) that struggle with hiring, prompting those companies to consider building their own company brand.

A key practical question in brand strategy is how an SME can create a brand that functions like McDonald’s: one that immediately supplies a recognizable clue or association as soon as the name is heard.

The discussion is framed as an interview with marketing researcher Hiroshi Tanaka (honorary professor at Chuo University and lecturer at the University of Tokyo Faculty of Economics) on the topic of recruitment marketing (採用マーケティング).
The conversation explores what, specifically, should be turned into a brand when a company decides it must construct its own brand identity.
Even global giants such as GAFA were nonexistent 20–30 years ago and began as SMEs; Zoom was founded only in 2011. SMEs should not assume they cannot build a brand.
Not every brand needs to become universally known like McDonald’s. Success depends on choosing which market to compete in; being recognized by a specific professional layer is often sufficient.
Shure (vocal-microphone brand) is commonly seen in karaoke venues, yet most users do not know the brand of the microphone they are using. Recognition among audio professionals is enough.
The same targeting logic applies both to product marketing (“which market”) and to recruitment (“which talent segment”). Identifying the relevant market/segment is critical in both cases.

When seeking STEM talent, categories such as agriculture or chemistry are too broad. Specify the exact expertise wanted (e.g., “people strong in this particular area of physics”). For new graduates, map how physics majors think, job-hunt, and reach the hiring decision.
Recruitment-branding process: (1) define the focused talent segment, (2) research thoroughly what that talent desires, (3) decide what the company can actually offer in response.

The central question in recruitment branding is “what to brand”—i.e., which facet of brand value to raise: awareness, company associations, perceived capability (perceptual capability), or CSR perception.

The branding object can be the product name or the corporate name depending on the target. Developers who want to build a specific product respond to product-name branding; long-tenure, multi-role organizations (e.g., banks) may be better served by corporate-name branding.

Recent talent often commits to a job type or product rather than to a company, making product-name recruitment branding legitimate. Mass new-graduate hiring, however, still favors corporate-name branding.
In engineering, people typically say they joined a service (AWS) rather than the parent company (Amazon).
Brand strategy can be strategically flexible: organizations may emphasize either product brands or the corporate brand itself, depending on what they are committed to.
The brand that should be strengthened (product vs. corporate) differs according to the organization's commitments.
Example: An acquaintance's company conducted Corporate Identity (CI) advertising to raise corporate image; an unexpected side effect was that student applicants for recruitment doubled.

Hiroshi Tanaka (Ph.D. in Economics, Kyoto University) specializes in marketing theory and brand theory; he spent 21 years as a marketing director at Dentsu, has taught marketing in business schools for 25 years, and authored Brand Strategy Theory (2018), which won the Japan Marketing Association Marketing Book Grand Prize, Japan Advertising Academy Award, and Chuo University Academic Research Incentive Award.
In HR (人事), distinct schools or factions (流派) exist, each with different foundational premises of thought; these differences often produce mismatches and talking past one another.
Talent Development (人材開発) school: Organization development is merely complementary or auxiliary. Talent management equals HR systems, which are tools that should be used well.

Organization Development (組織開発) school: Talent development and talent management are only parts of a larger purpose. Methods matter less than the way of being; depending on that way of being, those activities can themselves constitute organization development.
Talent Management (人材マネジメント) school: Talent development and organization development are elements inside a larger system; they should be made to function with both consistency and adaptability.

Recruiting (採用) school: Talent development, organization development, and talent management are merely proof of incompetence in organizations that failed at “who to put on the bus.” If disciplined talent is successfully hired, those other functions become unnecessary.
A shared characteristic of every school is the belief that its own domain is the most wonderful and that it surpasses the others.

Ken Wilber (Integral Theory): “Everything is right, but only partially.” The useful question is therefore not “which view is true” but “from which standpoint or paradigm am I speaking?”—i.e., self-awareness of one’s own lens.
The author’s own default stance is the Talent Management school, frequently judging phenomena by whether they possess consistency.
Deeply studying and growing inside one’s own school is valuable; denying and rejecting people from other schools is worse than not studying at all.

Do not impose one’s own school’s justice. Practice awareness plus dialogue: imagine and try to understand the paradigm from which the other person is speaking (compassion), and adopt a co-creation stance aimed at producing a better situation together.
A paradigm functions like a pair of glasses. Once it is brought into awareness, it can be consciously swapped.
Viewing recruitment (採用) as strategy (戦略) develops a thinking method that serves as the starting point for overall talent-system design.
Recruitment activity can be controlled through a time-based (時間) frame with three linked phases: securing talent (確保), enabling people to thrive/perform (活躍), and continuous improvement (改善).
The chapter’s core is recruitment design that incorporates strategy theory and a management perspective, not only operational hiring tactics.
Classic strategy concepts referenced include Chandler and Porter; readers without that background may find the material abstract.
Translating the chapter into practice depends on the reader’s ability to map ideas onto their own company’s situation, so a post-reading gap is common.
Recruitment often fails because there is no strategy; strategy must be defined before tactics or operations.

Alfred Chandler (1960s) defined strategy as setting the enterprise's long-term goals, deciding the courses of action needed to achieve them, and allocating resources. Top management makes long-term judgments such as whether to invest in new businesses and what organizational structure to adopt.

Michael Porter (1980s) defined strategy as creating unique value that other firms do not possess. Firms should analyze industry and competitors with economic methods and explicitly choose a path to sustainable competitive advantage along axes such as low cost or differentiation.

Henry Mintzberg (1980s) viewed strategy not only as a product of deliberate planning but also as a pattern that emerges from action. Strictly planned execution is rare; consistent direction often arises from on-the-ground trial-and-error and accumulated chance events (emergent strategy).

Ikujiro Nonaka (1990s) located the essence of strategy in the organizational process of sharing and utilizing both explicit knowledge (形式知) and tacit knowledge (暗黙知) to create new value. This view integrates planning and emergence, emphasizes human insight and ethics, and aims at realizing the common good rather than mere profit-seeking.

Four complementary strategy approaches useful for recruitment: (1) clarify long-term goals and resource allocation (plan), (2) offer value different from competitors (differentiation), (3) allow patterns to emerge from trial and error (pattern), and (4) create the future from explicit and tacit knowledge (knowledge creation).
All four approaches share the purpose of responding to environmental change while leveraging the organization's own strengths in order to produce continuous results and a coherent direction.

Recruitment strategy (採用戦略) is a series of decision-making and actions consisting of personnel planning (人員計画), recruitment marketing (採用マーケティング), winning patterns (勝ちパターン), and the recruitment team (採用チーム).

Alfred Chandler (1960s) defined strategy as the setting of a company's basic long-term goals together with the determination of courses of action and resource allocation needed to achieve those goals.
Ikujiro Nonaka (1990s) argued that the essence of strategy is developing the organizational capability to create and utilize knowledge.
Michael Porter defined competitive strategy as establishing a unique position that differs from that of other companies.
Henry Mintzberg (1980s) stated that strategy is something that is formed (Formed) and is not necessarily something that top management plans (Planned).
The value of new research is that it surpasses past research and also includes it (新しい研究の価値は、過去の研究を超え、かつ含んでいるのです).
Recruitment strategy is a series of decisions and actions consisting of personnel planning (人員計画), recruitment marketing, winning patterns, and the recruitment team.
Alfred Chandler defined strategy as a plan that sets an enterprise’s long-term goals, determines the courses of action needed to achieve them, and allocates resources.
Personnel planning is the part of strategy that specifies when, what kind of people, and how many are needed to realize long-term organizational goals, and how those people will be obtained.
The “how” of personnel planning includes not only hiring but also development (育成) and workforce turnover/replacement (代謝).
Long-term goals are formulated and executed to realize the organization’s mission and vision; those goals themselves change with internal and external environmental conditions.
According to a cited survey, 68.39% of organizations formulate personnel plans; recruitment staff should understand personnel planning as foundational theory.
Personnel planning should be formulated by internal stakeholders bringing different perspectives; it is most often compiled by HR, corporate planning, and top management.
HR’s role in personnel planning: grasp labor-market conditions, control medium- to long-term personnel costs, and take a company-wide optimization view.
Corporate planning’s role: judge what talent is needed while designing new businesses and growth strategies for existing businesses.
Management’s role: decide how the organization adapts to the external environment, realizes strategy, and governs internal decision-making as a whole.
Personnel planning (人員計画) is developed into three HR functions: 育成 (development/training of people), 採用 (recruitment), and 代謝 (metabolism—replacing or rotating people out).
Personnel planning answers when, what kind of people, and how many are needed; based on that plan, the organization develops people, hires people, and replaces people.

If one of the three functions is insufficient, the others compensate. Example: if development lags, recruitment fills the gap; if recruitment cannot keep up, metabolism (turnover/replacement) is delayed.
The three functions are organically linked. Progress across them is used to review (feedback) the personnel plan and keep it under control.
Among the three functions, the recruitment plan (採用計画) is the concrete specification of when, what kind of people, and how many to hire.
A staffing/personnel plan (人員計画) for achieving long-term organizational goals specifies when people are needed, what kinds of people, how many, and how they will be prepared or obtained.
Staffing/personnel plans (人員計画) are distinct from but related to recruitment plans (採用計画); Figure 092 illustrates this relationship.
Recruitment staff (採用担当者) must consider the extent to which they need to understand the broader staffing/personnel plan, not only the recruitment plan itself.
Personnel planning (人員計画) is formulated in order to maximize the possibility of realizing long-term goals (長期目標実現).
人員計画 (personnel plan) is defined as a plan that indicates 'when, what kind of people, and how many' are needed in order to realize strategy (戦略実現のための「いつ・どんな人が・何人」必要かを示したもの).

A January 2025 survey of 1,246 Japanese company workers (executives and employees) found that 34.4% (429 people) were involved in recruitment-related work. Among those involved, common activities were document screening (57.1%), interviews (48.5%), company information sessions (46.2%), and hiring decisions (30.1%).
Among people involved in recruitment, 68.3% reported that their company has a personnel plan, 25.2% said it does not, and 6.5% did not know.

Existence of a personnel plan correlates strongly with company size: only 26.5% of companies with 10 or fewer employees have one; this rises to 54.1% for companies with 11–30 employees and reaches approximately 80% for companies with 31 or more employees, with little further increase beyond that size.

Among respondents whose companies have a personnel plan (293 people), the main party responsible for compiling/formulating it is most often the HR department (28.7%), followed by the management/administration department (20.8%) and the executive layer (16.4%).

The primary formulator of the personnel plan shifts with company size: executives in companies of 10 or fewer people; corporate planning department in companies of 11–30 people; administration department in companies of 31–100 people; and HR department in companies of 101 or more people.
A survey found that quite a large number of corporate organizations formulate personnel plans (人員計画).
The quality of those personnel plans cannot be determined from the survey itself.

According to Tsutomu Okamoto of Deloitte Tohmatsu Consulting LLC (25 years of corporate consulting experience), companies that formulate personnel plans at a level that can be called '人事の管理会計' (HR management accounting) are 2–3割 (roughly 20–30%) or less of the total.
Substantial room for improvement remains in the quality of personnel planning.
The following section (ツボ094) addresses utilization of personnel planning.
In Japanese companies with 31 or more employees, approximately 80% have formulated personnel (workforce) plans (人員計画).
Chart 093 presents survey results on the presence/absence of personnel plans (N=429) and the primary entity responsible for formulating those plans (N=293).

Among formulating entities, the HR department (人事部門) accounts for 28.7%; 'don't know' (わからない) is 6.5%. Other mentioned entities include management layer (経営層), management/control department (経営管理部門 / 管理部門), business planning department (事業企画部門), and on-site management (現場マネジメント).
Results are broken down by company size: 10 or fewer employees (N=49), 11–30 (N=74), 31–100 (N=89), 101–300 (N=61), 301–1000 (N=44), and 1001 or more (N=93).
Size-specific 'don't know' or related rates shown include 6.8%, 2.2%, 4.5%, 6.6%, and 6.5% across the respective size bands.
For the person in charge of recruitment (採用担当者), confirming and understanding the personnel/staffing plan (人員計画) is the starting point of recruitment work (採用業務).
Personnel planning (人員計画) is for overall organizational optimization, not merely setting a hiring-headcount target from management such as “how many people to hire this period.”
Before recruitment starts, multi-factor analysis is required: business plans, organizational age structure, diversification of employment types, and future DX (digital transformation).
Without that whole-organization view, HR is driven only by short-term “we are short-staffed, hire immediately” requests, which does not produce sustainable organizational growth.

Treat personnel planning as a productivity plan (生産性の計画): decide how much productivity to secure and by what means over the long term, aligned with business direction and the future shape of the organization—not only “how many to hire.”

Method: visualize past and present metrics such as sales per person and efficiency per labor cost; set the future productivity level to aim for; then derive required headcount and capability requirements.

Options such as long-term new-graduate development, mid-career immediate contributors, IT-ization of work, or outsourcing to partners should all be judged on the productivity axis: where the firm’s competitive advantage comes from, and which work should stay in-house.

Personnel planning takes time (often six months to a year in larger firms) because it must incorporate each business unit’s future talent needs, financial conditions, and age-structure change. Realizing you need a personnel plan only when you start the recruitment plan is already too late.

Recruiters are not powerless even when personnel planning is a large project. By understanding—through dialogue with business units and leadership—why this skill set is needed at this timing, they can give candidates more convincing information, which in turn can raise offer-acceptance rates.
Quality-focused recruitment from a productivity viewpoint can reduce post-hire mismatch between employees and the organization.

Recruitment officers should not merely fill headcount in a risk-averse, numbers-only way; they occupy a position that can qualitatively raise the entire recruiting process by applying a productivity lens.

Holding an overall-optimization personnel-planning perspective lets recruiters look beyond filling the immediate openings and instead conduct high-quality hiring that anticipates the organization’s future.
The subsequent section (ツボ 095) covers how to formulate personnel plans.
Personnel planning should not be framed as deciding a headcount (how many people) but as a long-term plan for productivity.
Starting from the question 'How many people should we have?' typically yields no clear answer.
Instead, start from the question of what level of productivity the company should have.
Concrete target example: raise sales per person from 50 million yen to 70 million yen.
Once productivity is considered by business unit and by region, the required number of people follows from those productivity targets.
Do not evaluate goals solely by surface-level target numbers (表面の目標数字); also identify and grasp the underlying purpose (背景にある目的) those numbers are meant to serve.
Key statement: 表面の目標数字だけでなく、その背景にある目的を捉えましょう

Personnel planning (人員計画) is formulated using a four-step method, based on Deloitte Tohmatsu Consulting’s ‘Strategic Management of Staffing and Labor Costs’ (要員・人件費の戦略的マネジメント), reorganized by the author.

Step 1 — Visualize productivity from past to present: Gather roughly five years of data as planning judgment material. Headcount and labor costs alone are insufficient; the key data are productivity indicators.
Core productivity metrics: 人件費効率 (labor-cost efficiency) and 1人当たり売上高 (sales per employee). Review several years of these figures to grasp the organization’s productivity trend.
Formulas given: 人件費効率 = 売上 + APS; 1人当たり売上高 = 売上高 : 社員数 (symbols may reflect OCR of division operators).
If sales per employee is declining year by year, analyze the reasons and decide what should be done going forward.

Step 2 — Diagnose the gap between the natural course (成り行き) and the should-be state (あるべき姿): Simulate what personnel composition, labor costs, and productivity will become if no measures are taken. Then define the あるべき姿 required to achieve long-term goals (e.g., a mid-term management plan) and compare the two.
Critical comparison rule: Do not compare the current state with the should-be state; compare the natural-course trajectory (成り行き) with the should-be state (あるべき姿).
Step 3 — Consider HR/personnel measures (人事施策の検討) to close the identified gap.
To reach the desired/ideal state (あるべき姿), HR measures (人事施策) must be examined and planned.
HR measures consist of three functions: development/training (育成), recruitment/hiring (採用), and metabolism/turnover (代謝). See related point ツボ 092.
Step 4 in the process is annual goal setting (年度ごとの目標設定).
After considering HR measures, formulate a feasible company-wide personnel plan (全社の人員計画) for each fiscal year and set corresponding targets.
Deploy (展開) the company-wide personnel plan and goals down to each department (部門ごと).
The subsequent topic (ツボ 096) covers winning patterns in recruitment (採用の勝ちパターン).

Personnel planning is formulated in four steps: (1) visualization of productivity, (2) gap diagnosis between the natural course (if nothing is done) and the desired state, (3) consideration of HR measures, and (4) setting of annual goals with ongoing monitoring of actual-vs-target gaps.

Step 1 (visualization): Use historical data (e.g., five years) from past to present as judgment material for planning. Capture not only headcount but productivity metrics such as labor-cost efficiency and sales per person.

Step 2 (gap diagnosis): Simulate the unattended trajectory—personnel composition, labor costs, and productivity in a future year (20XX). Separately define the desired personnel composition, labor costs, and productivity required to realize long-term goals (the medium-term management plan). Identify the gap between the two.
Step 3 (HR measures): Design interventions—development (育成), hiring (採用), and workforce metabolism/turnover (代謝)—that close the gap and enable the organization to reach the desired state.

Step 4 (annual targets): Translate the chosen HR measures into a company-wide personnel plan with yearly goals, then cascade the plan and targets to individual departments. Continuously monitor the gap between actual results and targets each year.
The four-step framework is drawn from Deloitte Tohmatsu Consulting’s “Strategic Management of Personnel and Labor Costs” (supervised by Tsutomu Baimoto).

A planning or visioning exercise is to compare 成り行きの未来 (naruyuki no mirai: the future that unfolds if current trends continue without intervention) with あるべき姿 (arubeki sugata: the ideal or desired future state).
The Japanese instruction on the page is: 「成り行きの未来とあるべき姿を比較しましょう」 (Let's compare the unfolding/default future with the way things ought to be).
Successful new-graduate hiring (新卒採用) companies share identifiable winning patterns derived from differences versus struggling companies (採用成功企業 vs 採用苦労企業).

Pattern 1 — New strategy plus PDCA improvement: Review past hiring, analyze the market, and design a plan to win rather than repeating last year’s methods. Continuously consider new measures, run PDCA on recruitment activities, and keep improving tactics; this builds advantage in an intensifying hiring race.

Pattern 2 — Internal alignment and right people in the right interview roles: Recruiters, interviewers, and executives must coordinate so students hear a consistent message. Screening interviews that narrow a large pool require different skills than one-on-one interviews aimed at securing offer acceptance; interviewer selection therefore determines outcomes.

Pattern 3 — Channel mix and message refinement: Decide how heavily to use job boards, information sessions, advertising, and other channels. Then craft and broadcast messages and content that actually reach the firm’s target student segment.

Pattern 4 — Offer the right people: Extend offers only to candidates who fit the organizational culture. Deciding whom to offer is a process of judging both cultural compatibility (自社との相性) and the candidate’s own intent (本人の意思).
In large-scale, easily standardized new-graduate (shinsotsu) hiring, inertia (慣性) readily takes hold, so organizations tend to repeat past success recipes and fail to adapt.
What is required is double-loop learning that transcends that inertia: learning that goes beyond existing frameworks to incorporate new thinking and behavior.
Transformation must cover not only recruitment and selection processes but also HR systems and organizational culture; only then can a firm ride out environmental change and keep strong hiring power.
Recent reform examples include raising starting salaries and expanding the use of internships.
A viewpoint that identifies people who will actually thrive after they join is indispensable.
The next key point (097) will examine winning patterns for mid-career / experienced-hire recruitment.
Successful new-graduate hiring (新卒採用) requires going beyond uniformly running large-scale operations and instead continuously improving the recruitment framework (枠組み) itself.

The winning pattern for 新卒採用 consists of four linked elements: (1) new policies plus PDCA-cycle improvement, (2) internal cooperation and appropriate interviewer assignment, (3) channel design and message/content refinement, and (4) presenting job offers (内定) to the right talent.

Recruitment-successful firms versus struggling firms differ sharply on market-winning planning (59.5 % vs 7.5 %, gap 52.0 points) and on whether the PDCA cycle in hiring actually functions (55.1 % vs 20.0 %, gap 35.1 points); the text flags double-loop learning in this context.

Internal cooperation in hiring is rated sufficient by 77.7 % of successful firms versus 40.7 % of struggling firms (gap 37.0); interviewers/selectors are assigned to match each selection stage by 90.7 % versus 65.8 % (gap 24.9).

Channel design that makes the firm visible to target talent is achieved by 45.5 % of successful firms versus 24.4 % of struggling firms; messages and content aimed at those targets are well-refined by 69.1 % versus 45.7 % (gap 23.4).
Successful firms are far more likely to be able to extend 内定 to talent they judge appropriate (approximately 73.4 % versus 21.5 %).
The four-element comparison is drawn from Nakamura Amae’s book Recruitment Strategy (中村天江『採用のストラテジー』).
New graduate recruitment (新卒採用) is an activity that tends to generate 'inertia' (慣性) because it consists of repeating enormous volumes of operational work.
Key statement: 新卒採用は膨大なオペレーションの繰り返しによる「慣性」が生じやすい活動です。
The concept of operational inertia here refers to how large-scale, highly repetitive hiring processes (typical of Japanese campus/new-graduate recruiting) make the activity resistant to change.

Winning patterns for experienced (mid-career) hiring are derived from differences between companies that achieve hiring results (successful hiring companies) and those that do not (struggling hiring companies).

Successful experienced-hiring companies analyze their surrounding hiring environment and properly establish a 'plan to win'; their PDCA cycle functions; and they can present job offers to appropriate talent.

Double-loop learning in hiring is required: learning that goes beyond existing frameworks to incorporate new ideas and actions. Compared with new-graduate hiring, experienced hiring often lacks uniform methods and selection criteria, so interviews and pass/fail judgments easily produce individual differences; therefore building objective mechanisms is a key point.

Target talent must be clearly defined. Unlike uniform new-graduate hiring, experienced hiring requires different expertise by occupation and position, so messages and content aimed at target talent must be carefully crafted. Required talent profiles often split between 'immediate contribution (sokosenryoku) focus' versus 'company-likeness/culture focus,' making internal alignment necessary.

The entire hiring organization (all people involved in hiring) must be coordinated toward the goal and able to respond quickly to changing situations (agile). Because applicant numbers are often limited, the critical question is how to go after scarce talent. Executives and field staff begin wooing candidates from the early stages; hiring methods therefore emphasize 'attracting' talent.

A key practice is early-stage alignment with the candidate on 'what role the company wants them to play' versus 'what the candidate themselves wants to achieve,' so that both sides obtain mutual conviction/satisfaction.
In experienced-hire (mid-career) recruitment, compensation adjustments and the provision of flexible work styles are major deciding factors.
For experienced hires, comparison of annual income with the previous job is important; work-life-balance elements such as transfers and remote work are increasingly demanded.
Management-layer decision-making is the key to making these offerings possible.
Experienced-hire recruitment requires a design that delicately matches the company’s hiring needs with what the candidate wants to achieve.
The winning pattern for attracting diverse and scarce talent is: PDCA-based objective system-building, optimization of messages to the target, and an agile recruitment organization.
The next section (ツボ 098) covers a hiring-improvement model.

Delicate matching in mid-career (experienced-hire) recruitment is enabled by three conditions: double-loop learning in hiring, clear target definition, and an agile recruitment system oriented to the goal.

Winning pattern 1 — double-loop learning is operating: successful firms far more often have planning that can win in the hiring market (51.4 % vs 4.8 %, gap 46.6 points), a functioning PDCA cycle in recruitment (56.6 % vs 14.5 %, gap 42.1), and the ability to extend offers to truly suitable talent (95.3 % vs 73.4 %, gap 21.9).

Winning pattern 2 — the target is explicit: successful firms more frequently have verbalized talent requirements / target-person profiles (76.1 % vs 49.2 %, gap 26.9) and have refined messages and content aimed at those targets.

Winning pattern 3 — the hiring organization is agile toward its purpose: successful firms more often enjoy sufficient internal cooperation (64.9 % vs 36.5 %, gap 28.4) and train interviewers / selection staff (35.4 % vs 12.7 %, gap 22.7).
A core consistency requirement is alignment among (a) talent requirements (what is judged), (b) selection personnel (who judges), and (c) selection methods (how judgment is made).
Source framing: the patterns and figures are derived from Nakamura Tenae’s “Recruitment Strategy” and recast as Chart 097 on experienced-hire winning patterns.
To recruit scarce (rare) talent as an entire team, internal misalignments or discrepancies should be eliminated.
Key principle: 希少な人材を全員で口説くために、内部のズレをなくしていきましょう (In order for everyone to court/pursue rare talent, let’s eliminate internal gaps/misalignments.)
Nakamura Tenae's Recruitment Wheel Model (採用ホイールモデル), developed through research on recruitment strategy, is a framework for continuously improving a company's hiring.
The Wheel Model consists of six interconnected phases that companies should cycle through repeatedly, not treat as a one-time checklist.

Phase 1 — Premises of employment (雇用の前提): HR strategy, talent management policy, HR systems, compensation systems, employment security, workplace culture, work environment, corporate brand, reputation, HR technology, and related foundations.

Phase 2 — Premises of the recruitment/selection process (募集・選考プロセスの前提): recruitment goals, budget, department structure, hiring requirements, decision-making authority, accumulated know-how, and recruitment technology.
Phase 3 — Design of the recruitment/selection process: KPI design for recruitment and selection steps, choice of media, choice of tools, and building the operating structure.

Phase 4 — Execution of the recruitment/selection process: forming the candidate pool, document screening, interviews, pass/fail decisions, generating candidate interest, negotiating terms, reference checks, offer follow-up, contract signing, and tool use.
Phase 5 — Results of the recruitment/selection process: number hired, quality of hires, time to hire, hiring satisfaction, applicant volume, selection pass rates, and offer-decline rates.

Phase 6 — Post-employment results (雇用後の成果): retention after joining, onboarding/ramp-up, capability demonstration, performance, person-environment fit, individual satisfaction, supervisor/organizational evaluation, organizational outcomes, competitive advantage, and accumulation of hiring know-how.
The model is named after a bicycle wheel: when the hiring mechanism turns smoothly, better talent is attracted and the organization grows.
The critical mechanism is a feedback loop: after each hiring cycle, accumulate information and feed it into the next cycle so accuracy improves over time.
Example feedback actions: if desired talent did not apply, change sourcing methods; if many offers are declined, improve candidate communication; if retention is poor, strengthen post-hire follow-up.
Reflecting activity results into the next plan raises the precision of subsequent recruitment.
Recruitment (採用) is a process that involves not only the HR department (人事部) but also executives/management (経営層) and on-site/frontline managers (現場マネージャー).
In the Wheel Model (ホイールモデル), the function that connects all stakeholders and maintains consistency across the recruitment process is defined as the Recruitment Hub (採用ハブ).
Team-based approaches to recruitment are covered in Chapter 2.
The following section (ツボ 099) presents a practical example of the Wheel Model.
The defining feature of the Wheel Model is that it represents adoption not as an arrow-shaped linear process but as a cycle (循環).
Technical terms: ホイールモデル (Wheel Model); 矢羽型の直線プロセス (arrow-feather/arrow-type linear process); 採用 (adoption/recruitment).
The Recruitment Wheel Model (from tsubo 098) has six phases used to analyze hiring systems, illustrated by Yumemi, a company known for engineer recruitment.

Phase 1 (employment premises): Yumemi's goal is to be 'the No.1 company where engineers can grow.' It uses distinctive practices such as a salary self-determination system, unlimited paid leave, and a manager-less flat organization that emphasizes employee autonomy, plus tech events and SNS to raise industry awareness.

Phase 2 (premises of the recruitment/selection process): The company targets roughly 100 hires per year and strengthens new-graduate recruiting. Requirements stress 'autonomy, self-responsibility, and self-learning,' with dual evaluation of technical skill and culture fit. Data analysis is used to build candidate pools and optimize the selection flow.

Phase 3 (design of the recruitment/selection process): Multiple channels are used (direct recruiting, referrals, tech events). Candidates are screened rigorously via technical tests and portfolio review. The first interview is designed as an attractor; the final interview is for strict selection.

Phase 4 (execution of the process): The entire flow from document screening to offer is completed within one month for rapid decisions. Information is actively shared during selection to raise candidate interest; offers are sent the same day to encourage prompt decisions.

Phase 5 (results of the process): Offer-acceptance rate is maintained above 90%. Final-interview pass rate is about 25%, reflecting continued selective hiring. Thousands of applications are received annually, supporting a stable candidate pool.

Phase 6 (post-employment results): Early turnover is low and post-hire mismatches are few. New graduates typically reach lead-engineer level in 1–2 years. Hired talent's technical outreach creates a virtuous cycle that supports subsequent recruiting.

The recruitment hub function: Management is actively involved and the whole company participates. Data-analysis feedback loops continually refine strategy so that high-quality talent is acquired and organizational competitiveness is raised.
Yumemi Inc. (ゆめみ社) is a good example of accurately operating each phase of the Recruitment Wheel Model (採用ホイールモデル) and making recruitment a driving force for corporate growth.
Yumemi publicly discloses all recruitment-related data, covering goals, processes, and actual results.
The analysis of Yumemi was based on its disclosed document titled Recruitment Policy / Recruitment Marketing Policy (採用方針・採用マーケティング方針).
A culture of thoroughly documenting, reviewing, and disclosing recruitment information is a source of competitiveness for acquiring excellent talent.
The next section (ツボ100) addresses the core of recruitment strategy.
Yumemi Inc. (ゆめみ社) continuously polishes its recruitment cycle by thoroughly verbalizing, reviewing, and disclosing processes.
The company is analyzed using the Recruitment Wheel Model (採用ホイールモデル).
Management policy targets being the No.1 company where engineers can grow (エンジニアが成長できる会社No.1), with unique systems such as salary self-determination (給与自己決定制度) and unlimited paid leave (有給取り放題).
Organizational culture is a manager-less flat Teal-type organization (ティール型組織) that emphasizes employee autonomy.
Post-employment outcomes include low early turnover, few mismatches after joining, and many new graduates reaching lead engineer level within 1-2 years.
A virtuous recruitment cycle exists: hired talent performs technical outreach that leads to subsequent hiring.
Recruitment branding is strengthened via technical events and SNS to raise industry recognition.
Hiring goal is annual increase of about 100 people, with focus on new-graduate recruitment.
Requirements emphasize autonomy, self-responsibility, and self-learning (自律・自責・自学), evaluating both technical skill and culture fit.
Data analysis is used to accumulate know-how, form candidate pools, and continuously optimize the selection process.
Offer acceptance rate is maintained above 90%; final-interview pass rate is 25%, indicating strict selection.
Several thousand applications are received annually, successfully forming a candidate pool.
Recruitment channels prioritize direct recruiting, referral hiring (リファラル採用), and technical events.
Selection speed targets completion from document screening to offer notification within one month for rapid decision-making.
Offers are sent the same day to facilitate candidate decisions; information provision during selection is strengthened to raise candidate interest.
The CEO personally participates in hiring, making it a company-wide activity.
Selection data is analyzed to improve strategy continuously; a feedback loop uses hiring results to optimize the next cycle and raise organizational competitiveness.
Selection criteria include technical tests and portfolio evaluation for rigorous ability assessment.
Selection flow designs the first interview as an attraction (アトラクト) stage and the final interview as a strict-selection (厳選) stage.
The core of recruitment strategy is not 'numbers' (securing headcount) but 'time'.

Traditionally in Japan, the main goal of hiring was securing the required number of people; with population decline and a tighter labor market, firms must also create an environment in which hired talent can actually perform after joining.
Nakamura Tenae (中村天江) in 『採用のストラテジー』 defines hiring from a management-strategy viewpoint as 'the act of controlling the time required to acquire talent' (人材獲得の時間をコントロールする行為).
Three kinds of time are involved in this view of hiring; the first two are: (1) time until talent is secured, and (2) time until that talent becomes productive.
Time-to-hire: delays cause lost business opportunities and extra burden on remaining staff that worsens the work environment.

New-graduate hiring follows a fixed calendar, so firms can collect many applicants inside a set window; experienced (mid-career) hiring has irregular timing, creating the risk that time simply elapses without positions being filled.
The make-or-buy choice ('develop internally versus hire externally') itself arises from the managerial need to use time efficiently.
Because the share of experienced hiring is rising, companies must now confront 'time required for hiring' as a serious strategic issue.
Time-to-productivity: 'good hiring' is not merely acquiring excellent people but ensuring they deliver results after they join.
Japanese 'membership-type' (メンバーシップ型) employment culture expects post-hire development, so new joiners need support that lets them adapt quickly to the work.
Even highly skilled experienced hires now receive strengthened onboarding (入社後の立ち上げ支援) so they can start contributing sooner.
The more a firm expects high performance from a hire, the more important it is to prepare an environment in which that person can fully exercise their abilities.
Strategic hiring therefore requires the integration of recruitment strategy and talent-development strategy.
Recruitment is characterized by repeating similar processes over time.
Repeating the same hiring processes creates a risk that improvement stalls and inefficient processes continue.
A core challenge is the time lag until recruitment results become visible, which misaligns with the timing of the next hiring cycle.
Companies need to use past recruitment data to conduct more precise, higher-accuracy hiring.
Recruitment time (採用の時間) has two critical dimensions that must be shortened: (1) time until talent is secured, and (2) time until talent becomes fully productive/active.
Shortening time-to-hire (人材を確保するまでの時間) prevents loss of business opportunities (事業機会の損失を防ぐ).
Shortening time-to-productivity (人材が活躍するまでの時間) realizes early combat effectiveness / early contribution of new hires (早期戦力化を実現する).
When reviewing the recruitment process, time must be controlled by advancing data utilization and operational efficiency (データ活用・効率化を進める).
Framework source: based on Nakamura Tene, Recruitment Strategy (採用のストラテジー).
Peter F. Drucker (P.F. ドラッカー) stated that time is the most scarce resource: 「時間は最も希少な資源」.
This quote emphasizes time as a critical, limited resource in management and productivity thinking.
Recruitment (採用) is part of management strategy (経営戦略). The core question is how to allocate human resources (人材という資源) and thereby create the future.
Workforce planning (人員計画) perspectives (tips 092–095) and treating recruitment as management of time (経営の時間管理, tip 100) are insights that fundamentally support business competitiveness.
Recruitment should be positioned as a company-wide cycle (全社的な循環) and treated as a premise for management-level decision-making and consistency.

Field managers (現場マネージャー) are both executors of recruitment and co-designers of the team’s future. They must specifically consider what talent the team needs, how to accept people, and how to utilize them.

Hints for managers on needed talent, onboarding, and utilization are packed in winning patterns (勝ちパターン, tips 096–097) and workforce-planning thinking (tip 094). Managers should look beyond short-term response to long-term development (育成) and retention (定着).
Recruitment staff (採用担当者) are the existence that connects the “in-between” of company and candidates.
Winning patterns (勝ちパターン, tips 096–097) offer practical improvement perspectives; the wheel model (ホイールモデル, tips 098–099) stresses the importance of circulating mechanisms.
Tips 091–093 should be grasped as a strategic recruitment viewpoint (戦略的採用の視座).
Recruitment should be discussed not in terms of numbers (数) but in terms of quality (質) and sustainability (持続性).
Recruitment (採用) is not merely the act of selecting someone; it is an activity in which the organization and the individual meet and mutually nurture each other.
Recruitment functions as an entry point for reflecting on why one is currently in this organization and what kinds of people one wants to work with going forward.
Related topics to study alongside recruitment: personnel/workforce planning (人員計画, tips 092 and 094) and the time perspective (時間の視点, tip 100).
Treating recruitment as a personal matter (自分ごと) reveals new meaning both in one’s career and in how one relates to the organization.
Recruitment (採用) is framed as weaving “stories with hope” (「希望ある物語」を編むこと): assembling people so those present can hold hope.
Organization (組織) is explained as 組んで織りなす: 組む means putting shoulders together toward a common purpose; 織りなす means collaborating through division of roles.
Because a business has a purpose, people who agree on what they are trying to achieve and can work together should join (組む).

Purpose and means can interchange: unexpected organizational movements can give birth to businesses, and people who arrive at those moments can spark innovation—this is both difficult and interesting.

Interviewee context: Yamada Yuji (山田裕嗣), representative director of Reisan-sha, has visited about 80 interesting companies in Japan and knows advanced companies worldwide, speaking on organization and hiring.

Organizations viewed as living organisms survive by continually aiming at a fictional 'consistently continuing thing' (一貫して続くもの). Because both the environment and the self keep changing, organization-building consists of repeatedly trying to restore consistency amid ongoing fluctuation, course-correcting while attempting to hold the center.

The basis for that course-correction is '物語' (narrative/story). Humans live by consuming meaning; they therefore seek stories. Living without context is difficult, so people strive to align with a declared future such as 'we will create this kind of future.'

A usable (if incomplete) definition of a good organization is that the people inside it can keep having hope about remaining involved. The place should feel genuinely hopeful rather than excessively unhappy; a key signal is the felt sense that 'this story seems like it could become a good one.'

Organizational goals and direction are not fixed; they change flexibly with circumstances, yet some consistent core must still be maintained. That core includes mission and vision, but equally the human elements of narrative and the ability of involved people to hold hope.
Organizational consistency is therefore not merely a formal declaration; it is supported by a rich story that encompasses history, lived experience and culture.

Hiring is inherently difficult because fit must be judged in roughly three interviews, whereas real alignment and the sensing of discomfort occur only after people are already inside the organization.

High-performing companies worldwide often go beyond interviews: they spend about a full day actually working together. The interview is treated as the start of a relationship (analogous to dating); for mid-career hires the 'marriage' timing depends on mutual circumstances. Firms that invest in this kind of alignment tend to produce results.

Swedish self-management example (leadership-training firm active since ~1990–2000): candidates arrive dreaming of a workplace in which everyone works autonomously. The firm sends a 'Scare Them Away Letter' stating that self-management means taking responsibility oneself and that freedom is accompanied by responsibility.
In hiring, even after thoroughly explaining conditions, obtaining candidate agreement, and issuing an offer letter, mismatches and mistakes can still occur.
Giving extensive advance notice (予告) before key hiring steps is important because candidates may be fearful.
Psychological contract (心理的契約): both job candidates and companies often independently form unstated images and expectations of the role and organization.
Post-hire reality frequently differs completely from those pre-hire images; this mismatch is a commonly reported problem.
Converting implicit expectations into explicit, shared knowledge (形式知) between candidate and company is an important way to reduce such gaps.
Recruitment is commonly viewed as adding new strength to an organization, but its essence may lie in 'breaking' existing order rather than merely adding people.

Biologist Shinichi Fukuoka states that for life, destroying is more important than creating: oxidation and waste products arise and must be eliminated, otherwise new order cannot be generated. Life therefore constantly decomposes itself while simultaneously reconstructing itself, maintaining a precarious balance and flow known as dynamic equilibrium (動的平衡), which is the essence of life.

Takeshi Osawa, who shaped Recruit's organizational culture, argues in Psychological Management that an organization that merely preserves order becomes rigid and eventually stops growing. It is therefore necessary to intentionally introduce chaos (disorder) in order to break existing order once.

Hiring is an effective means of generating such chaos: when new people join, prior human relationships, ways of working, and atmosphere are shaken, producing temporary confusion and friction that constitute organizational metabolism (新陳代謝).

This process generates new questions, updates thinking, and reorganizes culture. Thus recruitment is not simply filling vacancies but an act of once destroying existing order so that it can be reconstructed.
Osawa advises: 'Intentionally create chaos' in order to introduce fluctuation into the organization and break its own shell.

If an organization is truly a living entity, its recruitment activity should likewise be a living process—destroying while creating, i.e., dynamic equilibrium. Corporate hiring therefore begins by breaking existing frameworks and previous methods; this is not something to fear but preparation for living toward the future.

Hiring interviewers often activate an unofficial “俺フィルター” (personal gut-feel filter), judging pass/fail with unfounded remarks such as “I can tell by intuition” or “it just didn’t click,” instead of evidence.
A small next step against gut-feel hiring is to ask every candidate in the next interview one behavioral question: “How did you actually do this action in the past?”

The fundamental fix is structured interviewing: share a common frame (e.g. STAR method) and evaluation criteria among interviewers so questions stay “behavior-based” rather than “feeling-based.” Related practices: understanding interview problems (ツボ045) and introducing structured interviews (ツボ047).
Hiring requirements are often never verbalized; the field only says “とりあえずいい人” / “a decent person,” so definition proceeds on unspoken “vibe and atmosphere.”
A small next step is, in a requirements meeting, to ask once: “What kind of episode would that person have?”

The fundamental fix is to structure requirements with Must / Want / Nice, or along four axes—skill, stance, behavior, and experience—and run a workshop that verbalizes them from concrete episodes. Related: structuring requirements (ツボ022) and verbalizing experience–behavior (ツボ025).
Management and the front line often want different people (e.g. field needs immediate contributors because of understaffing; the president wants future potential) and never discuss it.
A small next step is to schedule just one 5-minute gap chat between the president and a field leader during the selection period.

The fundamental fix is to design hiring requirements from both “ideal” and “real examples,” then institutionalize alignment meetings among management, field, and HR. Related: aligning hiring requirements (ツボ022) and prioritizing them (ツボ027).
Candidates who receive an offer (“please join us”) are often then left with no contact for weeks and decline.
A small next step is to offer the offer-holder one short online meeting (even 10 minutes) with a named field person.

The fundamental fix is a designed follow-up plan for offer holders (1on1s, contact with field members, intention checks) to keep engagement until join date. Related: experience design from offer to joining (ツボ077) and reviewing hiring CX (ツボ078).

Common hiring failure: field interviewers fail to appear or cancel at the last minute with excuses such as “an urgent meeting came up” or “I can’t leave another project,” which inconveniences candidates and leads to declines. A lightweight intervention is to ask at the start of the month whether they can block even 13-minute interview slots. The fundamental fix is to treat securing interviewer calendar time as part of their official work and to share with managers that the interviewer role is a mission that directly drives results (linked to points 013 on sharing roles/responsibilities and 043 on designing the interview experience).

Common hiring failure: interviewer evaluations split (one person praises, another opposes) and the decision collapses into 忖度 (reading the room / political deference). A lightweight intervention in the selection meeting is to ask once, fact-checking, “Which specific statement from the interview did you base that judgment on?” The fundamental fix is to align evaluation axes in advance, then run selection meetings as fact-based comparisons using STAR answers and to standardize recording of the reasons for each judgment (linked to points 045 on understanding interview issues and 046 on designing selection meetings).

Common hiring failure: newly hired employees immediately resign saying “what I was told was different” or “the culture doesn’t fit.” A lightweight intervention is to add one item to information sessions and interviews: “things you actually think are tough here.” The fundamental fix is to redesign the hiring candidate experience (CX) so that expectations are controlled, and to promote unvarnished, honest information sharing during briefings and interviews (linked to points 074 on sharing reality through information dissemination and 076 on sincere sharing of current conditions during the selection stages).

Common hiring failure: field interviewers have low skill and produce the opposite of the intended effect, lowering rather than raising candidate motivation through unconscious “cooling words” such as “we’re pretty strict here” or “someone like this might not make it.” A lightweight intervention is to ask the interviewer, before the next interview, to spend even one minute conveying a feeling of welcome. The fundamental fix is to introduce interviewer training that makes them conscious of the encounter as an experience for the candidate, using collections of common NG words plus role-play practice (linked to points 045 on interviewer behavior and 070 on designing the candidate experience).
STAR method is used as the factual basis for comparing candidates in selection meetings so that judgments rest on concrete Situation-Task-Action-Result evidence rather than impression or politics.

Hiring CX (candidate-experience) design and expectation control are presented as the systemic remedy for post-hire “it was different from what I heard” attrition; honest disclosure of difficulties is treated as a feature, not a bug, of the selection process.

The book 「人事と採用のセオリー」 (The Theory of Human Resources) by 曽和利光 (Sosumu, 2018) is a practical work by an author who served as HR and recruitment lead at Recruit, Lifenet Insurance, and Open House. It teaches practical ways of thinking to ensure the consistency required in HR work, and is distinctive for specifically addressing how to design personnel ‘metabolism’ (turnover/rotation), not only recruitment.

The book 「要員・人件費の戦略的マネジメント」 (Strategic Management of Staffing and Personnel Costs), authored by Ting Co. and supervised by Tsutomu Okamoto (Rodo Gyosei, 2013), lets readers vicariously experience the difficulties of drawing up personnel plans. Each theme features a different fictional company so that various cases can be examined; readers often feel ‘this is just like our company.’ Actual work processes are shown in detail so the content can be applied on the job.

The book 「「いい会社」はどこにある?」 (Where Are the ‘Good Companies’?) by Masahiro Watanabe (Diamond, 2022) presents the real picture of companies based on interviews the journalist-author conducted with more than 1,000 working employees. The raw, realistic information is highly interesting. For recruiters it can be used for competitor research and, by imagining one’s own company being listed with equally candid information, to train an objective view.

The Iceberg Model (McClelland, 1973) describes human abilities as a hierarchical structure of behavior, skills/knowledge, and motives/values, analogized to an iceberg with only the tip visible above water.

Spencer & Spencer (1993) systematized the Iceberg Model as competency theory, showing that deep-layer elements below the water surface (values, motives, personality) are closely related to job performance.

The Iceberg Model connects to the multilayered nature of hiring requirements (experience, behavior, skills, stance) and underscores the importance of observation and inference in interviews and evaluations.
Meta-analyses by Campion et al. (1997) and Schmidt & Hunter (1998) show that structured interviews have substantially higher predictive validity than unstructured interviews.
Structured interviews theoretically eliminate bias through standardization of evaluation and consistency of questions, thereby ensuring reliability and validity.
Practical introduction of structured interviews includes STAR-method question design and use of evaluation sheets.

Costa & McCrae's (1992) Big Five theory captures personality traits in five dimensions; relationships between these traits and both job performance and job satisfaction have been empirically demonstrated.
Schmidt & Hunter (1998) concluded that GMA (general mental ability) has the highest predictive validity among selection predictors.

Personality tests and ability tests are positioned as complements to interviews: they capture individual characteristics that interviews struggle to assess, while their introduction also has acknowledged limitations.
Realistic Job Preview (RJP), based on Wanous (1973), means disclosing the actual nature of the job to candidates in advance in order to reduce expectation gaps, early turnover, and disappointment.
Later RJP research has confirmed multiple mechanisms, including a 'vaccine effect' and a 'self-selection effect,' supporting the theory's validity.
Practical RJP implementations use work samples, videos, and similar methods whose design intent is to present a realistic picture of the work.

Employee Value Proposition (EVP), introduced by Ambler & Barrow (1996), is defined as the totality of functional, economic, and psychological benefits that constitute 'employment value' for employees.
EVP goes beyond traditional job information to include workplace culture and growth opportunities, and it correlates with application intention (aspiration) and employee engagement.
EVP design can be approached through four types of attraction, together with practical examples of how those messages are communicated.

Person-Job Fit (PJ Fit) is the compatibility between job requirements and an individual's abilities and experience; Person-Organization Fit (PO Fit) is congruence with organizational values and culture (Kristof, 1996).
Schneider's Attraction-Selection-Attrition (ASA) theory (1987) and Chatman's research (1991) empirically showed that high PJ/PO fit contributes to employee satisfaction, retention, and performance.
PJ Fit and PO Fit serve as foundations for recruitment requirement design, selection evaluation axes, and analysis of adaptation/retention outcomes.

The competency-based approach (McClelland, 1973) argues that evaluation should rest on job-performance behaviors rather than intelligence or education, identifying behavioral characteristics shared by high performers (competencies).

Spencer & Spencer (1993) integrated competencies with the iceberg model into a systematic framework used for multi-layered personnel-requirement design and as indicators in structured interviews (including STAR-method examples).
Vroom's Expectancy Theory (1964) models motivation as the product of expectancy (effort leads to performance), instrumentality (performance leads to rewards), and valence (value of those rewards).

Porter & Lawler (1968) extended expectancy-related work into a cycle model linking performance to satisfaction. Chapter 8 uses this as a theory for reading the psychological process by which candidates decide on job offers and joining, organizing how rewards, growth opportunities, and information provision affect those decisions.

Kahn (1990) defined engagement as a psychological state of investing the self in work and becoming absorbed. Schaufeli and colleagues’ UWES scale measures three elements: vigor, dedication (enthusiasm), and absorption.
Large-scale surveys by Harter et al. and a meta-analysis by Bailey et al. (2017) confirmed correlations of engagement with performance and retention rates.
Chapters 8 and 10 treat engagement as a foundation for building relationships with candidates, forming psychological contracts with accepted candidates, and designing retention measures.

Thaler & Sunstein (2008) argued that how options are presented (choice architecture) influences decisions and proposed nudges—light interventions that encourage desirable behavior without coercion. The approach has abundant empirical support as a behavioral-economics method.

Chapters 4–9 use choice architecture/nudge as theoretical background for non-verbal and structural design that supports candidate behavior: job-posting information design, entry flows, interview invitations, and offer notifications.
The Harvard Framework of HRM is referenced as a key model in Chapter 2 (point 013) and Chapter 10 (points 091, 100).
The Harvard Model of HRM is a comprehensive framework proposed by Beer et al. (1984).

Under this model, personnel (HR) policies should be designed by considering situational factors (e.g., management/business strategy, legal/institutional systems, labor-management relations) together with the perspectives of stakeholders (employees, managers/executives, society, etc.).
The four C's—Commitment, Congruence, Competence, and Cost-effectiveness—are to be used as outcome indicators for HRM.
The framework is applied (in Chapters 2 and 10) as a way of treating recruitment not as a standalone policy but as an integrated function that is linked with management and organizational strategy.
人員計画 (personnel planning) is defined as a plan that indicates when, what kind of people, and how many are needed in order to realize strategy.
The 人員計画実態調査 (personnel planning actual-conditions survey) was conducted in January 2025 by 株式会社専中天, targeting executives, officers, and employees, with 1246 valid responses out of 1321.
Survey method was self-administered online research using JustSystem Fast ask; the sample was allocated so that each age band (20s through 60+) and both genders had at least 120 respondents.
Survey period was 6–12 January 2025.
Respondents were asked whether they participate in any recruitment activities (company briefings, document screening, interviews, hiring decisions).

They were asked whether their company has a personnel plan, who primarily formulates it (management layer, corporate-planning department, business-planning department, administration, HR, field management, or other), and which realization methods are planned (hiring/onboarding, talent development, turnover/retirement, or other).
Company size was captured by number of employees in bands from 10 or fewer through 3001 or more.
A hiring or talent-analysis worksheet compares people who are thriving in a role (活躍している人) with people who did not succeed (うまくいかなかった人), examining stance, skills, culture, and job duties.
Hypotheses about what works in a role can be drawn from common points among ideal people outside the company (社外の理想的な人 / 共通点からの仮説), covering culture and job content.
For a given recruitment position (採用ポジション), requirements are split into must-have, nice-to-have, ‘desirable if present’ (あれば望ましい), and ‘would be glad if present’ (あればうれしい).
Each requirement is further checked for relevant experience and for how far the capability is realistically possible (できる可能性はどの程度か).
The sheet also flags items still under confirmation or not yet included (確認中・入っていない) and notes the need to protect potential and ethics.
